10063-happiness-and-marriage:
Elizabeth Towne's book on happiness and marriage belongs to the New Thought movement, which taught that attitude shapes life. She opens with verses from James Whitcomb Riley on turning clouds inside out to show the lining, and from Walt Whitman on turning whatever happens to beautiful results.

Towne applies that hopeful philosophy to married life, arguing that no imperfection in the present need spoil the future. Her tone is warm, encouraging, and practical. Readers interested in early twentieth-century self-help get a gentle guide to making a marriage happier by changing how one sees it.
10211-at-whispering-pine-lodge:
Lawrence J. Leslie published this boys' outdoor tale in 1919, set at a lodge in the Adirondacks. A group of boys, led by Max, halts on a carry, fishes, and builds a shanty shelter, while a strange lodge and a fur farm draw them deeper into the woods. The tone is hearty and comic, in the style of early camp fiction.

Obed Grimes bobs up, traps are set for night prowlers, and a tree bears strange fruit as plans to help Obed take shape. A young magician, taps on a cabin wall, and a big surprise push the plot on. Readers get a fun, old-style story of woodcraft, friendship, and small mysteries in the pines.
10473-the-heart-of-the-range:
William Patterson White published this western novel in 1921, dedicating it to Ranger, a good horse and a better friend. White, author of The Rider of Golden Bar and Hidden Trails, opens with a trail picked up three miles back, burning ground behind the riders. The range itself, with its horses, thieves, and bold bad men, drives the tale.

A horse thief, a yellow dog, a tall stranger, an old lady, and McFluke's place fill early chapters, while a riddle, a starlight, and a fire push the plot on. The hero must outwit foes and win trust. Readers get a fast, vivid western of horses, ranches, and frontier justice.
10767-courage:
J. M. Barrie, creator of Peter Pan, gave Courage as his rectorial address at St. Andrews University on May 3, 1922, to the students in their red gowns. He tells them his December roses, the people he has cared for most, have been simple folk, not the great. Memory, he says, gives us roses in December, long after summer has passed.

Barrie speaks as a Scotsman who walked the same academic groves, urging young graduates toward bravery in ordinary life. The address is short, tender, and full of quiet humor. Readers get a beloved writer's farewell counsel, still quoted at graduations a century later.
10812-the-worshipper-of-the-image:
Richard Le Gallienne published The Worshipper of the Image in 1900 as a tragic fairy-tale, dedicated to Silencieux. Its chapters follow smiling silence, the coming of Silencieux, the northern sphinx, lovers and whispers in the wood, autumn in the valley, and a human sacrifice. Antony judges Silencieux on the hills, and Beatrice fulfils her destiny at the end.

Le Gallienne writes in rich, dreamlike prose, blending myth, love, and doom. The tale's mood is that of the decadent nineties, beautiful and unsettling. Readers get a strange, poetic fantasy, unlike the author's lighter bookish essays.
11354-the-irrational-knot-being-the-seco:
George Bernard Shaw's Irrational Knot, his second novel, was written in 1880 soon after he left Dublin for London in extreme rawness about English life. No London or American publisher would take it, Shaw recalls in his 1905 preface. until Annie Besant published it as a serial in her propagandist magazine, after which it could not be recaptured. Shaw jokes that he is no longer, in any atom, the person who wrote it.

The novel itself, in four books and twenty-one chapters, follows love, marriage, and social convention with early Shavian argument. Its interest lies partly in the story and partly in Shaw's retrospective embarrassment. Readers of Shaw's development will find here a young writer learning to turn ideas into fiction.
11371-the-moorland-cottage:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Moorland Cottage, by the author of Mary Barton and published in New York in 1851. opens with directions to a dwelling between cottage and house in a basin among grassy hills near Combehurst. Past the lych-gate, a wooden bridge, a field path, gorse and heather common, and a grove of Scotch firs, the reader reaches Mrs. Browne's home, widow of Combehurst's late curate. The landscape, with larks dropping into nests among ling, sets the novel's mood.

Gaskell's story follows the Browne family through love, loss, and moral choice in a rural parish. Her descriptive opening is characteristic, grounding character in place. The novella shows Gaskell's shorter fiction at its most idyllic and most observant.
1144-in-the-cage:
Henry James tells of a young telegraphist in a London post office who, from inside her wire cage, reads the secrets of the rich in their coded wires. She pieces together a lover's plot, a scandal, and a marriage, and she grows to feel she knows the gilded world better than its own people.

The novella tracks her hopes and her disillusion as the truth proves smaller and sadder than her fancy. James writes her mind in fine, winding prose, with much left unsaid. The tale is a subtle study of class, knowledge, and longing, and it rewards patient readers.
11723-among-the-trees-at-elmridge:
Ella Rodman Church's 1886 book teaches trees chapter by chapter. It opens with a spring opening, then maples, elms, oaks, ash, and olive. Birch, poplars, and apple follow in turn. The peach, almond, plum, and cherry family comes next.

Later chapters cover mulberry, caoutchouc, and milk trees. Linden, camphor, beech, walnut, and chestnut appear too. Pines close the list of kinds. A story inside the book tells of a hussar officer at a father's house in Rebenheim after a battle. A child gave him cherries, and he lived because of her kindness. The book mixes botany with tales for young readers.
12669-marriage:
Susan Ferrier's novel, reprinted in this 1881 Edinburgh edition from the original texts, satirises the marriage market of her day. Young women of good family must choose husbands while parents, aunts, and fortune hunters press their own plans. Scottish homes, London seasons, and country visits form the shifting stage.

Ferrier aims her wit at folly rather than vice: vanity, snobbery, bad taste, and the small tyrannies of family life. Her heroines learn, sometimes painfully, that a fine match on paper can mean a poor life at home. Praised in its time by Walter Scott, the novel still reads as sharp, funny social comedy.
12744-in-his-image:
William Jennings Bryan's In His Image, the James Sprunt Lectures, defends a traditional faith against modern science and scepticism. Publisher's pages list Bryan's other books on prohibition, money, imperialism, trusts, labour, income tax, peace, religion and Pan-Americanism, with The Prince of Peace and Messages for the Times among them.

In His Image argues that man, made in God's image, cannot be reduced to animal descent, and that moral order rests on divine creation. Bryan writes in simple, unaffected language, as a populist preacher-statesman. The book is a key document of the fundamentalist movement, earnest, political and theological, on the eve of the Scopes trial era.
12857-cambridge:
Gordon Home's illustrated guide to Cambridge, in the Beautiful Britain series, walks readers through the university town college by college. Greater colleges like King's and Trinity get full chapters, with lesser colleges, the library, Senate House, Pitt Press, museums, and town churches following. Pictures show gateways, courts, chapels, and the Bridge of Sighs.

Home lingers on King's College Chapel, where vast windows leave only buttress widths of wall, yet a stone vault still rises above the glass. Comparisons with Oxford open the tour. The book works as a charming, picture-led companion for visitors and for armchair travellers.
12901-the-moon-voyage:
Jules Verne's Moon Voyage binds From the Earth to the Moon and Round the Moon in one volume, illustrated by Henry Austin. The Baltimore Gun Club, led by President Barbicane, plans a giant cannon, the Columbiad, to fire a projectile at the moon. The Cambridge Observatory answers questions, and Florida and Texas vie for the site. Michel Ardan, a French adventurer, joins the flight.

A Tampa Town march, with crowds at maximum cry and Ardan fleeing admirers to his hotel, shows Verne's comic touch. The sequel carries the travellers round the moon itself. The book remains a founding work of science fiction, bold, funny, and full of nineteenth-century faith in engineering.
1300-riders-of-the-purple-sage:
Zane Grey's most famous western follows Jane Withersteen, a Mormon rancher in Utah, who defies her church elders and shelters the gunman Lassiter. Lassiter is a rider in black who seeks revenge for his sister's ruin. The tale moves through purple sage, hidden valleys, and a siege on a cliff.

Grey writes the desert in glowing color and the action at full gallop, while his view of Mormon power stirred debate. The novel sold millions and fixed the western formula. It remains a rousing, sunlit adventure and the peak of Grey's fame.
13457-the-bed-book-of-happiness-being-a-:
Harold Begbie gathers cheerful writings from many quarters into a bedside book for 1914, meant as a friend to the invalid, a companion to the sleepless, and an excuse to the tired. He calls the collection a gathering of happiness, a throng of glad faces, and a muster of elated hearts, and dedicates it to Sir Jesse Boot.

Jokes, anecdotes, and light essays follow: a young gentleman praising a billiard screw as the most tremendous ever made. Ladies praising exquisite sights, and an old lady whose Alderney cow she loved like a daughter. The pieces are short, warm, and easy to dip into. Begbie's aim is simple comfort, a book to lift the mind without demanding it.
1379-a-straight-deal-or-the-ancient-grud:
Owen Wister was alarmed by the hatreds of the years after the Great War. He argues in this book that Americans should drop their ancient grudge against Britain and stand with her for freedom and law. The chapters, written as letters and essays, answer the angriest mail of his day.

Wister writes with a novelist's force and a patriot's bluntness, pleading for friendship between English-speaking peoples. The book is a document of its hour, earnest and partisan. It draws readers who like Wister beyond the westerns, as a public voice.
1393-amours-de-voyage:
Arthur Hugh Clough's verse novel is told in letters written from Rome in 1849, when French troops besieged the city. Its hero, Claude, writes to his friend Eustace about sights that bore him, churches that crowd him, and a young Englishwoman whose company stirs feelings he cannot quite trust.

In hexameter verse, Claude doubts art, faith, love, and himself in turn, and his letters shift between sharp jokes and sober thought. The romance fades as politics and pride pull the pair apart. The result is a witty, uneasy portrait of a clever young man who thinks too much to act.
1414-somebody-s-luggage:
Narrated by a waiter whose whole family waits at table, this Christmas book begins with luggage left unclaimed at a hotel. The waiter, curious and kind, opens the bags and finds manuscripts, and the stories inside take over the book, each in a different voice and mood.

From a lodger's romance to a comic ghost tale, the pieces range widely, all framed by the waiter's chatty asides. The humour is warm and the structure is playful. It is a fireside collection about the lives strangers leave behind in bags, and the tales a waiter overhears.
14571-life-and-gabriella-the-story-of-a-:
Ellen Glasgow's 1916 novel follows Gabriella Carr from a sheltered Virginia girlhood through marriage, motherhood, and a second start in life. The book divides into the Age of Faith and the Age of Knowledge.

Gabriella marries George, discovers his drinking and deceit, and rebuilds herself through work, success, and hard-won independence. Glasgow writes with irony about Southern womanhood and the price of illusion. The novel won praise for its heroine's growth, and it stands as a major work of Glasgow's Virginia fiction. Glasgow later won the Pulitzer Prize for a later Virginia novel.
14885-red-pottage:
Mary Cholmondeley's 1900 novel opens on a hot June night, with Hugh Scarlett in a hansom travelling from Portman Square toward Carlton House Terrace, his thoughts outrunning the horse. He says he will get out, seeing no bars but half conscious of a cage, in a life where passions spin the plot.

No villain need be, the epigraph warns, for betrayal comes from what is false within. Cholmondeley follows Hugh and the women around him through London society, love, ambition and moral choice, with the red pottage of the title standing for a bargain sold too cheap. The novel is sharp, witty and serious, a leading example of late Victorian society fiction.
15103-the-imaginary-marriage:
Henry St. John Cooper's novel opens with a masterful woman and a young man, Hugh, breaking news that sets a tangle in motion. Joan Meredyth, a typist, meets Hugh face to face, and a dream girl, a peacemaker, and a general all enter the story. Misunderstandings pile up through jealousy, spying, and waiting.

Chapters with titles like The Only Possible Thing and To Gain, or Lose It All signal a romance built on pride, honor, and near misses. Cooper writes for readers who like a long, emotional love story with social polish. The plot keeps turning on what each lover will and will not take back.
15432-henry-brocken-his-travels-and-adve:
Walter J. de la Mare, writing as Walter Ramal, published this fantasy in London in 1904. Its hero, Henry Brocken, wanders with a heart of furious fancies into the rich, strange, scarce-imaginable regions of romance, beyond the world's end, to a tourney of ghosts and shadows. An epigraph from Tom o' Bedlam sets the wandering tone.

Each chapter enters a famous literary world: Lucy Gray from Wordsworth, Jane Eyre with Mr. Rochester, and Julia, Electra, and Dianeme from Herrick's verse. Brocken meets these figures as living presences, not as quotations, and the book becomes a tour of English poetry and fiction. De la Mare's tale suits readers who love old books: a dream journey where beloved characters step out of their pages to greet a traveler.
15614-the-ragged-edge:
Harold MacGrath, author of Drums of Jeopardy, published this novel with Grosset and Dunlap in New York, illustrated with scenes from the photoplay by Distinctive Pictures Corporation. A front picture shows Mimi Palmeri as Ruth Emschede and Alfred Lunt as Howard Spurlock. The novel opens by declaring the Master inordinately fond of young fools, who rush in where angels fear to tread and survive their daring.

Later pages follow a trunk without labels, its linen stamped by Whiteaway, Laidlaw and Company, British merchants with branches all over the East. At the trunk's bottom lies a large manila envelope, unmarked, holding manuscripts with the author's name neatly cut from each title page. Ruth thrills: a novelist, realized in strange fashion. MacGrath writes a romantic adventure of dreams, identity, and daring, where young fools serve progress by dreaming gloriously.
15801-winning-his-w-a-story-of-freshman-:
A college story by Everett T. Tomlinson, issued in Chicago and New York in 1904. Peter John, a freshman, arrives at college hoping to win his W, the letter of the team. Tomlinson, a writer of school and college tales, follows one term of study, sport, and friendship. The book speaks to boys who dreamed of the college yard.

Peter John meets new friends, faces unsought attentions, and runs a race in darkness. A parade, a walk with Mott, and Wagner's advice shape his term, before telegrams and a downfall test him. The meet at the end decides his place. The tale praises grit, fair play, and steady work, and still reads as a cheerful picture of freshman life.
15894-the-lifted-bandage:
A short story by Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews, author of The Perfect Tribute, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1910. A man comes home staggering, lays down his hat, and drops on the edge of a divan in his library. Grief has left his face ashen and his eyes staring, unseeing, through the window. Andrews writes with restraint and deep feeling.

An old butler, Miller, leaves him in sorrow, and a young clergyman, his nephew Dick, follows from the court-house. Dick sits beside him, hand on his, waiting through a wintry afternoon. Talk comes slowly, and comfort slower still. The tale moves readers by what it withholds: a bandage lifted, a loss faced, and a nephew's patient love.
16125-the-judge:
Rebecca West's 1922 novel, published by George H. Doran in New York, takes its epigraph from a hard saying: every mother is a judge who sentences the children for the sins of the father. Book one opens in Edinburgh, where Ellen Melville sits crying by a window, though life around her looks beautiful. Across the street stand the black rock and bastions of the Castle, and the office of Mr. Mactavish James, Writer to the Signet, fills the grey New Town scene.

The novel follows Ellen through love, family judgment, and the weight of a past she did not choose. West writes with sharp wit and deep feeling about mothers, daughters, and men who fail them. Readers of serious modern fiction will find a rich, demanding story of conscience and desire.
16169-the-tragedy-of-dido-queene-of-cart:
Christopher Marlowe and Thomas Nashe wrote The Tragedy of Dido, Queen of Carthage, first printed in 1594. This file reproduces that earliest known edition in facsimile, from the Bodleian Library copy, as part of the Tudor Facsimile Texts under John S. Farmer. Other copies survive at Bridgewater House and Chatsworth, the notes record, but the Bodley text anchors this reprint.

The play retells Virgil's tale of Dido, Carthage's queen, and Aeneas, the Trojan hero whose duty pulls him away from love toward Italy. Marlowe's verse gives the queen passion, pride, and a tragic end. Readers and students of early English drama can study the play here in something close to its first printed shape.
16358-the-english-gipsies-and-their-lang:
Charles G. Leland stresses that every custom and word in this 1874 book came straight from English Gypsies themselves, not copied from earlier writers. He gathered speech from Gypsy mouths in talk, tales, and sayings, and he pointedly avoids repeating George Borrow or other authors on the Romany people.

The book mixes language samples with notes on ways of life, giving readers a direct record of a community often written about from outside. Two German Gypsy letters from other works are the lone exception Leland allows. For students of language and folk life, it remains a fresh, first-hand source.
16438-memoirs-of-arthur-hamilton-b-a-of-:
Arthur Christopher Benson drew these memoirs of Arthur Hamilton, a Cambridge man, from his letters, diaries, and a friend's memories of his talk. First published anonymously in 1886, the book follows a young mind wrestling with religious doubt and the divisions of thought at the universities. Benson dedicates it to a friend whose frank talk of sacred things helped him.

The memoir is quiet and reflective, more concerned with conscience than with events. Hamilton's letters carry the argument, while Benson's framing gives it shape. Readers of Victorian religious biography will find a gentle, honest portrait of faith seeking a settlement.
16464-the-ancient-irish-epic-tale-ta-in-:
Joseph Dunn, a professor at Catholic University, gives the first complete English rendering of the Tain Bo Cualnge, the Cualnge cattle raid, from the Book of Leinster and allied manuscripts. The tale opens with pillow talk, moves to the rising of Connacht at Cruachan, the march of the host, and the youthful deeds of Cuchulain, including the slaying of the smith's hound.

Facsimile pages of the manuscripts face the translation, and Dunn's notes guide readers through the old text. The epic's cattle raid, combats, and heroes unfold at full length. For readers of Irish myth, this is the landmark version that brought the Tain to English readers whole.
16532-the-plastic-age:
Percy Marks sets this 1924 college novel at a hilltop university, opening with the claim that an American founder hunts first for a hill. Harvard, indifferent to high places, grew vast and colorless, while Yale flounders among New Haven shops. Hugh, the hero, wins standing at athletic try-outs, dances, and faces joints, girls, and campus temptations.

Pictures from the photoplay illustrate the book, with captions like She's My Girl and Dance, Salome. Marks writes of college life between the wars: sports, slang, and growing up. Readers of campus fiction will find a lively, slangy portrait of youth in the Jazz Age.
16603-ladysmith-the-diary-of-a-siege:
H. W. Nevinson kept this day-by-day record while Ladysmith in South Africa was cut off in the Boer War, and Methuen put it out in London in 1900. It runs from the first fights on the edge of town through months hemmed in, to relief at last. Maps and photos of guns, camps, and ruins sit through the text.

Nevinson mixes battle news with small town life: shells on homes, sick wards, dull days, jokes, and sudden deaths. He also notes hopes raised and dashed by word from the relief force outside. The diary gives a close, on-the-spot view of siege life, not a grand plan of war but what it felt like day to day.
16907-greenwich-village:
Anna Alice Chapin wrote this 1925 book on Greenwich Village, New York, issued by Dodd, Mead, with pictures by Allan Gilbert Cram and a map of old Greenwich. It is dedicated to Vincent C. Peppe, who first urged the book and helped make the Village a popular home district. Chapters run from a city square's checkered past, through Sir Peter Warren, Richmond Hill, and Tom Paine, to restaurants, magic doors, and villagers.

Chapin mixes history, gossip, and walks, with Milligan Court and Jefferson Market among its sights. She shows how an old village became a home for artists and bohemians. Readers who love New York will enjoy a warm, illustrated ramble through streets, squares, and folk who made the Village famous.
17954-critical-miscellanies-vol-3-of-3-e:
John Morley wrote this fourth essay of his Critical Miscellanies, volume three, on the life of George Eliot, printed in London in 1904 by Macmillan. Morley, a statesman and critic, takes up Eliot's life and letters with a biographer's care.

He opens on Eliot's own plea against prying biography, then traces her Hebrew study, her tireless work, Romola, and the years of her great novels from 1856 to 1876. Morley praises her as an aesthetic, not doctrinal, teacher. The essay is a sharp, early verdict on Eliot, useful for readers who want to meet her mind through a contemporary critic.
17988-grace-harlowe-s-first-year-at-over:
Jessie Graham Flower wrote Grace Harlowe's First Year at Overton College in 1914, printed in Philadelphia by Henry Altemus. Grace, who won readers through high school, now goes off to college, with J. Elfreda soon finding friends.

Chapters run from off to college and first impressions to Miriam's unwelcome surprise, a disturbing note, and Grace taking matters into her own hands. A sophomore reception and disagreeable news test her pluck. Flower writes clean, cheerful college tales of loyalty and grit. It is a bright start to Grace's college years, for girls who liked school stories.
18413-prudence-of-the-parsonage:
Ethel Hueston wrote this children's novel, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1915, with pictures by Arthur William Brown. Prudence of the Parsonage is dedicated to Hueston's mother, who devoted her life to rearing a whole parsonage full of rollicking young Methodists. A frontispiece asks what Prudence put in the soup, and the book follows a minister's daughter learning her household.

Chapters introduce Prudence and the rest of the family, the ladies' aid, a secret society, and twins sticking up for the Bible. Later chapters bring an admirer, lessons in etiquette, the first dark shadow of winter, practising economy, a burglar's visit, and romance coming. Prudence orders her life, comes to grief, and lets fate take charge. Young readers get a parsonage comedy: a large family, a small town, and a girl growing into sense and kindness.
18856-the-settling-of-the-sage:
Hal G. Evarts published this western novel with A. L. Burt in 1922, by arrangement with Little, Brown. It opens with a lone rider on a big pinto horse, a led buckskin trailing behind, jogging north through sage toward hills and a ranch road fork.

Signs warn squatters not to let the sun go down on them, and a burned wagon with the bones of two horses proves the threat is real. Coldriver, a cluster of some forty buildings, lies thirty miles south behind him, and he heads for Brill's store at the end of the Coldriver Trail. Drought has browned the range and left the cattle lean, setting a hard land for the settling to come.
18860-shadows-of-the-stage:
William Winter gathered these stage papers for Macmillan in 1893, choosing them from hundreds he had written on the drama. For thirty years he had watched and recorded the contemporary stage, writing for the New York Tribune without a break since the summer of 1865.

The book is dedicated to Henry Irving, in honor of all he did to dignify the stage. Its chapters move from Irving in Faust and Ravenswood to Edwin Booth, Mary Anderson, Adelaide Neilson, and Charlotte Cushman. Jefferson's acting and autobiography, Salvini, Ellen Terry, Ada Rehan, and Richard Mansfield each get their turn. Winter wrote to save what he could of a passing theatrical age, and the volume stands as a record of its great players.
19403-murder-at-bridge:
Anne Austin wrote this mystery novel; its New York printing appeared in the early nineteen thirties. A murder in a bedroom at Nita Selim's house in Primrose Meadows sets the puzzle, with a ground-floor plan printed to help readers follow the clues. Bridge players, guests, and gossip all come under watch.

Bonnie Dundee and Penny, the young leads, piece together who stayed in whose room and who knew what. Austin, known for Murder Backstairs, keeps the talk sharp and the suspects many. It is a neat golden-age puzzle for readers who like to solve the crime ahead of the detective.
20003-the-infernal-marriage:
Disraeli's The Infernal Marriage is a satirical tale of gods and modern manners. It first appeared within his novel Henrietta Temple in 1837. Lady Ceres is promised to calm with time in its dialogue. What is done cannot be undone, the speaker soothes. A winter residence among the gods is even desirable, she is told. She may pay a visit by then, he predicts. Olympus here behaves like a London drawing room.

The tale retells Proserpine's marriage to Pluto as society comedy. Disraeli stuffs heaven with dowagers, dandies, and political talk. It is classical myth recut as a fashionable novel. Young Disraeli delighted in such blasphemous elegance. The piece shows his wit before Parliament tamed it. Readers meet the dandy-satirist in pure form.
2011-rudder-grange:
Frank R. Stockton's Rudder Grange follows a young couple, Euphemia and her husband, who take a houseboat, an old canal boat fitted as a home, and live on the water. The narrator explains that the proper way to find a house is not through an agent, but by word of mouth pointing to just the right house. The couple's search leads them to the Grange.

The novel's comedy comes from houseboat life: leaks, neighbors, and the small disasters of living afloat, told with Stockton's dry humor. Readers who like his stories of odd inventions and patient wives will enjoy the book. Its picture of a couple making a home in an unlikely place has kept it in print.
2024-diary-of-a-pilgrimage:
Jerome K. Jerome recounts a comic pilgrimage to Oberammergau for the Passion Play, travelling with a friend through Germany in 1890. The diary form lets him record mishaps, hotels, trains, and fellow travellers as they happen. Jerome travelled to see the Passion Play at Oberammergau, a pilgrimage thousands of Victorians made.

Jerome's humor comes from the gap between pious purpose and practical trouble, and from his own cheerful grumbling. First published in 1891, the book pairs well with Three Men in a Boat as a sample of his easy, talkative travel writing. His friend's practical worries balance Jerome's jokes, so the diary reads like a trip with a real companion.
20336-the-miraculous-revenge:
The Miraculous Revenge is a tale of Ireland, love, and a long-sought mystery. A man recalls first seeing a woman he hoped might solve his quest. On this night he watches and hears her only for that bygone hope. He applauds her generously as the curtain falls on her act.

Then he sups at a restaurant, returns to his hotel, and tries to read. Loneliness still sits with him despite the evening's bright show. Revenge in Irish tales often turns on wit, faith, and old wrongs. Readers get a moody, comic tale in the Irish storytelling vein.
20473-grace-harlowe-s-third-year-at-over:
In Grace Harlowe's Third Year at Overton College, published in 1914, Grace and her friends are deep into college life. The Eight Originals, as the friends call themselves, face a September parting. Miriam Nesbit and seven of the group spend a last evening on the Harlowes' wide veranda.

It is a warm night, and the talk turns on the day to come. The next morning will scatter the friends to their separate duties. The Grace Harlowe books followed their heroine year by year, and this volume catches the mix of freedom and farewell that college readers knew well.
20474-grace-harlowe-s-fourth-year-at-ove:
Grace Harlowe's Fourth Year at Overton College, published in 1914, brings Grace and the Eight Originals to their senior year. College rooms, parties, and old friendships crowd the chapters. Ruth and Grace plan one more gathering in a room they both know is too small.

Ruth remembers a Hallowe'en party in that same room the year before. It held eighteen girls one night, she says, and what a time they had squeezing in. The senior-year book closes Grace's college course with the warmth and loyalty that made the series a staple for girl readers.
20485-the-lunatic-at-large:
J. Storer Clouston's The Lunatic at Large is a comic novel that begins, as its title warns, with an escape. Its early pages introduce a young professional man in some detail. He may be described as amiable-looking, with a little fair moustache and still less chin.

He has no practice to speak of, and a considerable quantity of unpaid bills. A man of such features and in such circumstances, the narrator says, invites temptation. Clouston sends his characters through mistaken identities and absurd chases, in the brisk farce style that made this one of his best-loved books.
20667-a-canyon-voyage:
F. S. Dellenbaugh's A Canyon Voyage, published in 1908, narrates the second Powell expedition down the Colorado River in 1871 and 1872. Dellenbaugh went as a young artist and mapmaker. His book, written years later, is the fullest personal account of that voyage through the Grand Canyon country.

His figures give the canyon's scale. The gorge drops near six thousand feet on the north side and over five thousand on the south. Its total length, counting the Marble Canyon division, runs 283 miles. Dellenbaugh made sketches in colour on the spot, and the narrative keeps a painter's eye.
21197-diego-collado-s-grammar-of-the-jap:
Diego Collado, a Spanish Dominican missionary, published his grammar of Japanese in Latin in 1632, one of the earliest European studies of the language. Richard L. Spear edited and translated it for the University of Kansas East Asian series. His introduction compares Collado's account with the grammar by João Rodrigues.

Spear explains Collado's framework for Japanese sounds, word forms, and sentence structure before the translation begins. The 1632 original, Ars Grammaticae Iaponicae Linguae, also circulates as a separate text. For students of language history, the book shows how missionaries first fitted Japanese into Latin grammar terms, and where that fit strained. The book is old, rare, and hard to find in print now.
21405-the-loss-of-the-royal-george:
Ben Truscott's father was boatswain of the Royal George, and W. H. G. Kingston tells her loss through Ben's eyes. The great ship carried over a hundred brass guns and flew an admiral's flag. She had been launched in 1756 and was a pride of the navy.

Her sinking takes only a few pages, and the heart of the tale lies elsewhere. A small child brought aboard by a lady survives, while the lady drowns. A crewman raises the boy, who makes a good career at sea. In the last chapter his true parents are found, and all ends well.
21514-gryll-grange:
Thomas Love Peacock's Gryll Grange, his last novel, is shown here in the 1896 Macmillan edition. George Saintsbury writes the preface, and F. H. Townsend draws the pictures. Chapter heads promise squires, vicars, and a lord with a taste for grand dinners.

Peacock packs talk on science, exams, music, and the press into a country-house tale. A rustic lover, a thunderstorm, and the lottery of marriage stir the plot. Lord Curryfin's Siberian dinners and social tedium get sharp, funny treatment. The book is talk at its most sparkling, from a master of the comic dialogue novel.
21551-the-little-savage:
A boy grows up near alone on a rocky island in Captain Marryat's The Little Savage, published in 1848. His one companion, a morose and gloomy man, drags him over hard climbs and treats him unkindly. It was Marryat's twenty-sixth book, finished after his death by kin.

The tale was meant for children, and its religious tone sets it apart from Marryat's other works. Shipwreck, survival, and a child's slow schooling in faith and feeling drive the plot. Marryat died the year it appeared, leaving the book as a gentler last word. Its island scenes still hold young readers fast.
21639-when-patty-went-to-college:
Jean Webster sends Patty to a women's college in When Patty Went to College, published in 1903. Patty's roommate Priscilla drags pillows and curtains from a dry-goods box at term's start. Fifty girls, Patty jokes, have already begged the janitor Peters for his hammer.

Chapters treat an early fright, a question of ethics, and the elusive Kate Ferris. Patty comforts friends, pursues old English, and meets a bishop with grace. C. D. Williams draws the pictures, from Patty's portrait onward. Webster later won fame with Daddy-Long-Legs, and her wit and warmth are already here in full.
21701-the-settler-and-the-savage:
R. M. Ballantyne wrote adventure novels for young readers in the nineteenth century, and this one is set in South Africa. The story opens on the great dry plains called the karroo in the first quarter of that century. A young rider named Charlie Considine is lost there with his horse, Rob Roy, short of water under a hot sun.

From that hard start, the tale follows Charlie among settlers and the wild country around them. Ballantyne had a gift for plain, fast storytelling, and he fills the pages with travel, danger, and close escapes. Readers get a vivid picture of frontier life in southern Africa as English settlers saw it, told as a boy's own adventure.
2178-by-shore-and-sedge:
Bret Harte gathers California stories in By Shore and Sedge, opening with An Apostle of the Tules, set among four hundred campers in Tasajara Valley in October 1856. Sarah Walker and A Ship of '49 follow. Harte published By Shore and Sedge in 1885, gathering California tales from magazines.

Harte writes of miners, settlers, and the harsh, ague-haunted marshes with his usual mix of humour and pathos. The collection shows Harte's California at its most vivid, on shore and among the sedge. Tasajara Valley, barren and crowded, gives the opening story its strange, vivid setting.
21866-the-gundungurra-language:
An Australian Aboriginal language is set down on paper in R. H. Mathews's study of Gundungurra, read before a learned society in October 1901. The Gundungurra and Dharrook peoples held country from the Hawkesbury River to Mount Victoria and south to Berrima and Goulburn. Mathews notes features not before reported in Australia. Nouns, verbs, and pronouns carry rich inflections, and the first person has two forms each of dual and plural.

He spells every word phonetically in nineteen English letters and explains each sound. The little word for yes, ngee, opens his notes on the tricky ng. Such papers, dry as they look, preserve languages under heavy pressure. Mathews's record remains a source for Gundungurra descendants and linguists alike.
21995-philosophy-and-religion-six-lectur:
Materialism is impossible, argues Hastings Rashdall in Philosophy and Religion, six lectures delivered at Cambridge and published in 1909. Rashdall, fellow of New College, Oxford, begins with mind and matter. All we know of matter, he says, implies mind: color and sound plainly, but solidity and size no less. This was Berkeley's great discovery, though Berkeley blurred parts of it.

If matter cannot exist apart from mind, Rashdall reasons, there must be a universal mind in which all things exist: God. Yet he grants that theism is possible without idealism. The lectures move with a tutor's patience from Spinoza and Spencer to faith. They show Edwardian Oxford philosophy at its clearest, arguing for religion on reason's own ground.
22001-pastoral-poems-by-nicholas-breton-:
Three Elizabethan pastoral poets share this slim booklet of 1906, third in the Pembroke Booklets series from Hull. Nicholas Breton (1558 to 1626) leads with his pastoral poems; Ben Jonson praised his work as the habit of true passion in perfect strains. George Wither (1588 to 1667) follows with selected poetry. Charles Lamb's praise heads his section: Wither first found poetry a present wealth, not only a hope after death.

William Browne of Tavistock closes the volume with his pastoral poetry. The editor warns that the fate of poets is uncertain, and these three survive but slowly in public interest. The edition was limited to two hundred fifty large-paper copies. It is a small act of rescue for the singing shepherds of England's golden age of verse.
22183-wilton-school-or-harry-campbell-s-:
Wilton School; or, Harry Campbell's Revenge is a school story told as a tale. It opens on a sad summer evening in a little farm by Wilton church. The low, dim parlour, panelled in oak, looks across the quiet churchyard. Lindens shade the gravel path, and sorrow sits inside despite the sweet weather without.

From that farm the tale sends Harry Campbell to Wilton School. Schoolboy honour, injury, and the hunger for revenge drive the plot. The book belongs to the early school-story kind, before the genre found its classic shape. Its moral is worked out through friendship and disgrace rather than games, which came later to rule such fiction.
22244-miss-pat-at-artemis-lodge:
Pemberton Ginther wrote Miss Pat at Artemis Lodge in 1917, one of her Miss Pat books for girls. Patricia and her friends have settled at Artemis Lodge, an art colony. The story opens in a flurry: the train is in, and Judith begs Elinor to watch one corner while she watches the other. Bruce has gone for a taxi so as not to lose a minute, and a beloved arrival is expected any second.

Studies, models, pranks, and friendships fill the girls' days at the lodge. Ginther writes bright boarding-house comedy with art-school trimmings. The Miss Pat series followed its heroine from school to art study and beyond. This volume shows the series at its sunniest.
22845-the-beauty-of-the-village:
One good workman carries The Beauty of the Village, a character sketch by Mary Russell Mitford. Her subject is a man of the old school. He served his employers faithfully, never thought his work beneath him, and filled every family role with credit. A big family grew up well under his care. Drink never drew him into a tavern once.

Mitford's title plays gently against expectations. The village beauty here is not a face but a life. Through one man's steady record she praises the unnoticed virtues that hold a parish together. The sketch is brief, warm, and exact. It shows why her village portraits were loved. She found the remarkable inside the ordinary and made readers see it too.
23242-laramie-holds-the-range:
Frank H. Spearman's Laramie Holds the Range, from 1921, is a western novel named for its hero. Its opening rides a train west. All day, a heavy train of sleeping cars has climbed the long rise from the river, across a dull stretch of treeless, short-grass plains.

Those plains run from the Missouri River to the mountains. Then the train stops again, almost without a sound. Spearman builds the West from such quiet details: distance, grass, and rail lines crossing empty country. Readers get a range story where the land itself sets the pace before Laramie takes hold of it.
23374-the-dingo-boys-the-squatters-of-wa:
George Manville Fenn sent an English family to Australia in this long squatter tale, where they buy carts and gear and push up country to find land on Wallaby Range. Two grown daughters, three boy cousins near sixteen, and an old gardener make up the party.

On the road they gain an Aboriginal helper, first called Ashantee, then Shanter, whom the grown ups distrust even as he saves them again and again. Wild dogs, rough country, and tight scrapes test the boys, who learn bush craft, courage, and fair dealing. Fenn keeps the pace brisk and the perils close, so the tale reads as a lively lesson in how a new land tries newcomers and rewards pluck.
23422-essays-towards-a-theory-of-knowled:
Alexander Philip, a fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, wrote these nineteen fifteen essays on how we know what we know. Time and its cycles, the roots of physical ideas, two rival theories of knowledge, and the doctrine of energy form the four main essays.

Philip opens with a jest from As You Like It on clocks in the forest, then argues in a measured, learned voice about minds, matter, and the grounds of truth. Greek tags and long reasoning mark the text, which suits readers with some philosophy behind them. The book matters as a clear, early twentieth century attempt to join physics and thought, asking what science can truly claim and where its claims run out.
2343-the-adventure-of-wisteria-lodge:
A strange tenant, a murdered man, and a house full of secrets draw Holmes to Wisteria Lodge in Surrey. Arthur Conan Doyle weaves a tale of a Central American dictator's revenge, with voodoo trappings that turn out to mask a very human conspiracy. Watson narrates the gathering dread as footprints and strange visitors multiply.

The story's exotic surface gives way to a solid detective solution. It shows Conan Doyle's taste for the sensational within the Holmes formula. Mystery readers get a vivid, two-part adventure. The story first appeared in two parts, a rarity among the Holmes shorts.
23449-behind-the-beyond-and-other-contri:
Stephen Leacock, author of Nonsense Novels and Sunshine Sketches, wrote this nineteen thirteen book of comic essays and tales, with pictures by A. H. Fish. The title piece, Behind the Beyond, leads a set of contributions to human knowledge that are anything but solemn.

Leacock mocks learned talk, social fads, and grand theories with a straight face, letting absurd logic run until it trips itself. The humour stays genial even when the satire bites, and the short pieces suit reading in small doses. Fans of Leacock's light touch will enjoy the book as a prime sample of his art: learned jokes, everyday follies, and a world that takes itself far too seriously, gently deflated.
23452-the-trial-of-william-tinkling-writ:
Charles Dickens wrote this child voiced tale as the trial of William Tinkling, set down by himself at the age of eight years. The boy editor insists the opening part is real, not made up. He begs the reader to believe it most, while his cousin Bob Redforth shakes the table and wants the editorship himself.

Nettie Ashford is William's bride, wed in a dancing school closet with a green ring. The trial that follows plays out in full child logic, with scorn, papers, and courtroom pomp in miniature. Dickens catches a boy's voice with glee, from boasts to grudges to solemn oaths. Readers who love Dickens at play will enjoy this short, funny glimpse of childhood law, love, and pride.
23768-the-squirrel-cage:
Dorothy Canfield published The Squirrel-Cage in 1912, a novel in four books about Lydia and the marriage market. Book One, The Fairy Princess, follows an American family, Lydia's godfather, and the shadow of a coming event. Paul stands by her, looking down into her eyes, confident and masterful, on the frontispiece.

Book Two puts Lydia in the locomotive cab of decision, weighing what is best for her and choosing in perfect freedom. Book Three, A Suitable Marriage, tests that choice through evenings, voices in the wood, and a black milestone. Canfield writes with sympathy for a young woman learning what freedom costs when society offers her a gilded cage.
23792-the-ruba-iya-t-of-bridge:
Carolyn Wells published The Rubáiyát of Bridge with Harper and Brothers in 1909, with pictures by May Wilson Preston. It is a parody of Omar Khayyam's Rubáiyát, rewritten for the card table, where the wine, the wilderness, and the beloved become bridge, the rubber, and a partner.

Verses open with the new rubber rousing new desires, and the thoughtful soul aspiring to doubling hearts. Dummy's red hand is laid down, hope of the odd trick expires, and players throw down high cards sans lead, sans score, sans honor, and sans stake. For bridge players, it is a witty companion to the game, best read between rubbers.
24333-the-privet-hedge:
J. E. Buckrose, the pen name of Annie Edith Jameson, wrote this novel, published by Hodder and Stoughton in London in 1921. Its chapters run from The Cottage and Caroline through The Promenade, The Three Men, and The Dance on the Promenade. Morning Calls and Sea-Roke lead to The Height of the Season, Wedding Clothes, and Sunday Night. The Gala, The Cliff Top, The Cinema, New-Comers, The Benefit Concert, Uprooting, and St. Martin's Summer close the book.

It opens at the far end of Thorhaven, where a little house behind a privet hedge stands apart. Its green door under a wooden canopy defies rows of terraces and villas creeping toward it. Behind lie flat fields under a wide sky, gulls screaming inland from mud cliffs. The ladies of the Cottage, nicknamed the Misses Canute, face a changing town. Readers get a seaside novel of a cottage holding out.
24479-the-nursery-june-1873-vol-xiii-a-m:
Published at Boston in June 1873, this was the sixth number of volume thirteen of The Nursery, a monthly magazine for youngest readers. Its prose opens with children at grandmother's, where fourteen little grandchildren gather, and goes on to a flying wood-sawyer, a papa's story, and notes about bees.

Other pieces tell of bad luck, Cherry and Fair Star, some Indians, and playing tableaux, with Little Mischief returning. Verses include an old blind man and his granddaughter, Dixie, fat little piggies, a song of noses, and A-Maying. The issue closes the volume's first half with summer stories and songs for small children.
24495-the-golden-judge:
Nathaniel Gordon wrote this short science-fiction story, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in December 1955 and illustrated by Freas. It imagines a device called the Golden Judge, found twenty-five years before a great ceremony at the United Nations in 1981. The story suggests a new way to settle disputes between nations.

Its problem is face-saving: how can rival powers back down without shame? The Golden Judge offers an answer that is both ingenious and unsettling. Gordon's tale is brief, clever, and very much of the Cold War age. Readers get a neat idea-story about pride, peace, and the price of both.
2496-our-village:
Mary Russell Mitford's Our Village sketches the life of a Berkshire village in essays and tales of neighbors, seasons, and small events. The book follows village characters through walks, fairs, and harvests, with Mitford's sharp eye and warm humor. Our Village made the country sketch famous and influenced a generation of writers.

The sketches charm with their detail: cottages, lanes, and the talk of ordinary people. Readers who love English rural life will find a classic. It reads best in small, leisurely doses. Mitford's sketches first appeared in the Lady's Magazine in the 1820s.
25910-the-long-portage:
Harold Bindloss sets a northern tale of love, pride, and rescue around the Gladwyne expedition, printed in 1912. Chapters move from the divide and the cache to a painful choice, Millicent Gladwyne, and Nasmyth's story. Lisle gathers news, Bella finds a champion, Crestwick makes trouble, and Mrs. Gladwyne pleads, while Gladwyne takes shock after shock.

The frontispiece shows a day of paddling up a gleaming lake, and the plot turns on who will hold Jim and who will sway him. One woman begs a friend to keep hold of the uncontrollable lad, though Gladwyne holds more sway than he does. Protests fail, rescues come, and Gladwyne at last gives way. Bindloss writes of moors, lakes, and portages with a steady, outdoor vigor.
25939-a-bibliography-of-the-writings-in-:
Thomas J. Wise catalogs the writings in prose and verse of George Henry Borrow in this 1914 bibliography, printed for private circulation in only one hundred copies. The book tracks first editions and later printings with close detail, from half titles and page counts to wrappers, signatures, and imprints. A manuscript of the Lord's Prayer in Romany fronts the work, fitting for Borrow's gypsy lore.

Entries spell out collations that collectors prize. One song book runs half title, title page, and text pages five to thirty, with head lines naming each song, then a leaf on American copyright. Issued in bright green wrappers with untrimmed edges, that small book ran to thirty copies only. Wise's list remains a key guide to Borrow's scattered and scarce books.
26069-robert-toombs-statesman-speaker-so:
Pleasant A. Stovall's 1892 life of Robert Toombs follows the Georgia leader through four roles: statesman, speaker, soldier, and sage. Chapters cover his career in Congress and on the hustings, his work in the courts, his record with the army, and his life at home. The book draws on the aid of Robert Toombs Du Bose, to whom it is dedicated.

Stovall quotes Toombs at length, including his appeals to Georgia's mountain people and his claim that the blood mingled at Cowpens and Eutaw could not stay at enmity forever. The biography presents Toombs as a Southern voice of courage and candor, firm in his views and loyal to his state through war and its aftermath.
26239-the-forester-s-daughter-a-romance-:
Hamlin Garland's 1914 romance of the Bear-Tooth Range centres on Berea McFarlane, called Berrie, the forester's daughter. His foreword says the tale grew from two trips in 1909 and 1910, though neither lay in the Bear Tooth Forest itself. The golden trail, the camp on the lake, and the rain and snow of those trips live again in fiction.

Contents list a happy girl, a ride in the rain, a warning for Wayland, the supervisor of the forest, and a storm-bound camp. Berrie teaches a youth to chop wood and cook, rigs a tarpaulin kitchen, and faces gossips and a summons. Later chapters bring a death grapple, a private car, and millinery matters. The novel mixes mountain weather, work, and romance.
26520-the-fighting-edge:
William MacLeod Raine published this western novel in 1922. It opens on Piceance Creek, where June Tolliver keeps house alone with her father. She rarely sees another woman from one month's end to another. A ragged, resentful girl at the start, June is drawn out of her lonely cabin life by cowboys, neighbors, and newcomers.

Chapter titles trace elopement talk, scandal, prayer, and a growing claim on her future. Raine mixes ranch work, horseback chases, and range quarrels with a recruit's path into the Rangers. An outlaw trail runs through Houck and his rivals. June's choices sit at the center of it all, as she tests courage, loyalty, and love against the rough code of the range. The novel reads as a fast, old-style western with a strong heroine and a crowded, talkative cast.
26644-friendship-village:
Zona Gale published this book of village stories with Macmillan at New York in 1908, after chapters appeared in The Outlook, Harper's Monthly, and other magazines. Gale says Friendship Village itself is not known to her, commending instead real home towns, their kindly companionship, and their quiet opportunities. Her note is dated from Portage, Wisconsin, in September 1908.

Twenty stories follow one long street from sun to sun, from the side door and a debut to nobody sick, nobody poor, the grandma ladies, and a tea party. Telephones bring modern gossip, as Central reports who is awake all night or invited to tea. Gale finds a medieval flavor in modern improvements, and warmth in neighbors who know everything and forgive most of it.
26674-the-life-and-times-of-john-wilkins:
P. A. Wright Henderson, himself Warden of Wadham College, Oxford, wrote this short life for the college's tercentenary, published by William Blackwood and Sons in 1910. John Wilkins, born in 1614 and dead in 1672, served as Warden of Wadham, Master of Trinity College, Cambridge, and Bishop of Chester. Henderson claims no deep research, only brevity, and leans on Jackson's and Wells's college histories, Wood, Aubrey, and the Dictionary of National Biography.

Chapters run from the college's foundation to Wilkins's wardenship and his life after Oxford. Civil War Oxford fills the background, as the university put itself in a posture of defence in August 1642 and surrendered to Fairfax in June 1646. Wilkins emerges as a remarkable man shaped by the most interesting age in British history, in Henderson's judgment.
26772-a-question-of-courage:
J. F. Bone wrote this science-fiction story, illustrated by Finlay, opening with a narrator who smelled trouble the moment he stepped on the lift for the long climb up the Lachesis's side. Five years in the Navy, he says, gives a man a feeling for such things. From outside, the ship is beautiful, a gleaming shaft of duralloy with paint and brightwork glistening.

Lieutenant Thomas Marsden reports as executive officer, saluted by white-gloved sideboys and an immaculate ensign, Halloran. Everything is standard operating procedure, yet the ship is not taut but tight, and not happy: blank, hard-eyed, unsmiling faces, no laughter, no clatter, no deviation. The cause is Lieutenant Commander Charles Augustus Chase, Rule-Book Charley, By-The-Numbers Chase, known to every midshipman at the Academy. Marsden must serve under the man he dreads, and prove his own courage.
26930-over-the-top-with-the-25th-chronic:
Lieutenant R. Lewis's 1918 memoir follows a Newfoundlander from a coastal steamboat to the trenches of France with the 25th Battalion. Turned away by the already full Newfoundland Regiment, Lewis crossed to Canada to enlist, and his chronicle runs from training to the fighting at Vimy Ridge and Courcellette.

Lewis writes as a junior officer who saw the war at close range: planes dueling overhead, the Somme guns, and the daily grind of battalion life. Published in Halifax while the war still raged, the book gives a firsthand Canadian account of two battles that became landmarks of the war.
27129-lyrics-from-the-song-books-of-the-:
A. H. Bullen's Lyrics from the Song-Books of the Elizabethan Age, published by John C. Nimmo in 1887, anthologizes songs from the old song-books. This large-paper edition ran to 250 numbered copies, this one number 221, as a companion to the poetical miscellanies of the late sixteenth century.

Bullen went through the song-books in the British Museum library, finding many poems unknown even to specialists. Lyrics from William Byrd's Psalms, Sonnets and Songs of 1588 sit beside pieces from England's Helicon and Davison's Poetical Rhapsody, preserving love songs of the Elizabethan age.
27196-cheap-postage:
Joshua Leavitt's Cheap Postage, published in Boston in 1848 for the Cheap Postage Association, gathers remarks and statistics on postal reform in Great Britain and the United States. Leavitt, the association's corresponding secretary, opens with a statute of Charles II on the well-ordering of the posts.

His arguments run through reduction of price increasing consumption, cheap postage as the only way to suppress private mails, and the postage law of 1845. Leavitt questions the repeated rule that the post office must support itself, pressing a case for low, uniform rates. The pamphlet was printed for general circulation under the publishing committee. Dr. Howe, Dr. Webb, and Leavitt formed the committee of publication.
27320-st-john-s-college-cambridge:
Robert Forsyth Scott, fellow and senior bursar of St. John's College, Cambridge, wrote this illustrated history of his college in 1907, with drawings by Edmund H. New. It appeared in the College Monographs series from J. M. Dent in London and E. P. Dutton in New York, and it treats buildings and people together.

Chapters move from the courts and interiors to the Hospital of St. John, which stood from about 1135 to 1511, then through the college's first, second, and third centuries, ending with social life in Scott's own day. Plans, gateways, halls, and the old bridge are all pictured. The book gives a compact, well-illustrated tour of one Cambridge college.
27511-the-free-range:
Elwell Lawrence published this western novel with Grosset and Dunlap in New York in June 1913, with illustrations by Douglas Duer. Lawrence dedicates it to Mathew White Jr., editor, author, critic, and friend.

Chapters run from Flinging the Gauntlet and A Late Arrival through The Six Pistol Shots, Strategy and a Surprise, and The Man in the Mask. They go on to War Without Quarter, Made Prisoner, Juliet Asserts Herself, and A Battle in the Dark. An illustration shows two riders swinging clasped hands like happy children. The novel mixes range warfare, mystery, and romance.
27518-change-in-the-village:
George Bourne published this study of English village change with George H. Doran in New York in 1912, printed in Great Britain at Guildford. Bourne dedicates it to his sisters, and he arranges it in five parts, from the village itself to the forward movement.

The opening warns that this parish is, strictly, no village at all. It has no central green, and no squire ever lived there, and it had no resident parson until some thirty years before. Later parts treat self-reliance, drink, the peasant system, new thrift, competition, and notice to quit. Bourne then names resulting needs, from book-learning to the children's need.
27520-a-sailor-of-king-george:
Captain Frederick Hoffman, R.N., kept these journals from 1793 to 1814, edited by A. Beckford Bevan and H. B. Wolryche-Whitmore and published by John Murray in London in 1901. Hoffman entered the Navy in October 1793, aboard H.M.S. Blonde for his first ship.

He saw the siege of Martinique in 1794, served in the West Indies until 1802, and survived yellow fever twice. He fought in upwards of eighteen boat actions, was wounded in the head at Tiberoon Bay, and lost the hearing of his left ear. While first lieutenant of the Volage, he was taken prisoner at St. Jago de Cuba for six weeks. The journals give a sailor's wars at first hand.
27756-revenge:
Arthur Porges wrote this short science-fiction story in the voice of a scorned biochemist who has found the core of the drug problem. He addresses the officials and citizens who profited from his work but refused to act on it.

The narrator argues that enforcement alone cannot kill a flourishing trade, comparing it to pruning leaves from an Upas tree instead of striking at the root. Darkly comic and furious, the story turns a revenge plot into an attack on panic-driven drug policy and punishment of addicts. The narrator's targets include a new narcotics bureau headed by Myron P. Bishop, modeled on the Federal Bureau of Investigation.
27860-the-message:
A. J. Dawson wrote The Message, published in Boston and London in 1907 with illustrations from color sketches by H. M. Brock. The novel is divided into two parts, The Descent and The Awakening, following a journalist through London life toward a religious and national revival.

Early chapters cover a journalist's equipment and surroundings, a girl and her faith, Saturday night in London, and a demonstration in Hyde Park, while later chapters turn to ancient lights, conferences. Dawson's book blends social observation with spiritual earnestness, in the manner of Edwardian moral fiction.
28436-a-handbook-of-the-english-language:
R. G. Latham's Hand-Book of the English Language, published in New York in 1864, was written for university students and the higher classes of schools. Latham, formerly professor of English language and literature at University College, London, treats English as a language with a long, mixed history.

The first part traces its Germanic origin through the Jutes, Angles, and Saxons, then weighs Celtic, Latin, Danish, and Norman French elements. Later parts follow the stages of English and explain sounds, letters, pronunciation, and spelling. The handbook remains a clear Victorian guide to how English grew into its modern form.
28454-heart-of-the-blue-ridge:
Waldron Baily's Heart of the Blue Ridge, copyrighted in 1915, is a mountain romance set in the Blue Ridge country. It opens with Zeke setting out from his mother's lonely cottage, carrying only a hickory cudgel and a small oilcloth bag, and looking back toward home at dawn.

Ahead lies the valley where the Siddon cottage stands hidden among the trees, and the story follows Zeke into new country, new work, and new attachments. The edition is illustrated with scenes from the photoplay starring Clara Kimball Young, under the direction of Lewis J. Selznick. The novel offers old-fashioned romance against a vivid mountain landscape.
2860-framley-parsonage:
Anthony Trollope's Framley Parsonage follows the young clergyman Mark Robarts, whose friendship with the wealthy set at Chaldicotes pulls him toward debt and trouble. Lucy Robarts, Griselda Grantly, Lady Lufton, and the formidable Mrs. Proudie move through a Barsetshire world of Sunday mornings, lectures, and country-house visits. The chapter list promises money dealings, a little bill, and delicate hints long before the crises arrive.

Trollope balances comedy of manners with a serious study of ambition, as Lucy resolves to end a dangerous friendship with Lord Lufton while he wants to reopen it. The novel's strength lies in its patient attention to parish life, social rank, and conscience. It remains one of the most readable entries in the Barsetshire series.
28641-the-history-of-dartmouth-college:
Baxter Perry Smith's History of Dartmouth College, published by Houghton, Osgood and Company of Boston in 1878, prefers reliability to unity of style. Smith lets history tell its own story where possible, noting that older colleges survive mainly in records of their teachers' lives and labors. Friends of the college, libraries, and historical societies supplied letters, lists, and aid.

Hon. Nathan Crosby's money kept publication from delay, and many hands checked the work before print. A drawing of the original college edifice adds a visual record. Readers get a documentary history of one American college, built from archives rather than polish.
28873-track-s-end-being-the-narrative-of:
Hayden Carruth edited this 1911 narrative, told by Judson Pitcher himself, of a strange winter spent at Track's End. Pitcher leaves home, meets Pike, and stays through a fire and a blizzard that empties the place of many people and brings others in. Chapters follow his fight with robbers, a trip to Bill Mountain's house, days alone at headquarters, and a fight with timber-wolves beside his dog Kaiser.

The book is told in Pitcher's own plain voice, with a map drawn by the author and pictures by Clifford Carleton. Carruth frames it as a true account, now first printed in full, of escapes from death and rough winter adventure. Readers get a lively frontier yarn, part tall tale and part survival story, set at the end of a railroad line in winter.
28980-the-life-of-sir-james-fitzjames-st:
Leslie Stephen wrote this 1895 life of his brother, Sir James Fitzjames Stephen, judge of the High Court of Justice. The book opens with family history: James Stephen on imprisonment for debt, as master in chancery, and as colonial under-secretary, with the Venns among the family circle. Later chapters follow Fitzjames through childhood, Eton, King's College, Cambridge, and reading for the bar.

Further chapters treat the bar and journalism, with two portraits, including one drawn by G. F. Watts in 1863. Leslie Stephen writes as both brother and biographer, frank about a formidable Victorian judge and thinker. Readers get a full Victorian life, useful for the history of law, India, and letters, told by one of the age's great biographers.
29088-polly-of-lady-gay-cottage:
Emma C. Dowd wrote this 1913 girls' novel, Polly of Lady Gay Cottage, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, with illustrations. The story opens with a telephone call breaking into Polly's tale of merry hours with Mrs. Jocelyn. Her father summons her to the hospital, where Mr. Bean, who married Aunt Jane, lies hurt and wants to see her.

Later chapters bring a rosewood box, Leonora's wonderful news, a whiff of slander, and a blizzard, through an intermediate birthday party to Polly in New York and Mrs. Jocelyn's dinner party. Dowd writes warm family fiction for girls, with cousins, uncles, and small mysteries. Readers get a cheerful period novel of a girl, her cottage, and her widening world.
291-the-golden-age:
Children ruled by aunts and uncles turn holidays into kingdoms in Kenneth Grahame's Golden Age. The prologue calls adults Olympians, kind to bodily needs but deaf to imagination. Aunts, uncles, and governesses stand far above the children's world.

Chapters follow a white-washed uncle, alarms and excursions, the finding of a princess, and the secret drawer. The Argonauts, the Roman road, and a falling out fill the year. Grahame writes childhood from inside, with wit and longing. The book preceded his Dream Days and Willows. Grahame's childhood tales influenced later writers of children's fantasy.
29230-the-indian-princess-or-la-belle-sa:
James Nelson Barker wrote this operatic melodrama in three acts, first acted in Philadelphia on April 6, 1808, and performed in Philadelphia and Baltimore. Barker, born in 1784, had already written a one-act piece from Cervantes and a masque called America. The Indian Princess tells the Pocahontas story under the French title La Belle Sauvage, the beautiful savage.

Songs punctuate the action, including a song to Aresqui, and the play mixes spectacle with romance. Barker wrote from wide reading and a love of the stage. Readers get an early American musical drama, important in theatre history as one of the first American plays on a Native American theme, staged with music and pageantry.
293-paul-prescott-s-charge:
Paul Prescott's dying father leaves him a charge: keep integrity and duty through every campaign of life. Horatio Alger Jr.'s Paul Prescott's Charge, second in the Campaign Series, follows Paul from a boarding school at Potowome through hardship. The preface states Alger's idea plainly.

Paul battles adverse circumstances, earns his way, and holds to his father's charge under discouragement. Alger dedicates the book to boys who remember that school. The story's moral energy made it a staple of boyhood reading. It shows Alger's formula at its most earnest. Alger's campaign moral gave generations of boys a model of steady duty.
2934-on-the-advisableness-of-improving-n:
Thomas Henry Huxley delivered On the Advisableness of Improving Natural Knowledge in London, opening two hundred years after January 1666. His listeners sat yards from where plague had appeared in late 1664 and smitten the capital with unknown violence the next year, between the shocks of plague and the coming fire. Huxley uses that setting to ask why natural knowledge matters at all.

He mocks the fantasy that science will give telegraphs to Saturn and a view of the moon's far side, leaving us to thank God we are better than benighted ancestors. If that were the payoff, he says, he would as soon chip a flint axe like his forefathers. The essay defends science as a discipline of mind and a public good, not a gadget shop.
29742-the-long-voyage:
Carl Jacobi's short tale opens with a soft, gentle rain as travelers emerge from dark woods onto a gray, sullen shore, flecked with green-white foam. The secret, Jacobi promises, hid at the end of nine landings, and one man's Medusa-dark hunt for it made the strangest journey ever. Above the sound of the sea, strained breathing marks the crew, while only Navigator Norris stands calm, smoking.

Jacobi, praised in the headnote as a uniquely gifted science-fantasy writer newly radio-active on the entertainment meter, returns with shining nuggets of wonder. The long voyage becomes a quest through strangeness. Fans of Jacobi will enjoy a moody, atmospheric tale of sea, secret, and search.
30054-a-virginia-village:
Charles A. Stewart wrote A Virginia Village, reprinted in April 1985 by the Centennial Committee of the Falls Church Village Preservation and Improvement Society, for its centennial year of 1885 to 1985. The society thanks the Mary Riley Styles Public Library of Falls Church for permission to use its copy for the reproduction. Sue Bachtel served as president of the committee, with Rowland Bowers as vice president and a long list of directors.

The book itself portrays Falls Church around the turn of the century, when a village was becoming something more. Its value lies in that close, local view: streets, houses, people, and the slow work of preservation and improvement. Reprinted for a centennial, it lets modern readers see Falls Church as its own people saw it a hundred years before, before the suburb grew around it.
30522-the-etiquette-of-engagement-and-ma:
G. R. M. Devereux writes The Etiquette of Engagement and Marriage, describing modern manners and customs of courtship and marriage, with full details of the wedding ceremony and arrangements. First published in January 1903, this text follows the March 1919 reprint by C. Arthur Pearson of London.

Devereux, author of Etiquette for Women, opens with introductory remarks, then treats the beginnings of courtship: favorable opportunities, intellectual affinity, artistic fellowship, athletic comradeship, amateur acting, and social intercourse. Later chapters cover introductions, love at first sight, following up an acquaintance, and kindly offices of relations and friends. The guide suits readers planning a wedding in its own era. The tone is calm and kind. It tells a young couple how to act at each step, what to say, and what to do, so no one feels lost.
3053-signs-of-change:
William Morris delivered Signs of Change as seven lectures on various occasions, published by Longmans in 1896. The lectures include How We Live and How We Might Live and Whigs, Democrats, and Socialists. Feudal England, The Hopes of Civilization, The Aims of Art, Useful Work versus Useless Toil, and Dawn of a New Epoch follow. Morris, author of The Earthly Paradise, speaks as a socialist craftsman. The opening lecture admits the word revolution sounds terrible even after socialists explain it, then argues for a life of useful work and beautiful surroundings.

A feudal lecture traces Simon de Montfort's burgesses and Edward the First's parliamentary foundations, used to augment crown power and crush town liberty. The book remains a key statement of Morris's socialism, practical and poetic.
30560-music-an-art-and-a-language:
Walter Raymond Spalding writes Music: An Art and a Language, published in Boston and New York in 1920 by the Arthur P. Schmidt Company, priced at two dollars fifty net. Spalding dedicates the book to colleagues in Harvard's music department, including William Clifford Heilman, Edward Burlingame Hill, and Archibald Thompson Davison.

Supplementary illustrations follow the text, and transcriber notes correct obvious printer errors and mark questionable text. Spalding treats music both as an art to hear and as a language to read, teaching listeners how form, melody, and harmony speak. The book serves students, teachers, and concert goers who want to listen with more understanding.
30617-a-danish-parsonage:
An angler writes A Danish Parsonage, published in London in 1884 by Kegan Paul, Trench, with rights of translation and reproduction reserved. Ten chapters open with an introduction, the Danish parsonage itself, and trout fishing on the Gudenaa river, followed by Rosendal.

Later chapters cover the Danish church and its clerical party, Danish parishioners, pianos, and English and Danish horses. Pike, perch, and eel fishing join a silver wedding at a Danish proprietor's, horse breeding, and a fatal accident. Superstitions of the Huldr, the Gefion tradition, sunken mansions, and the boar Limgrim add folklore. The book blends fishing, travel, and Danish life.
3071-the-golden-slipper-and-other-proble:
Anna Katharine Green wrote The Golden Slipper and Other Problems for Violet Strange as detective stories centered on a young society woman with a gift for solving crimes. The problems include The Golden Slipper, The Second Bullet, and The Intangible Clew. The Grotto Spectre, The Dreaming Lady, The House of Clocks, The Doctor, His Wife, and the Clock, Missing: Page Thirteen, and Violet's Own follow. The first case opens at the opera, where a clubman turns his glass toward three young ladies in a box near the proscenium.

A later client protests she has done nothing foolish or wicked, only been very unfortunate and sensitive, and begs Violet to help her tell the story clearly. Green, a pioneer of detective fiction, gives Violet cases that turn on observation and sympathy.
30832-nor-iron-bars-a-cage:
Jonathan Blake MacKenzie wrote this dark science fiction and crime story, printed in Analog in May 1962, about a murder and the binds that hold people tighter than iron. A young girl, Angela Frances Donahue, is found dead in a sewer, just short of her seventh birthday. Inspector Kleek of Homicide South calls the narrator, whom he addresses as Roy, to the morgue. The case starts with grief and shock, not with a puzzle alone.

The title points to the story's theme: bars may hold a body, but subtler ties can hold a person far more firmly. MacKenzie follows Roy and Kleek through a future city of video phones and police work, where a killer's cruelty and a victim's fate raise hard questions about guilt and freedom. It is a grim, tense tale, best for readers who can face its sad subject.
30846-the-tragedy-of-caesar-s-revenge:
Held here is a Malone Society reprint, printed at Oxford in 1911, of an early play on Julius Caesar called The Tragedy of Caesar's Revenge. The reprint was prepared by F. S. Boas with the help of general editor W. W. Greg. Its introduction untangles a title puzzle: the head title points toward Chapman, while the running title was long linked with Shakespeare, so the piece is best known by its second title.

The Stationers' Register entry of June 1606, for John Wright and Nathanael Fossbrook, shows the play in print in the early seventeenth century. The reprint gives the old text with care for students of early drama, without settling every question of authorship. Readers of Renaissance plays will find a bloody Roman revenge tale, in the style of its age, and a useful case in how old plays reach modern readers.
30869-thin-edge:
Johnathan Blake MacKenzie wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in December 1963, about inventions that one society can use well and another would find nastily deadly. The tale opens aboard tugship 431, where a man at the pickup controls hears a radio beep. He marks in his log that the beep's frequency and rate show an asteroid found and set with anchor by Captain Jules St. Simon.

Direction and distance go at once to the pilot's instruments. The pilot, with a cry of Jazzy-o, swivels his ship until its nose lines up with the beep, then fires the forward accelerator for a few seconds. In the dark of space only points of light show as the tug moves toward the rock. MacKenzie builds a tense story of salvage, invention, and the thin edge between a tool and a weapon.
30911-the-demi-urge:
Thomas M. Disch wrote this science fiction story, published in Amazing Stories in June 1963, about a survey report that turns Earth's story upside down. The report, sent from Dira Four to the Central Colonial Board, says intelligent life flourishes on Earth after ages of lifelessness, multiplying with an energy that amazes the survey team. Terrans have filled their small solar system and now reach for the stars.

The survey can no longer hide the existence of its empire from them, and the report adds a stranger claim: the Terrans are slaves. Disch pairs that shock with the myth named in his title, a demi-urge, a lesser maker, as if one mystery of creation were not enough. Readers get a short, sharp tale about empire, freedom, and who truly made the human race.
30993-the-spectacle-man-a-story-of-the-m:
Mary F. Leonard, author of The Big Front Door, wrote this children's story, published by W. A. Wilde in Boston and Chicago in 1901, with pictures by Frank T. Merrill. Its opening verse says that out of a song the story grew, and that song and story, it all came true. The book is dedicated to one whose love has been from childhood an unfailing inspiration, and whose friendship has made dark paths light.

Its chapters follow Frances as she meets the Spectacle Man, leaning his elbows on the show-case, then a certain person, Gladys, a flat, new acquaintances, an informal affair, and a portrait. The story of the bridge, finding a moral, the portrait again, Mrs. Marvin perplexed, and Christmas time complete the tale. It is a warm, old-fashioned story of a missing bridge and the people who find their way across it.
3102-their-pilgrimage:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote Their Pilgrimage as a novel of American resort life, opening at Fortress Monroe on March twentieth. Irene looks from her stateroom at soft, luminous horizon clouds prophesying spring, as a steamer from Baltimore's arctic temperature nears the wharf. Passengers crowd the guards to scan the Hygeia Hotel, which Irene calls more conservatory than hotel, its glass corridors above and below.

The pilgrimage moves through watering places, hotels, and summer society, with Warner satirizing fashionable travel and the search for health, scenery, and company. A later passage mocks a noble tower pierced irregularly with factory-like square windows. The novel charms as a period picture of Gilded Age tourism, gentle and observant.
31300-peonage:
Lafayette M. Hershaw's 1915 paper, number fifteen in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, examines peonage as the afterlife of slavery's labor system. Hershaw opens with the African kidnapped to the Western Hemisphere in the early sixteenth century to meet a labor problem. Spaniards seeking gold found Native peoples unwilling or unable to bear the mines' heavy work.
