He notes how slavery looks different to each judge. To the moralist it is the sum of all villainies, to the reformer the negation of right, to the economist a system of labor. To the historian it is a step from killing captives to living by the sweat of other men's faces. Noting that the Panama Canal's opening marks four hundred years since Black slavery's introduction, Hershaw turns to the debt-labor system that succeeded it. The paper is a sharp, early study of unfreedom after emancipation.
31640-crestlands-a-centennial-story-of-c:
Mary Addams Bayne's novel Crestlands, a centennial story of Cane Ridge, was published at Cincinnati by the Standard Publishing Company, with copyright in 1907, and illustrated by O. A. Stemler. Its frontispiece shows Abner gently checking his mare and sitting to watch a woman. The book is set at Cane Ridge, a place of meeting houses and revivals.

Its chapters open with the coming of the schoolmaster, then getting to work, and the Cane Ridge meeting house. A great revival follows later in the book. Bayne's novel tells a centennial story of a Kentucky community, its school, its church, and its people across a changing time.
31758-call-him-savage:
John Pollard's short story was printed in Amazing Stories in March 1954. It is told by a writer working on a tale of a Sioux rising against a white settlement at the fork of the Platte. As he writes of Chief Spotted Horse and an attack set for dawn, his wife interrupts him, and the frontier story keeps breaking into his home life.

The humor comes from that split: the narrator's imagined war whoops and heroic speeches sit beside midnight talk, a cold, and a chapter still unfinished. Readers get a playful story about a writer whose invented West refuses to stay on the page.
31833-the-wedge:
H. B. Fyfe's short story The Wedge was printed in If in September 1960. It opens with a man named Barnsley sitting on the floor of a cylindrical chamber, slumped against curving, pearly plastic. He is careful not to glance toward translucent ovals he knows to be observation panels. He is large but thin and bony-faced, in a dirty gray coverall too big except at the shoulders.

When a concealed gong sounds, Barnsley rises and gazes in turn at each of three doors spaced around the chamber, adopting an expression of simple-minded anticipation. Readers get a science-fiction puzzle story whose title gives its clue: finding his way out of this maze is only half the job.
32431-the-model-of-a-judge:
William Morrison's tale, printed in Galaxy in October 1953, centres on Ronar, a reformed former outlaw whom his neighbours still fear and distrust. People move awkwardly near him, and fear looks out of their eyes, though Ronar hopes time will let them see him as one of themselves. At a gathering run by Mrs. Claymore of the Presiding Committee, Mrs. Silver modestly enters a contest, praising the fine women taking part.

The story's joke, set out in its sidenote, asks whether a reformed outlaw could serve as judge when the only verdict concerns a layer cake. Morrison uses a small-town contest and its polite talk to test how far reform, trust, and second chances can go. The tale mixes gentle satire with a serious question about judging others.
32438-the-book-of-courage:
John T. Faris's Book of Courage, published in Philadelphia and London in 1920, opens the Sunrise Inspirational Books series with short readings on courage in everyday life. Its foreword tells of a teacher who fitted a room for children with pictures, plants, goldfish, and a canary. She then faced a cold snap the night before the welcome, when a janitor let the room chill. That small disaster frames the book's question: what courage looks like when plans fail.

Contents divide courage into self-conquest, facing obstacles, industry, facing consequences, courage for others, golden-rule courage, and courage through companionship. Topics include restraining self, forgiving injuries, persisting, toiling, conquering infirmity, truth telling, and duty doing. Faris writes plain, encouraging prose for readers seeking moral examples rather than abstract theory.
32442-gertrude-s-marriage:
W. Heimburg's novel, translated from German by Mrs. J. W. Davis and published in New York in 1889, opens with an unexpected inheritance. Judge Weishaupt teases his friend Assessor Linden, who has just gained a small estate. It holds several hundred acres of meadow and woodland, a wild garden, and a neglected house. Its stock runs to four spavined Andalusian horses, six dried-up old cows, and an old aunt. Linden sits in mute despair before an empty Rhine wine bottle.

From that comic opening, the story follows Linden, Gertrude, and their circle through money, family claims, and the making of a marriage. Heimburg writes with humour about German middle-class life, pride, and affection, as an unwanted estate becomes the ground for a new household. Readers who enjoy domestic novels of manners will find the book warm and readable.
32445-the-pain-and-sorrow-of-evil-marria:
The Pain and Sorrow of Evil Marriage preserves an early humorous tract in verse on marriage. It was reprinted in London in 1840 for the Percy Society from a unique copy printed by Wynkyn de Worde. Its introduction notes three early tracts on the subject, all printed by de Worde, with only one dated, 1535, and the other two assigned to about the same period. Their titles concern those married too soon, those married too late, and the pain and sorrow of evil marriage.

This volume prints the third tract entire, while a brief account of the other two appears in Dibdin's edition of Ames. The Percy Society editors promise a fuller description of these ancient, facetious relics, which mock bad matches with Tudor bluntness. Readers interested in early English verse, printing history, and marriage satire will find a rare, short text in a scholarly reprint.
32501-the-golden-age:
Kenneth Grahame's Golden Age, companion volume to Dream Days and illustrated by Maxfield Parrish, recalls childhood as a world apart from grown-ups, whom children call the Olympians. Published in London and New York in 1900, with copyrights in 1899 and 1904, it opens with a prologue on the Olympians. Chapters follow on holidays, a white-washed uncle, alarms and excursions, and the finding of a princess. Sawdust and sin, young Adam Cupid, burglars, and a harvesting follow.

Later chapters cover snowbound days, what children talked about, Argonauts, and a Roman road. A secret drawer, Exit Tyrannus, a blue room, a falling out, and a Latin farewell follow. Grahame writes from inside a child's imagination, where orchards seem elf-haunted and gardens lead to roofs and adventure. The book remains a classic of childhood memory, warm, witty, and gently rebellious.
32577-dorothy-page:
Eldridge B. Hatcher's Dorothy Page, published in Louisville in 1912, follows a young woman home from college in the North. Dorothy arrives at six-twenty in the evening, beautiful in her neighbor Sterling's eyes, and that night he feels an epoch in his life has occurred.

Sterling, twenty-nine, a Presbyterian elder with a two million dollar fortune, states his case through chapters on conversion, deep water, wronging the little ones, and Baptist principles on the march. Hatcher writes a story of faith, courtship, and conviction, where Dorothy's arrival tests what both families believe.
32701-kant-s-theory-of-knowledge:
H. A. Prichard, Fellow of Trinity College, Oxford, examines Kant's Critique of Pure Reason. His book appeared from the Clarendon Press in 1909. Thirteen chapters move from the problem of the Critique to phenomena and things in themselves. Later chapters treat time and inner sense, knowledge and reality, and the deductions of the categories.

Prichard states Kant's questions plainly. Reason cannot decline questions about God, freedom, and immortality, yet it cannot answer them. He tests each stage of Kant's argument in turn. He presses hardest where Kant assumes what he must prove. The book closes with the postulates of empirical thought and a note refuting idealism.
32764-manners-of-the-age:
H. B. Fyfe tells of Robert, a man living in gracious solitude on a practically deserted Earth, in this story from Galaxy Science Fiction of March 1952, illustrated by Marchetti. Robots serve him: a red tennis robot returns his shots, a referee box calls the game, and serving robots fetch his racket and clothes.

Robert swims in a hundred-foot-square pool and wonders how far he must go to meet another human face to face. It has been ten years since he saw one. A televised invitation brings him to Marcia-Joan, whose robots serve a dinner of raw vegetables and a tiny portion of protein-concentrate. Her robots found the diet in the city library, but they looked up song-birds, not humans.
32803-letters-from-a-father-to-his-son-e:
Charles Franklin Thwing, president of Western Reserve University, writes twelve letters to a son entering college, published by Platt and Peck in 1912. Parts were first read to his own students starting a college year.

The letters treat thought, the essential gentleman, and health as an asset. They treat appreciation, scholarship, and the intellectual life. They treat the use of time, culture, college morals, weakness of character, the genesis of success, and religion. Thwing urges his son to become a thinker. He urges him to choose the better over the good, and the best over the better, and to take time in large pieces, not cut into bits.
32856-lectures-on-the-science-of-languag:
Max Müller delivers nine lectures on the science of language at the Royal Institution of Great Britain in April, May, and June 1861. The volume appeared in New York by Charles Scribner in 1862, from the second London edition, revised. He dedicates the volume to the members of the University of Oxford.

Lectures treat language as a physical science, its growth against its history, and its empirical, classificatory, and theoretical stages. Müller weighs genealogical and morphological classification, comparative grammar, and the origin of language. He quotes Bacon: words shoot back upon the understanding of the wisest, and entangle judgment. Iceland's skalds and fifty thousand inhabitants illustrate his history.
32920-a-question-of-marriage:
Mrs George de Horne Vaizey opens in a London consulting room, where a doctor gives a young woman his hardest advice. She carries a family history he calls a curse, and he tells her plainly that marriage is not for her. Anxiety, depression, and loneliness, he warns, are her worst enemies, and a wife's strains might unbalance her mind. The girl answers only, Thank you.

The novel then tests that ban against living people: Jean, Vanna, and Robert, whose grey eyes and brown eyes exchange an unspoken duel in a railway carriage. Jean, spoiled by Robert's devotion, calls herself a continual enigma to him, puzzling and shocking him by turns. Vanna sticks obstinately to her post between them. The question of the title is whether the doctor's verdict, or the heart, will govern.
32931-harley-greenoak-s-charge:
Bertram Mitford's novel opens on a ship's deck, where Sir Anson Selmes, an elderly, refined baronet, asks a sun-tanned, iron-grey-bearded frontiersman to look after someone in his charge. The second man, hardened by forty-five years in southern Africa, man and boy, accepts with absolute assurance. His keen blue eyes and rough, mahogany-brown hands mark him as a man who has lived by rifle and open country.

The charge of the title becomes Harley Greenoak's trust, and the novel follows what that promise costs him in a land of farms, feuds, and sudden violence. Mitford, at home in colonial Africa, builds his story from that trust and its dangers. It is a period adventure about duty kept under pressure, told with the confidence of a writer who knew the veldt and the men who rode it.
33043-windyridge:
W. Riley's Windyridge, published by Herbert Jenkins in London in 1915, is a Yorkshire novel of moors, farms, and village life. Its chapters open with the call of the heather. A farmer stats his terms, Grace meeting the squire, and a studio, then follow Farmer Brown photographed, a walk over the moor to Romanton. A cynic discourses on woman, and Christmas Day at Windyridge. Widow Robertshaw, Ginty running away, and Barjona falling into a trap carry the plot forward.

Later chapters bring Rose, a carrier's notice to quit, a visit to Zermatt, and a great storm followed by calm after storm, as the heather pulls its people back. Riley writes with affection for moorland folk and their talk, and the novel's humor and sentiment made it popular in its day. It remains a warm, old-fashioned story of a community finding its way through change.
33105-hymns-in-the-chinook-jargon-langua:
Rev. M. Eells, a missionary of the American Missionary Association, compiled Hymns in the Chinook Jargon Language, in a second edition revised and enlarged at Portland, Oregon, in 1889. The hymns grew out of Christian work among Native peoples, and they repeat often because they were meant chiefly for singers who could not read and had to memorize them. Once learners could read, Eells notes, they sang in English.

The book's notes explain its singing practice, as when two syllables must be sung to one note. The examples are nika to the first note of Happy Land, or skookum to one note in another hymn. As a document, it preserves a trade language turned to worship, and the missionary effort to carry hymns across languages. For students of the Pacific Northwest, Native languages, and mission history, it is a small but revealing source.
33409-the-ranch-girls-at-rainbow-lodge:
Margaret Vandercook's Ranch Girls at Rainbow Lodge opens her Ranch Girls series, a set of tales for girls who love horses, ranches, and friendship. The series went on to a pot of gold, boarding school, Europe, home again, and a great adventure, but Rainbow Lodge is where the ranch girls first gather. Vandercook writes with warmth for young readers, in a style that made the series a favorite.

The book's charm lies in its outdoor life, its lively girls, and its sense of a ranch as both home and adventure ground. Its chapters move briskly through rides, scrapes, and good times. For fans of girls' series books, Rainbow Lodge offers a bright, wholesome start to a long and much-loved run.
33554-nancy-of-paradise-cottage:
Shirley Watkins tells the story of Nancy Prescott, a capable girl who keeps house for her sister Alma and manages the shopping, cooking, and daily chores of their cottage home. Alma drifts and daydreams while Nancy plans, and their different tempers shape much of the household comedy. A stern man known to the girls as an ogre, a fashionable visitor, and a school term add new pressures.

Across fifteen chapters Nancy faces quarrels, scrapes, and a great adventure before the cottage itself becomes the center of the story. The novel follows her growth from a hardworking sister into a young woman who can stand up to difficult people and protect the home she loves.
34001-challenge:
Louis Untermeyer published this book of poems in New York in April 1914 with the Century Company. Three sections hold the poems: Summons, Interludes, and Songs of Protest. Early poems include a prayer to arms, a poem on the birth of a child, God's youth in the Berkshire hills, downhill on a bicycle, and midnight by the open window.

Interludes add Sunday night at Kennebunkport, a folk-song in the streets, Isadora Duncan dancing, and a Heretic sequence of blasphemy, irony, mockery, and humility. Songs of Protest close with Caliban in the coal-mines, strikers in the subway, and a voice from the sweat-shops. The book shows a young poet of fire and conscience.
34017-deep-moat-grange:
S. R. Crockett wrote this mystery romance, published in London in 1908 by Hodder and Stoughton. Deep Moat Grange opens with an empty mail gig, a poacher named Davie, a bailiff, and a golden farmer. Elsie, her visitor, a brom-water mystery, an iron trapdoor, and a bricked passage deepen the plot.

Later chapters bring a monks' oven, a breaking dam, comrades in captivity, and a night when Elsie dances for her life. Crockett writes with old-fashioned color and suspense. The novel offers a rich, tangled tale of a moated house and its secrets.
34088-a-poached-peerage:
Sir William Magnay's 1909 novel runs through forty-two chapters of English country life, where a disputed peerage sits at the heart of the plot. Lalage, a young woman met at a village inn, presses a prior claim on a man named Gage. Rival hopes for rank and marriage pull the households around them into open conflict.

The story moves between inn parlours, country houses, and sharp talk among suitors, kin, and hangers-on, as each side works to secure the title. Magnay keeps the tone light and brisk, with comic servants and scheming guests. The question of who truly holds the peerage drives the tale to its close. Readers who enjoy a tale of rank, rivalry, and village wit will find the pace quick and the cast large.
34552-danger-at-the-drawbridge:
Mildred A Wirt wrote Danger at the Drawbridge, a Penny Parker mystery tale issued by Cupples and Leon Company in New York. The copyright is nineteen forty. Wirt had written many mystery tales for girls. Penny Parker is a girl reporter and sleuth. Twenty five chapters carry this case from assignment to victory. A list in front names fifteen Penny Parker books.

Chapter one gives Penny an assignment, and chapter two warns that reporters are not wanted. A gift to a bride, a talk behind bushes, and a missing bridegroom launch the case. A ring of white gold, a forbidden pool, and a thrown stone add clues. Later chapters bring a stone tower, a cameo pin, and a search for Jerry. A daring rescue over the drawbridge and a secret of the lily pool close the hunt. Girls of the age got a brisk heroine in Penny.
34595-the-english-language:
The English Language is a philological treatise by Robert Gordon Latham, printed at London by Taylor, Walton and Maberly in 1850. It is the third edition, revised and greatly enlarged. Latham had been professor of English language and literature at University College, London. The dedication is dated November 1841, the time of the first edition.

Latham's preface states the book's plan. Those views, so received, might stand as established facts. To that extent the work was strictly a grammar of the English language. An educated Englishman, Latham held, should know the results of modern criticism applied to his native tongue. The enlarged third edition carries the historical and comparative study of English further. The book is a landmark of the years when English philology became a science.
3482-voyages-in-search-of-the-north-west:
This volume draws on Richard Hakluyt's great collection of voyages to tell the search for a northern sea route to Asia. The introduction recalls the editor's own small boat voyage to Arctic seas and his reading of early accounts in Dickens's Household Words. The narratives that follow come from English sailors who sailed toward ice, fog, and unknown coasts.

Readers meet whaling grounds where a hundred Dutch ships might crowd a bay, rival claims to fishing islands, and crews who wintered in harsh places. The book gives the raw material of exploration: logs, letters, and reports rather than a modern history. It suits readers who enjoy first hand adventure and the slow, dangerous opening of the Arctic.
34902-basque-legends-with-an-essay-on-th:
Basque Legends is a set of folk tales of the Basque land, got in the main in one of its shore parts by Webster. He was a priest and a master of Oxford. An essay on the Basque tongue, by a Paris sage of speech lore, stands with the tales.

A set of Basque poems is bound in at the end. This is its second form, put out at London in the late eighteen seventies. Its gift word makes it out to a great lord of that land, a member of a high house of France. It thanks him for kind aid at all times. The tales he gave in his own old tongue are here in English dress, with his help.
35055-a-pasteboard-crown-a-story-of-the-:
A Pasteboard Crown, a story of the New York stage, by Clara Morris, was printed in New York by Charles Scribner Sons in 1902. Morris had written Life on the Stage. Howard Chandler Christy drew the front plate. She had been a famed actress of strong feeling roles.

The plate line has an actor manager say, I will place the crown upon your head, only promise not to reproach me when you find it is only pasteboard. Chapters open with the Lawtons arrive, a powerful neighbor, and shopping under difficulties. The Woman of Fate, a prayer and a promise, and the promised crown follow. The costuming of Juliet, a lover plea, a family scene, and a working lesson pace the later tale. Stage fans get a novel of greasepaint dreams by one who lived them.
35068-the-car-that-went-abroad-motoring-:
Albert Bigelow Paine wrote The Car That Went Abroad, motoring through the golden age, printed in 1921 with drawings by Walter Hale. Paine had written lives and letters of Mark Twain and the Hollow Tree books for the young. A plate shows the Normandy road to Cherbourg, as fine as any in France. Contents open with part one, under the book's own title.

Do not hurry through Marseilles heads the first chapter. Motoring by tram and across the Crau follow. The mistral wind, the Rome of France, and the way through Eden come next. To Tarascon and Beaucaire, glimpses of the past, and in the citadel of faith fill the early run. An old custom and a new experience, wayside chances, and the lost Napoleon lead on. The house of heads stands later in the part. The trip runs through the south of France by motor car.
35071-the-boy-scouts-on-the-range:
The Boy Scouts on the Range is a western adventure for boys by Howard Payson, published by Hurst and Company at New York in 1911. The first chapter, Rob Surprises a Cow-Puncher, opens north of Truxton, Arizona. There the desert stretches a red-hot, sandy arm about baked hills with a thin growth of chaparral.

Twenty-four chapters carry the scouts through news of the Moquis, a desert water hole, and a silver tip bear. At the Harkness ranch Rob turns broncho buster, and a stampede hems the boys in with the herd. The home of a vanished race, capture by Moquis, and the grip of a grizzly follow. Black Cloud's visit and the maverick raid lead to scouts to the rescue.
351-of-human-bondage:
W. Somerset Maugham follows Philip Carey from a lonely childhood to adult life in this long novel. Philip, born with a club foot, loses his mother early and grows up under strict kin. He tries school, clerk work, art in Paris, and medicine in London, each path testing his pride and his need for love.

A cruel affair with a waitress named Mildred breaks his heart and his funds more than once, while steadier friends offer a saner path. Maugham writes in plain, steady prose, with little show. The book endures as a study of how a sensitive man learns to live with limits, and to want less yet feel more free.
35338-marriage:
Marriage is a novel by Wells. A list of his books stands at the front, from Tono Bungay and Kipps to The War of the Worlds and The First Men in the Moon. His books on social and political questions are listed too, A Modern Utopia among them. The novel itself opens on a train crossing middle England.

An extremely pretty girl rides in a second-class compartment. The train percolates through rural quiet from Ganford in Oxfordshire to Rumbold Junction in Kent. She is going to join her family at Buryhamstreet after a visit to Gloucestershire friends. Wells sets his courtship story in motion on the railway, among the small towns and family houses of the England he knew so well.
35364-ethel-morton-at-sweetbrier-lodge:
Mabell Smith's Ethel Morton at Sweetbrier Lodge was published by the World Syndicate Publishing Company. Seventeen chapters fill the contents, from A New Craft and Playing with Concrete to the club selecting the benches. A trip off to Philadelphia in the morning, preparations for the housewarming, Columbus Day, and the parting breakfast follow.

Chapter one is at the incubator. Ethel Blue Morton and her cousins, Ethel Brown and Dorothy Smith, are helping seven-year-old Dicky move his hatched chickens into the brooder. Dorothy drops one; the dinky thing runs about as chipper as ever. Ethel Brown finds one with a twisted leg, fallen off the tray when first hatched. Dicky judges, lispingly, that it will live if he feeds it by itself, so the strong ones will not crowd it from the feed pans. He examines the cripple with a farmer's care learned from his big brother Roger.
35472-euripides-and-his-age:
Euripides and His Age is a study of the Greek stage poet by Gilbert Murray. The author held the Greek chair at Oxford in his prime years. The book stands in a home set of short guides to great themes. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

First parts ask what wells of fact stand for a life of the poet. His plays, his gods, and his bold new mind fill the brief keen study. Murray turned the poets works for the stage in his own famed verse. The set aimed sound lore at home readers in small cheap books. The life shows a poet mocked at home and crowned long past death.
35534-how-to-be-happy-though-married-bei:
Press notices hail this handbook to marriage and its earthly paradise. Punch rhymes a strong plug for the book on its first edition. The Pall Mall Gazette calls its author the Murray of Matrimony. The Morning Post finds it clever, practical, and full of wise precepts.

The Standard calls it a new guide to matrimonial felicity here. Queen says it is tastefully got up, fit for a young bride gift. The Whitehall Review dubs it a companion to the honeymoon itself. Girls weighing marriage get special mention in the notices list.
35684-at-large:
At Large, a novel by E W Hornung, was printed by Charles Scribner's Sons at New York in 1902. Hornung's Raffles tales head the front list. The tale opens far from home: a hooded wagon creeps through red mud in mid Australia. Two hawkers ride the box, their gear in brass-bound drawers below. Recent rains clog the wheels at each yard, and the day crawls as the horses crawl.

Heads ahead jump four years and bring Dick home. Graysbrooke, a first night, and South Kensington set the stage. A dancing lesson bears fruit, an old friend stirs an old grief, and the Admirable Miles works his way. A photo and a song each turn the plot late on. Novel fans get bush trade, home ties, and a slow debt paid in Hornung's clean prose.
35748-christian-phrenology-a-guide-to-se:
A phrenology manual by Joseph Bunney, in its second edition of 1839. A Drewett published it at Regent Street, London. Its Greek motto is know thyself. The full title calls it Christian phrenology, a guide to self-knowledge. An introduction defines the system as mental philosophy. Phrenology measures the mind's faculties through its agent, the head.

Self-love blinds even gifted minds to their faults, Bunney argues. Flattery from others deepens the blindness. Phrenology escapes both esteem and partial praise, he claims. It avoids metaphysical error on one side and materialism on the other. Such a science suits an era of intellectual cultivation, he writes. Might made right in rougher ages, needing no standard of intellect. Bunney baptises the bump-reading science for Christian readers.
36075-the-king-s-pilgrimage:
The King's Pilgrimage is a photographic record of King George the Fifth's visit to the war cemeteries of France and Belgium in 1922. Hodder and Stoughton published it in London. By the king's desire, the profits went to the charities helping relatives visit the cemeteries abroad. The motto on the graves is carved at the front: their name liveth for evermore.

A letter from Buckingham Palace, dated May 1922, opens the book. Photographs by the great press agencies show the king standing beneath the cross of sacrifice at Terlincthun. He faces the stone of remembrance there. The pilgrimage, made four years after the armistice, honoured the empire's dead where they lay.
36179-the-rover-boys-on-a-tour-or-last-d:
The Rover Boys on a Tour, or Last Days at Brill College, is a boys' novel by Arthur M Winfield. Winfield was Edward Stratemeyer, who also wrote the Putnam Hall series. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York, copyrighted 1916. It stands twentieth in the first Rover Boys series. The arrival at the Barlow farmhouse fronts the book as an illustration.

Thirty chapters carry Sam, Tom, and Dick Rover out of college. A snowball fight opens the action. Something about the Rover Boys and something about Songbird follow. Blackie Crowden enters as the villain of the piece. A baseball game fills the middle chapters, opening and ending across two of them. Good-bye to Brill comes at chapter eighteen. The tour itself brings a moment of peril and news of Crowden. A telegram from New York speeds the climax. Cloudburst and flood lead to a rescue on the river.
36353-the-invisible-lodge:
Jean Paul Richter wrote this early romance, translated by Brooks and copyrighted in 1883. Brooks had translated Richter's 'Titan' and 'Hesperus' before this cradle work. The book was the forerunner of his principal later romances, the translator's preface states at the front.

Spazier called it the Genesis of Jean Paul's poetic world and its people, that preface quotes. Man is the great unknown in the book of nature, runs the motto from the Devil's papers. A boy raised underground by a strange lodge comes up into a world of tutors, soldiers and love, in Jean Paul's wild, tender first novel.
36383-a-canterbury-pilgrimage:
A Canterbury Pilgrimage is a travel book by Joseph and Elizabeth Robins Pennell, published by Seeley in London in 1885. The Pennells rode, wrote and illustrated the record themselves. Their pilgrimage was made not by rail but on a tandem tricycle, from London to Canterbury at the end of August.

They dedicate the book, unknown to him, to Robert Louis Stevenson, in gratitude for the hours spent travelling with him and his donkey. Their aim was reverent imitation: to follow Chaucer's road as far as possible. The first morning takes them out of Russell Square before anyone is stirring. The book helped invent the literary cycling tour: part homage, part holiday, all charm.
36533-bastien-lepage: Bastien-Lepage is the volume on the French painter Jules Bastien-Lepage, who lived from 1848 to 1884, in the Masterpieces in Colour series. Henry Roujon edited the series. Its companion volumes treat Reynolds, Chardin, Velasquez, Millet, Turner, Sargent and many more. The plates show the painter's work in colour. The first plate is The Song of Springtime, in the museum at Verdun, one of the artist's earliest works.
36960-a-classified-catalogue-of-selected:
A Classified Catalogue of Selected Works is the publisher's list of George Bell and Sons, dated London, November 1892. The catalogue sorts the firm's books by kind. Its sections run from poetry and biography to theology, botany, economics, art, and books for the young. The Aldine Poets series leads the poetry pages.

Entries give each book's size and price: Hamilton Aidé's songs at five shillings, the poems of Robert Bridges in several forms, and a cantata with words by Bridges. Fiction and the All-England sports series close the list. Such catalogues show what a serious London house offered the reading public in the eighteen nineties, and at what prices.
36967-a-west-country-pilgrimage:
Eden Phillpotts wanders in A West Country Pilgrimage, from Leonard Parsons of London, first published in May 1920, with pictures by A T Benthall. Phillpotts had written Dance of the Months and A Shadow Passes. The contents name the shrines: Hayes Barton, the Sad Heath, Dawlish Warren, Berry Pomeroy, and Berry Head.

Bagtor, Okehampton Castle, a Devon cross, Old Delabole, and Tintagel close the road. The first chapter opens east of the Exe, in a green valley of red earth, clover fields, and buttercup pools where lambs play. Devon and Cornwall receive a lover's slow attention, page by page.
37294-the-red-cross-barge:
Red Cross Barge is a war novel by Mrs Belloc Lowndes, published at London in 1916. Lowndes had written The Chink in the Armour and The Lodger before this work. Part one opens in occupied France at a table split between dessert and a war map. A German doctor pushes back his chair from coffee cups and liqueur bottles.

The large scale map of the French countryside spreads across half the table in the scene. That clash of fine dining and invasion sets the tone of the tale at once. A Red Cross barge on the rivers of France gives the book its title and craft. Mercy work amid armies drives the story of love and duty.
375-an-occurrence-at-owl-creek-bridge:
Ambrose Bierce sets this short Civil War tale on a railroad bridge in northern Alabama. A Southern planter, Peyton Farquhar, stands bound with a rope round his neck, guarded by Federal soldiers. As the trap drops, his mind races through a vivid dream of escape, flight through woods, and a rush home to his wife.

Bierce times the dream with care, letting each sense sharpen as Farquhar runs. The final twist snaps the dream shut and restores the grim fact of the bridge. The story endures for its tight craft and its stark view of war, hope, and self-deceit in a few short pages.
37618-queens-of-the-french-stage:
Williams wrote Queens of the French Stage for Scribner's Sons of New York in 1905, telling the lives of six famous French actresses. Portraits after Coypel, Lancret, and Van Loo illustrate the volume, with Adrienne Lecouvreur as frontispiece.

The first and longest life is Armande Béjart, the wife of Molière, married to him in Paris on February 20, 1662, when her father had just died and the family was poor. The other lives follow Marie de Champmeslé, Lecouvreur herself, the dancer Camargo, Justine Favart, and Clairon. Williams draws on deeds, letters, and theatre records to rebuild each career. The book preserves the glamour and the gossip of the Paris stage in the age of Racine and Voltaire.
37636-charles-lewis-cocke-founder-of-hol:
W R L Smith's Charles Lewis Cocke, Founder of Hollins College, was published at Boston by Richard G Badger, the Gorham Press, with a 1921 copyright. The contents promise the early years, the call of the Southwest, Hollins Institute in struggle and growth, the clearing skies, and expansion and achievement.

Later chapters treat the president and his girls, commencements and addresses, his religious enthusiasms, his characteristics, and his comrades and co-workers, closing with his monument. The chronology begins: born on February 21, 1820, at Edgehill, King William County, Virginia. Cocke entered Richmond College in 1836 and Columbian College at Washington in 1838, graduating in 1840. He married Susanna Virginia Pleasants on December 31, 1840, and in 1845 was called to take charge of the Valley Union Seminary at Botetourt Springs.
37667-three-hours-after-marriage:
Three Hours After Marriage is a comedy by John Gay, written with Alexander Pope and John Arbuthnot, the wits of the Scriblerus circle. This copy is the Augustan Reprint Society edition of 1961, edited with an opening essay by John Harrington Smith.

The editor's notes worry over a puzzle from the first edition of 1717. Gay's advertisement says the play is printed exactly as acted, yet he also says the players broke it into five parts while the action properly falls in three acts. The printed play has three acts, and only the later Dublin printings show five. Smith works through the tangle as a case study in how Augustan plays reached print. The farce itself mocks a fossil-hunting doctor and the lady who marries him for his collection.
37871-dandelion-cottage:
Carroll Watson Rankin wrote Dandelion Cottage, first published in 1904 and reprinted in 1977 by the Marquette County Historical Society in Michigan. Rankin dedicated the book to three girls whose lively interest made the writing a joyful task. Her heroines are four friends: Bettie Tucker, Jeanie Mapes, Mabel Bennett, and Marjory Vale.

The girls rent a small cottage from Mr. Black and take possession as the Dandelion Cottagers. They furnish it, face poverty in the cottage, and take in a lodger to the rescue. Neighbors pleasant and unpleasant fill the street, from kind Mrs. Crane to the Milligans and their dog. Surprises, a hurried retreat, and a telegram carry the tale. The book is a warm picture of girlhood in a Michigan lake town.
37963-miss-arnott-s-marriage:
Miss Arnott's Marriage, by Richard Marsh, author of The Beetle, was published by John Long at London in 1904. The chapters open with Robert Champion's wife and a woman on the pavement, then bring the heiress into her own and give her a proposal from the Earl of Peckham.

Later chapters turn on the law of marriage, on Mr Morice presuming, and on a solicitor's clerk, a note, and a somnambulist. Hugh Morice explains, two men confront each other, and the buttons come off the foils before the close. The marriage at the heart of the plot is no simple love match.
38300-boy-scouts-tenderfoot-squad-or-cam:
Alan Douglas, a scout master, wrote this boy scouts story, copyrighted in 1919. A carload of khaki-clad boys piles in with their camp gear and heads for Raccoon Bluff, arguing cheerfully about a rifle brought along just in case of trouble.

The contents promise a game poacher named Jem Shock, a bargain made with Conrad, a peril lying in wait, a strange message, and a cabin in a clearing. Later chapters bring a storm, a call for help, and scouts to the rescue. The boys include Elmer, George Robbins the doubter, and Lil Artha at the wheel. Readers get a hearty camp adventure of the squad's first season.
38521-a-drake-by-george:
John Trevena wrote A Drake by George, a novel put out by Knopf at New York in 1916. It opens with rumor flying about the town of Highfield. Captain Drake has come, a man of two hundred and fifty pounds who blocks the one narrow street. His voice rings from the church at the hill top to the post office below. Talk says lawyers work about two old cottages of an absent landlord. A man who needs two homes, folk think, must have plenty of money.

Wealth, in Highfield, is the shortest cut to fame that the town knows. Chapters bring a show day at Windward House, a tangled inheritance, and scandal laid bare. George, of the title cry, takes control in time. Parts named for ploughing, sowing, and reaping hint at land at its heart.
39082-a-desperate-voyage:
Desperate Voyage is a novel by Knight in the Milne Express Series. John Milne of London issued the book in eighteen ninety eight. Knight wrote The Cruise of the Falcon and Where Three Empires Meet. The series mate, The Rome Express by Major Arthur Griffiths, heads the list.

Chapter one sets solicitor Henry Carew in his Carey Street office block. The firm of Peters and Carew faces the Law Courts in Chancery Lane. Peters, the senior partner, died of gout two years before the tale opens. Carew comes in late one August evening, white faced and haggard with care. He mutters to himself, a man plainly crushed by some secret dread.
39340-the-surprising-adventures-of-sir-t:
Crockett wrote this boys' book, copyrighted in 1897 by Stokes of New York. Gordon Browne illustrated the history for its young readers throughout. A mock order at the front bans too good boys from reading the book, by command of Field Marshal Napoleon Smith.

Prissy, Hugh John and Sir Toady Lion open the contents in chapter one. Hugh John becomes General Napoleon in the third chapter, and Castle Perilous follows in the list. A declaration of war and a Highland charge, likened in a plate to troopers at Balaclava, promise mock-heroic games played in deadly earnest by children.
39617-curiosities-of-the-american-stage:
Laurence Hutton wrote Curiosities of the American Stage, published by Harper and Brothers in New York in 1891. Hutton, author of Plays and Players, presents the book as chapters from the annals of the American theatre. A portrait of Junius Brutus Booth serves as frontispiece. He dedicated the volume to Brander Matthews.

In his argument, Hutton says the book considers plays and players in their less familiar aspects. It does not pretend to be critical, and he took the greatest care to verify its facts, many printed for the first time. Chapters on the American stage negro, on burlesque, and on a century of American Hamlets first appeared in Harper's Magazine. Hutton writes for dramatic collectors and old play-goers, the specialists and veterans of the American stage.
39803-an-explanatory-discourse-by-tan-ch:
An Explanatory Discourse, put in the mouth of Tan Chet-Qua of Quang-Chew-Fu, comes from the pen of Sir William Chambers. The Augustan Reprint Society reissued the work in nineteen hundred seventy eight. The Clark Memorial Library at Los Angeles held the copy. Richard E Quaintance the younger wrote the long front essay.

Chambers first wrote on Chinese buildings in seventeen hundred fifty seven. His later piece on eastern garden art came in seventeen hundred seventy two. The discourse defends wild, free garden plans in the Chinese taste. Notes trace the rage for that style in his day. At page one hundred fifty nine, the notes say, Chet-Qua drops his mask. Scholars of garden art get a key text with full help.
40015-a-boy-scout-s-courage:
Edward Griggs wrote A Boy Scout's Courage, the tenth of twelve volumes of boy scout tales issued by the Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron, Ohio, in 1921. Its hero is Harry Fleming, an American boy scout living in London. The eleven chapters run from a friend in need through an unexpected blow, the silent wire, a treacherous deed, the trap, the cipher, and a capture from the skies, to vindication.

Harry looks back on a wild week: his scoutmaster Grenfel gone, his parents recalled to the States, and he and his chum Dick Mercer sent on a mission. They found heliographs flashing signals to the enemy across the North Sea, from a guarded estate by a village. Harry is caught in a trap set for trespassers and sends Dick away. The tale is a wartime spy chase for boys.
40385-rutledge:
Miriam Coles Harris wrote Rutledge, a novel printed at New York in eighteen sixty. The tale opens on a gloomy November dusk at the school of St Catharine. Lamps are not yet lit, and black stoves warm the rooms. The narrator walks a dim hall with her friends Nelly and Agnes, and all three are low in spirit.

Her trunk stands packed by her dorm door, full of school books and keepsakes. She leaves the next day, parted from the girls who were her world for five years. Old feuds have been healed in the face of parting, and old friends cling with new warmth. Even the staff, who had much to forgive in her wild ways, wish her well. The book follows her out into grown life.
40452-the-twickenham-peerage:
The Twickenham Peerage is a mystery novel by Richard Marsh, author of The Beetle, published by Methuen at London in 1902. The book is built in four parts. The first, The Sleeping Man, opens with a side show and a dinner party given by Lady Desmond. Montagu Babbacombe awakes, a message comes from the Marquis, and the part ends with chapters named Dying, Dead, and Buried.

The second book, The Lost Husband, brings an encounter in Piccadilly and the opening of a coffin. The third follows a gentleman with nine lives toward a marquis in fact. The fourth book is called The Sinner. Marsh mixes peerage secrets, hidden identity, and strange returns in his brisk, startling manner.
40757-the-nursery-june-1881-vol-xxix-a-m:
The Nursery for June 1881 is Volume Twenty Nine Number Six of a monthly magazine for the youngest readers, issued at Boston. Prose and verse lists fill the front pages. The Careless Nurse leads the prose. Master Baby, Two Small Boys, and a piece on how Georgie fed his fawn follow.

Verse holds Feeding the Fowls, A Polite Dandelion, and The Rose. Margie's Trial and a piece on why the chick came out sit in verse too. The lead prose writer says his charge is the rights of children. He faults careless nurses and tells a case from the seaside last summer. Pictures and short pieces suit home reading with small children.
40800-an-imperial-marriage:
An Imperial Marriage is a novel by Arthur Marchmont, author of By Right of Sword and When I Was Czar, printed in 1909 at London, Melbourne, and Toronto. Thirty chapters carry the tale from complications and a stroke of luck to murder, a charge of murder, and a bride elect. The narrator tells the story in the first person.

He had been Berlin correspondent for the London Newsletter, and the marriage was almost the last news he sent home. The Kaiser plans to wed his kinswoman, the Princess von Altenvelt, to his handsome favourite, the Prince von Graven. Court gossips call it the Imperial Marriage. The narrator stays on in Berlin, ostensibly to help his successor, in truth for the sake of Althea.
40949-the-outrage:
Annie Vivanti Chartres wrote this novel, issued by Knopf in New York in nineteen eighteen under the title The Outrage. Book One opens at Westende, a Belgian sea resort, where two girls are racing to bathe. Chérie flings on her robe and seizes Amour, her small dog, while little Mireille struggles with knotted tapes and begs the governess for help.

Frieda, the hard-faced German nursery governess, answers the French chatter with an order. This is their English day, so both girls must speak English, and nobody leaves for the street without stockings and a hat. The bright bath-house scene sets the resort world of French girls, a German servant, and small rules of respectability just before that world breaks.
41378-coleridge:
Coleridge is a short life of the poet by Bensusan, printed at London. Jack issued it, and Dodge published it at New York. Six chapters and an introduction fill a brief book, ending with an index. A portrait of Samuel Coleridge stands inside.

The introduction opens with a lament. Dryden, Pope, Goldsmith, Gray, Crabbe, and Thomson are little more than names to the new generation, Bensusan says. Readers cannot keep pace with the ever-growing task of reading. Only steady reading, with knowledge of a poet's life and times, makes the dead man a living force again. Chapters then treat Coleridge's early years, his search for the ideal, his troubled years, and his place as poet and critic.
41659-the-swiss-family-robinson-a-transl:
The Swiss Family Robinson comes from the original German of Johann Rudolf Wyss, in the title page's naming. William H G Kingston edited this translation, issued by Grosset and Dunlap at New York. Walter S Rogers drew the illustrations. The frontispiece shows something taking wonderful, flying leaps. The first chapter's long heading tells the whole opening: storm-tossed, wrecked, and deserted. The family makes swimming-belts for the children and passes an anxious night.

The gale moderates, and the cargo is examined. Jack finds two new acquaintances among the stores. A tub-boat is built with the use of a lever, and another night passes on the wreck. The family collects the cargo and embarks for the shore. A tent, glue soup, and a lobster mark the first day on land. Fritz returns with a sucking pig, and the dogs devour the agouti.
41671-double-challenge:
Double Challenge, a boys adventure novel by Jim Kjelgaard, was issued by Dodd, Mead and Company in New York in nineteen fifty eight. The title page notes a copyright of nineteen fifty seven. Ted Harkness is the young hero. His fine collie Tammie walks at his side. Twelve chapters carry names such as The Jolt, The Camp, and The Fugitive.

The story opens on Hawkbill, the high point of the Mahela hills. Ted climbs without a rest and feels proud of the feat. On the way down Tammie finds young grouse on a fallen tree. Later chapters promise a flight of woodcock, a black bear charge, and a friend who turns false. Young readers get wild woods, dogs, and risk.
42045-the-curate-in-charge:
The Curate in Charge is a novel by Mrs Oliphant, published by Macmillan in 1883, set in the parish of Brentburn in Berkshire. The first chapter paints the parish where rich forest meets pine moor, with its too correct new church and plain red brick rectory.

The story follows the curate St John, who holds the parish together while rectors come and go, and the girls whose work and hopes fill the middle chapters. Aunt Jane, a new rector, and an enemy stir the quiet. Oliphant wrote parish life as few could, with patience for small duties and the money worries behind them.
42182-the-hyborian-age:
The Hyborian Age is an essay by Robert E. Howard, first printed in The Phantagraph in 1936. Howard wrote it as the invented history behind his Conan stories. He says plainly that it is not a theory against accepted history. It is a made-up background meant to lend Conan and his sagas a greater air of realness.

Howard tells how he kept to the facts and spirit of this history in every Conan tale, as a writer of true historical fiction keeps to real events. The essay begins with the Pre-Cataclysmic Age, known only in legend. Its great kingdoms were Kamelia, Valusia, Verulia, Grondar, Thule, and Commoria. Beyond them lived the Picts on isles of the western ocean, the Atlanteans on a small continent, and the Lemurians on isles in the east. The piece is the seed chart of the Conan world.
42760-the-myth-in-marriage:
Alice Hubbard wrote this short book on marriage, published by the Roycrofters at East Aurora in 1912. The contents move from romance and revelation through facts and an awakening, then classify the natural marriage, the social marriage, and the marriage of convenience.

Later pieces treat the business of marriage, primitive bondage, economic freedom, enforced dependence, and citizens. The opening chapter argues that love is a sacred mystery whose secret stays locked from mortals; we can know only its absence or its presence. Hubbard quotes Emerson on taking oneself for better or worse. Readers get aphoristic, reforming counsel from the Roycroft circle.
43349-an-irishman-s-difficulties-with-th:
An Irishman Difficulties with the Dutch Language is a laugh book by Cuey na Gael. A Rotterdam house brought out this fourth print of the work. Friend O'Neill trips through Holland on word traps in the tale set. A Haarlem note of March nineteen eight thanks the man for the fun. Dutch folk who fight with English will love the flip side view, it says.

Sweet thanks in Dutch means no thanks at all, one tale trap shows. O'Neill says it at each kind gift and gets no food for his pains. Call word traps with notes and day trains fill more jest heads. A D train runs by night since D means day in the jest logic. The book holds a place fit for school book rooms, the note claims.
439-the-vital-message:
Arthur Conan Doyle argues for spirit contact in this 1919 sequel to The New Revelation, written after the Great War. Doyle claims the war's vast loss opened minds to a new relation with the unseen. He sets out the evidence and the changes he expects in science, faith, and daily life.

Chapters treat the dawning light, the great argument, and the coming world, with notes on spirit photos and clairvoyance. Doyle writes with earnest conviction, as a public man pleading a cause. The book stands as a clear record of his later faith, and of a generation seeking comfort beyond the grave.
44185-the-fighting-starkleys-or-the-test:
Captain Theodore Goodridge Roberts wrote this war novel for boys, published by the Page Company at Boston in 1922 with pictures by George Varian. The Starkleys farm at Beaver Dam, a New Brunswick settlement of farms, a gristmill, a meetinghouse, and a store. John Starkley and his wife Constance Emma have raised three boys and two girls to an early-rising, robust life. Their house was built by the sons of old Major Richard Starkley, the settler.

When the call comes, the boys go to the war their grandfathers' generation only remembered. The chapters follow Jim Hammond, who does not return to duty, Private Sill, Dave Hammer's commission, Peter's letter, and the 26th as it mops up. Frank Sacobie, heir of the major's Malecite friend Two-Blanket, objects and serves. It is a test of courage, as the subtitle says.
44672-stronghand-or-the-noble-revenge:
Stronghand, or The Noble Revenge is a frontier novel by Gustave Aimard. Ward and Lock published it in London in 1864. Aimard had written Prairie Flower and Buccaneer Chief before it. The first chapter is called An Exchange of Shots. It opens in the country between the Sierra de San Saba and the Rio Puerco. The narrator calls that land one of the most melancholy regions imaginable.

Skeletons bleach unrecognized on the accursed savannah. Grey rocks shelter snakes and wild beasts among black shrubs. Travellers cross the solitude only when forced. Forty chapters carry the tale across the border country. A council of sachems, a spy, and the assault on Quitovar mark the middle. The vengeance of heaven and the funeral of a sachem come near the end. Kidd reappears among the complications of the plot.
44820-the-evolutionist-at-large:
The Evolutionist at Large is a set of popular science essays by Grant Allen. Chatto and Windus published it in London in 1881. The essays first appeared in a London gazette. A poem to the author's mother opens the volume. It recalls the Canadian wildflowers of his boyhood.

The preface states the book's object plainly. Allen wished to make evolution's principles familiar to unscientific readers. Biologists dwell on minute structure, he notes. Ordinary people care little for such points. His essays take up the living creatures around them instead. Allen had earlier written on beauty and on the colour-sense. The tone stays light and conversational throughout. Even the dedication poem lists bloodroot and trilliums with love.
45184-later-queens-of-the-french-stage:
Later Queens of the French Stage, by Noel Williams, was published in London and New York in 1906. Williams had already written Queens of the French Stage, and lives of Madame Recamier, Madame de Pompadour, and others. Six lives make up this second set, each with pictures.

Sophie Arnould comes first, at near a hundred pages. Then come Guimard and Raucourt, both dancers and players of their age. Dugazon and Contat follow, and Saint-Huberty closes the book. Portraits after Greuze, Boucher, Gros, and Isabey face the text. Readers get short lives of women who ruled the Paris stage, told with care for their art, their fame, and the world that watched them.
45282-the-history-of-the-devils-of-loudu:
An eye-witness told the history of the devils of Loudun, here in English. Edmund Goldsmid edited the set, printed at Edinburgh in 1887. The run held 275 small-paper and 75 large-paper copies only. The French source first came out at Poitiers in the Roman year MDCXXXIV.

Ursuline nuns at Loudun were said to be possessed by devils in the tale. Urbain Grandier, their priest, stood trial for magic and was put to death. The writer, des Niau, believed the charges and took part in the scenes. Students gain a chilling, first-hand record of a famed witch panic.
4531-the-secret-passage:
Fergus Hume built this detective novel around a cottage, a crime, and a mysterious death, with a secret entrance waiting to explain them. Susan Grant, a parlour-maid of twenty-five, comes to work for the sharp Miss Loach, and the household soon fills with suspects: Lord Caranby, Juliet, Basil, Cuthbert, Mrs. Octagon, and a detective who asks hard questions. Chapters follow the crime, the details, the course of true love, and one mystery after another.

Juliet's story, told in two parts, and Susan's discovery slowly open the hidden passage and the revenge behind it. Hume keeps the plot moving through parlour talk, admissions, and experiments, until nemesis catches the scamp at the centre. Readers get a brisk Edwardian mystery, with romance and detection side by side, and a secret that rewards patience right up to the final chapters.
45317-a-memorial-of-mrs-margaret-breckin:
A Memorial of Mrs Margaret Breckinridge came out at Philadelphia in 1839. Martien published the book, entered that year under the law. It stands in two parts, as the title page lays them out. Part one holds a memoir of her life and a funeral sermon. Part two holds letters to her surviving children, the title adds.

Her life, her religious character, and her work for foreign missions fill part one. Her sacrifices for the church and her last sickness close the memoir. A sermon on submission follows the closing reflections there. Part two is called letters of a grandfather to the young. Human nature and the way of salvation stand in its heads. Margaret Breckinridge was taken into the saints' everlasting rest, the opening says. The memorial gives a pious life for the family's keeping.
45421-theodore-roosevelt-an-address-deli:
Henry Cabot Lodge delivered this address on Theodore Roosevelt before the Congress of the United States on February 9, 1919, a month after Roosevelt's death. The McGrath-Sherrill Press privately printed it at Boston in three hundred copies. An inscribed photograph of Roosevelt, dated September 20, 1904, faces the title page.

Lodge opens with a lament from an old Moorish ballad: a tower is fallen, a star is set. He describes how the news emptied every other concern, pushing aside the absorbing reports of those fateful days while newspapers gave pages to the man who had died. The pulpit found a text in his life, the judge and the schoolchild paused, and sorrow came from rich and poor alike. Lodge argues that Roosevelt, though a private citizen with no power to reward or punish, was unusual even among the leaders of men.
45666-little-peter-a-christmas-morality-:
Lucas Malet wrote Little Peter, a Christmas morality for children of any age. Kegan Paul, Trench and Company published it at London in 1888, with many pictures by Paul Hardy. Malet was the author of Colonel Enderby's Wife. She dedicated the story to Cecily, in token of affection toward her, her mother, and her stately home. The frontispiece line runs: remember, my ears are so quick I can hear the grass grow.

The first chapter deals with the opinions of a cat and the sorrows of a charcoal-burner. A Grasshopper-man and an admirer of the ancient Romans follow. A dinner party and an unpleasant walk come midway. The pine forest opens the tale, its trees standing in ranks like soldiers. Malet writes a fable of beasts, spirits, and a small boy for the Christmas shelf.
45695-the-memorials-of-the-hamlet-of-kni:
Henry George Davis compiled The Memorials of the Hamlet of Knightsbridge, with notices of its immediate neighbourhood. His brother Charles edited it after his death, and Russell Smith published it at London in 1859. The preface sketches the author: born in 1830, schooled at the Philological School, kept from sports by lung disease, and dead at twenty-nine after labouring at the book to its end. His notices had already appeared in Notes and Queries and the local papers.

The work gathers a London hamlet's history from notes made since boyhood: its sites, among them the ground of Albert Gate, its schools, and its old residents. Charles Davis issued the volume as a duty to his brother. The transcription follows the 1856 printing.
45718-the-blocking-of-zeebrugge:
The Blocking of Zeebrugge is a war account by Captain Carpenter of the navy. Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York brought it out in 1922. Carpenter held the Victoria Cross for the raid he here describes. Admiral Earl Beatty wrote the introduction to the sailor's own tale. Marshal Foch, Rear-Admiral Sims, and the Burgomaster of Bruges add appreciations.

Storming the mole fronts the book, drawn from details the author supplied. Beatty recalls the naval situation at the beginning of 1918 first. The German High Seas Fleet lay contained in the Heligoland Bight then. German submarines waged vast operations against Britain's trade and communications. Destroying them, or barring their egress, stood as Britain's two aims. Convoys, patrols, and mining served the first aim with great results. Yet submarines were built almost as fast as they were destroyed. Blocking their bases thus became the needful stroke of the war.
45728-the-happy-average:
The Happy Average is a novel by Brand Whitlock with pictures by Howard Chandler Christy. Burt Company of New York put out this copy of the popular tale. Bobbs-Merrill held the rights from October of the year 1904. Whitlock had writ Her Infinite Variety and The 13th District before. The tale opens with a young man's fancy on a summer evening call.

Lawrence leads the way to the Carters' veranda with a jaunty step. Marley lags behind, fresh from college and stiff with new dignity. He wishes Lawrence would not speak so loud before the girls. White figures stir on the veranda, then a screen door bangs shut. Lawrence bows low to Mrs Carter and greets the captain there. Marley bows and says something, lost in the dark presentation. Lawrence fans himself with his hat, easy where Marley stands stiff.
46059-the-adopting-of-rosa-marie-a-seque:
The Adopting of Rosa Marie is a girls' novel by Carroll Watson Rankin. Holt issued it in New York, with copyright in 1908. It is the sequel to Dandelion Cottage. Florence Shinn drew the illustrations. The four chums of the first book meet again here. Their summer of playing house knit them close. Now they take up the care of a small Indian baby. Press praise on the wrapper calls them a lovable group.

Jean, Marjory, Mabel, and Bettie are the four friends. Borrowed babies open the contents in fun. Rosa Marie arrives, then must be returned. A dark secret and a fugitive soldier stir the plot. Fire and alarm come in the middle chapters. A Boston paper praised the girls' humour and pranks. The book aims at readers from eight to fifteen.
4613-at-large:
Arthur Christopher Benson published At Large in 1908, as a book of essays by a bachelor tied to college for half the year and free for the other half. He asks what such a man should do with his free months. He cannot live on in college rooms for economy, and he will not drift from house to house like a wandering dove. The essays that follow are his answer, written from a love of independence and quiet study.

Contents run from the scene, contentment, friendship, humour, and travel. They go on to specialism, our lack of great men, shyness, and equality. Later essays cover the dramatic sense, Kelmscott and William Morris, a speech day, literary finish, symbols, optimism, joy, and the love of God. Readers get a calm, civilised set of reflections on how to live well, in Benson's easy, bookish voice.
46348-over-there-with-the-canadians-at-v:
Over There with the Canadians at Vimy Ridge, by Captain George H Ralphson, was printed in Chicago and New York by M A Donohue and Company under a 1919 copyright. Ralphson wrote twin boy war books on Cantigny, St Mihiel, and Chateau Thierry.

Chapters open with shells and minenwerfer, Irving idea, and in no man land. Kamerad, the turtle is wounded, and a little history follow. Tourtelle apologizes, cubist art, and Bob letter pace the mid tale. Quizzing a spy, studying to be a spy, and last preparations raise the stakes. The blowing up of Vimy Ridge, behind the German lines, and off for Berlin drive the close. The text opens with two soldiers crouching in a camouflaged pit in no man land at Vimy. Boys of 1919 got a spy chase on the western front.
46476-the-idea-of-god-as-affected-by-mod:
John Fiske wrote The Idea of God as Affected by Modern Knowledge, dated eighteen eighty-five and issued at Boston in eighteen eighty-six. The book follows his Destiny of Man as a sequel. Fiske gave it to his wife, recalling a Sunday talk under an apple-tree.

Fiske argues that the word Unknowable, much abused by Herbert Spencer's follower Harrison, holds real worth. Rightly grasped, it says that God in himself is not only unknown but beyond knowing. That claim, Fiske holds, strengthens rather than weakens belief. Goethe's lines on the world-soul head the book. The small volume sold for one dollar.
46699-judge-elbridge:
Judge Elbridge, a novel by Opie Read, was published at Chicago and New York by Rand, McNally and Company in 1899. Read was already known for books such as An Arkansas Planter and A Yankee from the West. The story is told in short chapters with picture like titles. Early heads include The Student and the Orator and The Family Joke.

Later chapter titles hint at the turns of the tale. Readers meet the Wexton Club, a night scene in an alley, and a visit to the old office. A front plate shows a piece of silver thrown upon a banner of salvationists. That image points to the public and moral scenes in the book. The novel belongs to the popular fiction of its day, built on character and incident in American life.
47019-cambridge:
Cambridge is a full guide to the town and the great school of that name, writ by Tuker and put out for sale in towns on four shores of the world. The title leaf names her as the hand of past parts of a like guide to Rome. A plate at the front shows the Bridge of Sighs at one of the halls. That bridge joins two courts of the hall, and the book room of sixteen twenty four stands past it.

The work walks the town in set parts. First come the old inns and hostels where the first bands of young men lodged. Then come the halls in their full line, from the first small house to the great ones of a late age.
47113-the-message:
The Message is an adventure novel by Louis Tracy, published by Clode in New York in 1908. Joseph Cummings Chase drew the illustrations. The contents promise a tale that travels far from home waters.

The first chapters are called Derelicts, and How the Message Was Delivered. A figure named Warden sets a new course as the plot gathers way. Figuero makes a discovery, and Hassan's tower joins the Colonial Office in one chapter title. A blue man and a white stand opposed in another heading. Evelyn, the heroine, receives unexpected visitors and then enters the fray herself. The drums of Oku sound before a five minutes' fight near the climax.
4723-a-treatise-concerning-the-principle:
George Berkeley, 1685 to 1753, wrote A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge. It inquires into the chief causes of error and difficulty in the sciences, with the grounds of scepticism, atheism, and irreligion. He dedicates the work to Thomas, Earl of Pembroke, knight of the Garter and lord of the privy council. He wonders that an obscure person unknown to his lordship should presume to address him in that manner.

Berkeley argues that a man who writes to promote useful knowledge and religion may properly choose such a patron, since Pembroke ornaments and supports church and learning. His treatise then sets out the idealist philosophy for which he is famous. Material things exist as perceived, and abstract ideas mislead science. Readers get a short, demanding classic of philosophy, best read slowly, with its dedication as a window into its age.
47475-chronicles-of-london-bridge:
Chronicles of London Bridge gathers the history of the famous crossing, written by an unnamed antiquary. Smith, Elder published the book at London in 1827. The work is dedicated to the lord mayor who laid the first stone of the new bridge in 1825. Pictures and old songs with music fill its pages.

The preface defends the chronicle plan by the example of old law books. All sources are quoted in English, the author promises, so no reader is lost in Latin. Gathering the matter proved a longer labour than he looked for. The old bridge had stood since the middle ages, crowded with houses and shops. Its tales run from saints and kings to traitors' heads on its gate. The book appeared just as the old bridge faced its end.
47613-the-mystery-hunters-at-the-haunted:
Capwell Wyckoff's The Mystery Hunters at the Haunted Lodge was copyrighted in 1934 by the Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron and New York. The frontispiece has a boy crying out over a rifle shell he has found. The story opens at Cloverfield High School in Vermont, where Barry Garrison, star halfback and the school's most popular boy, waits with Kent Marple, the fullback whose father owns the local hotel. The Ford twins complete the four.

Twenty-five chapters take the Mystery Hunters upriver to a haunted lodge: its story told, an expedition planned, a strange conversation overheard, and Bronson's cabin reached. An upstairs window, a disturbed night, mysterious knocking, a quarry shed, and a black shadow build the haunting. Barry's great discovery and a fight with the Black Shadow lead to the mystery of the lodge explained. The book is a boys' series mystery of the Depression years.
4787-the-story-of-julia-page:
Kathleen Norris published The Story of Julia Page in 1915, with a frontispiece by C. Allan Gilbert. Its pictured line says it never occurred to anyone to ask why the heroine differs from other women, or what made her so. Chapter one opens with Emeline, wife of George Page, slowly reaching, in her thirtieth year, a sullen conviction that life is monstrously unfair.

From resentment at an unhappy marriage, Emeline's mind returns to a pert, precocious childhood and a restless, discontented girlhood, feeling with smouldering fury that she never had a fair chance at all. It took years to reach that conclusion, since Emeline, shrewd among women she knew, was in essential things unintelligent, and mental effort was strange to her. She scrambled through grammar school and five further years of schooling. Readers get a Norris novel of a woman's discontent, marriage, and slow awakening.
47966-frank-armstrong-at-college:
Frank Armstrong at College, by Matthew Colton, was copyrighted in 1914 at New York. Burt published the boys college tale in the Frank Armstrong series. A plate shows a Yale quarter driving a forward pass to Armstrong in play. The freshman rush opens the contents as chapter one of the book.

A brush with the police and the Codfish creating news follow in the list. Making the eleven and Frank learning to tackle the dummy fill the football chapters. The great freshman battle and a wreck at the harbour come next in the contents. Fun at the theatre and a jump in baseball stand further down the roll. College sport and pranks of the 1910s fill this series volume for boys.
481-in-the-bishop-s-carriage:
Miriam Michelson tells of Nancy, a young pickpocket who poses as a Bryn Mawr girl to dodge police, in this brisk novel. After a theft at a station, Nancy slips into a bishop's carriage and talks her way into a new life among polite folk. Her thief friend Tom watches from the shadows, torn between love and the law.

Michelson writes in Nancy's quick, slangy voice, full of nerve and humor. Each chapter tests whether Nancy can keep her act, or fall back to the streets. The novel charms as a tale of disguise and second chances, where a sharp girl outwits both cops and society.
48426-the-heroic-age:
H Munro Chadwick, a fellow of Clare College, Cambridge, wrote a study of the heroic age published at the University Press in 1912 and reprinted in 1967. A map of central Europe illustrates the heroic age of the Teutonic peoples. Where a name occurs in capitals and italics, the front matter explains, the former marks an early position and the latter a later extension. The book belongs to a Cambridge archaeological and ethnological series.

Chadwick compared the heroic societies of Greece, Ireland, and the Germanic world. His age is the era of war bands and gift giving kings behind the epics. The reprint kept a standard work in print. Library editions reissued it unrevised.
48937-the-wiving-of-lance-cleaverage:
Alice MacGowan tells a hill tale in The Wiving of Lance Cleaverage, printed in New York and London in 1909. Putnam made the book, with plates in color by Robert Edwards. She gives it to Emma Bell Miles, who could have writ this story of her own home country much better, she says.

Twenty nine chapters map a mountain courtship and its storms. A dance and a serenade lead to the asking and the wedding. An interloper, pride in poverty, and broken chords strain the match. A stubborn heart, a flight, and a spell in hiding raise the stakes. The sheriff scores near the end, and the island waits at last. MacGowan had writ Judith of the Cumberlands.
49019-kirkcaldy-of-grange:
Kirkcaldy of Grange, by Louis Barbé, is a biography in the Famous Scots Series, published by Scribner's at New York. Its subject is Sir William Kirkcaldy of Grange, the soldier whose holding of Edinburgh Castle closes the book.

Chapters follow the Kirkcaldy family from its seat at the Grange in the parish of Kinghorn, on the north shore of the Firth of Forth. They pass through the tragedy at Saint Andrews and the conspirators at bay. The narrative takes him to France and home again, through the uproar of religion, the harassing of the French, and the battles of Carberry and Langside. A chapter titled Defection, with a question mark, precedes the holding of the castle and the final scene at the mercat cross.
49465-the-three-bears-of-porcupine-ridge:
The Three Bears of Porcupine Ridge, by Jean Thompson, was copyrighted in 1913 and published at Boston and Chicago, with pictures by Charles Copeland. Thompson gives the book, subtitled Wild Dwellers of Forest, Marsh and Lake, to the loving memory of her mother. A front picture shows Mrs Bear fiercely tugging at a cruel chain.

The title tale opens the set. Ring Neck, leader of the flying wedge, follows. Later tales treat the revolt of Timothy, a little red doe, and Dame Woodchuck and the red monster. A catamount tracks one hero, and a moose calls another. Porcupine, weasel, bobcat, beaver, crow, owl, and coon all get tales. Readers get animal stories of the north woods for young readers, each built round one wild dweller.
49827-pygmalion-and-the-image:
Pygmalion and the Image is a poem by William Morris, issued in New York in 1903 with pictures by Edward Burne-Jones. The poem comes from Morris's Earthly Paradise. Burne-Jones, Morris's lifelong friend, had made a full set of designs for it in 1866 and 1867, one of only two poems of that work so honoured.

Four finished paintings carry the tale. Their titles chart the sculptor's progress: the heart desires, the hand refrains, the godhead fires, the soul attains. Pygmalion carves the woman of his dreams, falls in love with the stone, and prays until the statue warms to life. A portrait of Morris, from the painting by Watts, forms the frontispiece. The small volume is a monument of the two friends' shared art: Morris's verse in medieval dress, and Burne-Jones's dreamy figures beside it.
50023-the-economics-of-the-russian-villa:
Isaac Hourwich's study, issued at New York in 1892 as the first number of the second volume of Columbia College's Studies in History, Economics and Public Law, examines the Russian village. An introduction treats the rise of what he calls peasantism. His first chapter sketches the growth of landholding in Russia from the old village community onward.

That history runs through serfdom, the poll tax, the rising under Pougatchoff, and the statute of 1861 that ended bondage. Later chapters take up the community of land, the working forces of the peasantry, and the weight of taxes on the peasant. Hourwich notes that taxes fell in inverse ratio to income, and that arrears bore hard on the peasant's live stock.
50611-the-pillar-of-fire-or-israel-in-bo:
Ingraham, rector of Christ Church in Holly Springs, Mississippi, wrote The Pillar of Fire, a tale of Israel in bondage in Egypt. Roberts Brothers of Boston issued this edition in 1881; the work was first entered for copyright in 1859. Ingraham had already won readers with The Prince of the House of David, named under his name.

The book is built as a series of letters, and a picture of the finding of Moses faces the text. In a note to readers, Ingraham says his aim was to show the Egypt of the bondage years from a view outside the Mosaic account, yet in strict accord with it. He inscribes the book to the men of Israel in this generation. Bible readers get the Exodus world rebuilt as story, palace, river, and slave gang.
51133-how-to-use-the-popular-science-lib:
Garrett Serviss wrote how to use a sixteen-book home science set. Volume sixteen came out in New York in 1922. Collier and Son put the whole Popular Science Library out. A plate calls the Majestic the world's largest steam ship. Selwyn-Brown's history of science fills most of this last book.

Serviss tells where to find each theme in the set's shelves. Word lists and a master index close the whole work. The history runs from cave man to the science of that day. A host of pros wrote the set's parts on each art. Home shelves in 1922 could hold all man's facts in one row. This book is the key to that row.
5129-the-prodigal-judge:
Vaughan Kester's novel is set in the pine woods of the American South after the Civil War, where the last of the Quintard family has died at the old Barony house. A boy left at the margins of that household crosses paths with a wandering judge, river men, and tavern fighters, and the story follows their fortunes toward Tennessee.

Courtroom scenes, raft journeys, shooting matches, and jailbreaks give the book the flavour of a Southern picaresque. Beneath the adventure, Kester tells a story of inheritance, loyalty. Second chances follow, as a rootless judge and a homeless boy each look for a place to belong.
5131-childe-harold-s-pilgrimage:
Lord Byron's long poem follows Childe Harold, a weary young nobleman, on a pilgrimage through Europe in four cantos. Harold travels from Portugal and Spain to Greece, the Alps, Italy, and Rome, and Byron uses each place to reflect on history, liberty, war, and the ruins of empires.

The poem made Byron famous overnight, and its melancholy traveller became a model for Romantic heroes. Readers will find famous passages on Waterloo, Venice, and Rome, alongside Byron's own voice breaking through Harold's, as the poet turns a journey into a meditation on his age.
51370-life-of-father-ignatius-of-st-paul:
Life of Father Ignatius of St Paul is a biography compiled chiefly from the man's own autobiography, journal, and letters. It was put together by Father Pius, a Passionist of the same order, and published at Dublin in 1866. The subject was born George Spencer, son of an earl, and bred in the Church of England. As a Passionist priest he took the name Ignatius of St Paul. The book is dedicated to his old director in the order. That director had found the Anglo-Irish province a handful and made it a host.

The life traces a strange road for an English lord's son. Spencer gave up rank and ease for the Roman faith and a hard rule. He worked for the conversion of England, as his order saw it. His letters and journal let him tell much of the tale himself.
51571-subject-to-change:
Subject to Change is a short tale set on the bay town's streets. Ron Goulart wrote it for a star book of the year 1960. Pendleton comes home from two months off and takes a long walk. He walks through the east part of town to the flat of his girl Beth.

The day is warm, and he smiles at the bright shops as he goes. Small busts of the sage stand in row on row in the panes. Torn fate slips crack on the walk as the throng steps past them. Three boys chase a fourth round a nook till he draws Pendleton's eye. An old curio shop with tin troops in its pane stops his walk there. An old man with a white beard steps out of the door to meet him. What Pendleton saw and kept still about weighs on the tale.
51650-innocent-at-large:
