Innocent at Large is a tale of the far days past, by Poul and Karen Anderson. It first ran in a press sheet of tales of the stars in July of nineteen fifty-eight. The front note calls its lead a hayseed man of Mars among sharp men of a big world. He is sure to land in strife, yet worse strife waits if he does not.

The tale opens as a rich girl takes a call in her rooms and drops a date. A fixer begs her to spend the night with his guest from Mars. That guest is on state work with a vast pile of funds to spend. The fixer's pitch sets the con in train, with the girl, the funds, and the wide eyed guest all in play.
5183-the-unexpurgated-case-against-woman:
Sir Almroth E. Wright's 1913 treatise argues against giving women the parliamentary vote in Britain. Its three parts first answer the arguments for suffrage, from natural rights, justice, and taxation. They then present Wright's own case, resting on what he calls woman's disability in physical force, intellect, and public morality. Finally they consider the wider aims of the suffrage movement.

Wright, a distinguished physician, wrote at the height of the suffragette campaign. His book is now read as a document of opposition rather than as a persuasive case. It offers a clear, if dated, view of the arguments suffragists had to defeat before the vote was won.
52410-peace-in-friendship-village:
Zona Gale's Peace in Friendship Village was published by Macmillan in October 1919. Gale, author of Friendship Village and its love stories, gives the tales in the words of Calliope Marsh. She signs a note at Portage, Wisconsin: wherever she has intruded a word of her own, it is with apology. Calliope's closing line runs through the book, that life is something other than what we believe it to be.

Fourteen chapters of village affairs follow: the feast of nations, the story of Jeffro, Nick Nordman coming back home, and being good to Letty. An art and loan dress exhibit, a cable, and the hero coming home fill out the list. A motto from Tarasov, in Ernest Poole's The Village, stands at the front, on the brotherhood those first weeks in Russia revealed.
52609-captain-carey-or-fighting-the-indi:
Captain Carey is a frontier adventure novel by Lieutenant Lounsberry. Its subtitle names the fight at Pine Ridge. McKay of Philadelphia published the book. Street and Smith held the copyright of 1896. Lounsberry also wrote Won at West Point. The tale opens with orders from a post commandant. Carey has won a step in rank and new duty.

Colonel Crandall tells Carey he is to report to General Miles. Carey owes his start to the colonel, he says. A border boy, he was sent to West Point by that patron. Trouble with the Indians is brewing, the colonel warns. Carey's own report has proved right so far. A frontispiece shows a rescue scene with Kit. Dime-novel officers of this kind filled boys' shelves. The Pine Ridge campaign of 1890 gives the tale its ground.
53250-the-golden-age:
The Golden Age is Kenneth Grahame's book of childhood, first copyrighted in 1899. John Lane published this edition in New York and London in 1914, with illustrations in colour by Moony. Grahame, later famous for The Wind in the Willows, here looks back at the world of children from the far side of the gate.

The contents are sketches of a country childhood: a holiday, a white-washed uncle, alarums and excursions, and the finding of the princess. Sawdust and sin, the burglars, a harvesting, and snowbound follow. Later pieces take the children to the Roman road, a secret drawer, and the blue room. A prologue, The Olympians, names the grown-ups as children saw them: remote gods, aunts and uncles rather than parents. Looking back, Grahame writes, he can see that children with a proper equipment of parents would have seen things otherwise.
53268-murder-at-large:
Lesley Frost, editor of Come Christmas, wrote Murder at Large, issued in New York by Coward McCann with copyright in nineteen thirty two. Ordway Belknap is the sleuth, an ex judge of the magistrate courts. He is a detective of amateur standing, on call at the Homicide Department. Chapter one opens in his penthouse den on the East River at Gracie Square. James, his man servant, announces a call.

Judge Whittaker is on the wire, James says in a cotton wool voice. Belknap slowly ground out a fresh lit cigarette and studied the telephone, the tale says. His face gathered seriousness as a window gathers steam. Whittaker had said at the club that he would ring soon on a matter of life and death. Though the matter had slipped his mind, Belknap now hesitated to lift the receiver. Mystery fans get a suave amateur detective novel.
534-an-inland-voyage:
Robert Louis Stevenson recounts a canoe trip through Belgium and France in this early travel book. With his friend Cigarette, Stevenson paddles the Sambre and Oise canals, past Antwerp, Maubeuge, and Noyon, camping, portaging, and dining with canal folk. A preface jokes that a small book needs a large welcome.

Stevenson writes with light, witty prose, keen on rain, inns, and cathedral towns. The voyage is less about distance than about talk and temper on the water. The book charms as a young writer's ramble, where a canoe proves a fine lens for foreign life.
53515-the-mystery-boys-and-captain-kidd-:
The Mystery Boys and Captain Kidds Message, by Van Powell, was published in New York in 1931. The book is one of a series of thrilling stories in far distant lands. Other titles in the set name Inca gold, Chinese jewels, and Hindu treasure.

The tale opens with Nicky and a voodoo woman, then turns to one half of a cipher. A Mystery Boy meeting follows, and the ghost of Captain Kidd. Chapters move on the way to the Keys, to Crocodile Key, and to Black Caesar buccaneers. Sam shows his true colours, one mystery is solved, and modern pirates appear. Readers get a boys adventure of codes, ghosts, pirates, and chase, built for pace and surprise.
53769-floreat-etona-anecdotes-and-memori:
Floreat Etona, anecdotes and memories of Eton College, was written by Ralph Nevill and published by Macmillan in nineteen eleven. Nevill filled the book with stories of the school that educated Britain's rulers. The frontispiece engraves the Great Court of the college.

Nevill thanks Lewis Harcourt for access to a unique collection of Eton books. The Earl of Rosebery also lent prints and volumes. The dedication mourns a dear old Eton friend whose pleasant voices death could not take. Anecdote is the method throughout: masters, boys, customs, and games pass in review. Such school memoirs fed the public image of Eton as a world apart. Nevill writes as an insider preserving a vanishing nineteenth-century Eton for its old boys.
53909-a-short-history-of-newnham-college:
Alice Gardner, once a lecturer and fellow of Newnham College, wrote this short history, published at Cambridge in 1921. Ten illustrations support the text, including a portrait of Henry Sidgwick by Myers. Gardner dedicates the book to the honored memory of two figures named only by initials.

Chapter one treats Newnham in idea, from 1871 to 1880, before the college took shape. Adolescence, from 1880 to 1881, and progress, from 1881 to 1892, follow in her scheme. Newnham was a college for women at Cambridge, and Gardner tells how a bold experiment grew into a lasting institution.
53941-the-theatrocrat-a-tragic-play-of-c:
The Theatrocrat, a tragic play of church and stage by John Davidson, was printed at London by Grant Richards in 1905. Davidson heads the volume with verses To the Generation Knocking at the Door, bidding youth break it open and take the lead. A long prose piece, Wordsworth's Immorality and Mine, argues that poetry is immoral because it will state any and every morality.

Poetry, he says, can sing alike the worship of Aphrodite and of the Virgin, triumph and martyrdom. To be immoral, in his new sense of the word, is simply to be different. Without that difference, he holds, life would rot in place.
54033-when-she-came-home-from-college:
When She Came Home From College is a novel by Hurd and Wilson, published in 1909 with illustrations by George Gibbs. The story begins on the last night of college, in a stripped suite where a set of friends sit dejectedly among packing boxes. One of them, nicknamed the Infant, refuses the mood and demands to know why the crowd cannot smile.

Diplomas are hidden in the tops of the trunks, and tomorrow the friends scatter to the four corners of the United States. The contents promise the real subject after graduation: home, the theory and practice of philosophy, a character called the Idgit, applied philanthropy, real trouble and the end of the interregnum. The book follows its heroine from college into the harder curriculum of the family home.
54214-a-story-of-the-golden-age:
James Baldwin wrote A Story of the Golden Age, illustrated by Howard Pyle. Charles Scribner's Sons published it at New York; the copyrights run from 1887, this printing from 1927. The book stands in the Heroes of the Olden Time line. A front plate shows Pyrrhus finding Philoctetes in a cave. Baldwin dedicated the volume to May. His fore word addresses the reader who has heard of Homer but never read him.

No one knows whether Homer made the Iliad and Odyssey, or many poets did, Baldwin says. The poems begin in the midst of things. His book is no simplified version, he insists. The way to read Homer is to read Homer, in Greek or in a true translation. Bryant, Derby, Chapman, and Butcher and Lang get his praise. His story paves the way to that reading.
5430-preface-to-a-dictionary-of-the-engl:
Samuel Johnson wrote this preface for his great Dictionary of the English Language, published in the mid-eighteenth century. He begins with the lonely labor of the dictionary-maker, a worker driven more by fear of failure than hope of praise, and considered a servant of learning rather than its master. The preface explains what he set out to do and why the task was so hard.

Johnson defends his choices about spelling, meaning, and usage, admitting where the language resisted order. Readers get both a window into eighteenth-century English and a famous piece of literary prose. It remains the best short introduction to how one man tried to fix a living language in print.
54943-how-to-teach-a-foreign-language:
Otto Jespersen, who taught English at the University of Copenhagen, wrote a guide to teaching a foreign tongue, turned from Danish into English by Sophia Bertelsen. Swan Sonnenschein brought it out in London in 1904, with Macmillan in New York. Jespersen was known as a sound scholar of speech sounds.

Press praise on the front pages hails Jespersen as a clear thinker who sees with his own eyes. One paper calls his work a new start in the study of tongues, far from the dry tone of most such books. His guide brings that same fresh eye to how a new tongue should be taught in class.
54955-the-suffragette-the-history-of-the:
Sylvia Pankhurst writes The Suffragette, a history of the militant suffrage movement from 1905 to 1910. The book came out in New York in 1911. A front plate shows Pankhurst at work on decorations for the Prince's Skating Rink.

Plates show Christabel Pankhurst and Annie Kenney side by side. One shows the first suffrage rally in Trafalgar Square, on May 19, 1906, with Keir Hardie at the stand. One shows women who sell Votes for Women in Kingsway. One shows Mrs Pankhurst with a petition for the prime minister. Pankhurst writes as a chief actor in the fight, and her tale is both record and plea.
55257-at-close-range:
Hopkinson Smith published a book of stories at New York in 1905, opening with a letter to his readers about the magnifying glass on his writing table. With it, he says, he deciphers at close range the cutting of intaglios, the brush-marks on miniatures, and the fusings in a Samurai sword-guard. At the same range he tries the minds and hearts that cross his nomadic path.

Tenderness hides behind suspected cruelty, he finds, and the joy of giving forces through crusts of pretended avarice. At the bottom of almost every heart-crucible a drop of gold can be found. Nine stories follow the theory: a night out, an extra blanket, a medal of honor, the rajah of Bungpore, and a pot of jam among them.
55463-owen-clancy-s-run-of-luck-or-the-m:
Burt L Standish wrote a boys' weekly story for the New Tip Top Weekly, copyrighted in 1914 by Street and Smith and sold at five cents a copy. The weekly calls itself an ideal publication for the American youth. Subscription terms run from sixty five cents for three months to two dollars fifty for a year. Owen Clancy, the motor wizard, takes his run of luck in a garage setting.

Street and Smith built the Tip Top line around Frank Merriwell, Standish's creation. Owen Clancy carried the formula into the motor age. Garage adventure replaced the diamond and gridiron for a new generation. Weekly numbers like this one reached boys by mail across the country.
55571-whom-god-hath-joined-a-question-of:
Whom God Hath Joined, a novel by Fergus Hume, reached a third edition at London in 1894. Hume had won his name with The Mystery of a Hansom Cab. His new book takes marriage itself as its question. A wife and mother, he warns, serves two masters, and woe follows when she loves one side to the shutting out of the other.

Forty chapters track two friends, a honeymoon that wanes and a bride brought home. Husband and wife each get a chapter told from their own side. Gossip, fascination and an undesirable acquaintance press the pair. The death of the first-born and a last temptation bring the marriage to its test.
55837-the-rainbow-bridge:
Frances Margaret Fox tells a child's story in The Rainbow Bridge, from W A Wilde of Boston and Chicago, copyrighted in 1905, with pictures by Frank T Merrill. Its heroine is Marian Lee, and the contents follow her growth: a little pilgrim begins a journey, her first day in school, a new home, and a diary. Diphtheria and a botany professor mark the later chapters.

The tale opens at the Home for Little Pilgrims, where Mrs Moore runs the nursery by strict rule and never rocks the babies. Then comes the night she rocks one: Marian, six months old, eyes wide open, compelling kindness.
56308-when-i-was-your-age:
Laura Richards wrote When I Was Your Age, a book of family memories issued at Boston in 1894. She had also written Captain January, Melody, and Queen Hildegarde. The book is given to the dear and honored memory of her father, Samuel Gridley Howe. A poem at the front praises him as God's servant against tyranny and wrong. He is a warrior who could stoop like an angel to raise the fainting.

The chapters treat ourselves, Green Peace, the valley, our father, Julia Ward, our mother, our teachers, our friends, and our guests. Pictures show the young Julia Ward, Julia Ward Howe, and Richards herself. The book tells how the Howe household lived and learned, through the eyes of a child of that famed family. It gives young readers a warm view of a great reformer's home from inside.
56316-the-campaign-round-lie-ge:
J M Kennedy wrote The Campaign Round Liège as volume four of the Daily Telegraph War Books, published in London in 1914 with an introduction by W L Courtney. The series sold in cloth at a shilling. Publisher copy calls this volume the key book to the military situation.

Chapters open with the outbreak of war, the invasion of Belgium and Luxemburg, and the first fighting at Liège. French troops join the Belgians, German spies and uhlan raids appear, and the battle of Haelen follows. Later chapters move to life at Brussels and the capital's removal to Antwerp. Readers get instant history of the war's first weeks, written while the defence of Liège was still news.
56527-in-a-quiet-village:
Baring Gould published this set of village tales in London in 1900, and it was reprinted within a month. Dan'l Coombe opens the contents, followed by Timothy Slouch and Doble Drewe in the list. Mary Trembath, an old post-boy and a figure called simply Auntie come next among the village folk.

Brother Augustine, Haroun the carpenter, Shone Evans and Henry Frost fill the middle of the book. A bride's well, a plum-pudding, a Christmas tree and folk-prayers add custom and season to the sketches. Old Dan'l, the first portrait, was a character indeed and a mystery for many years in the telling.
56620-ruby-roland-the-girl-spy-or-simon-: Ruby Roland, the Girl Spy is number 282 of Beadle's Dime Novels, in the semi-monthly novels series from Beadle and Adams of New York. Its second title names her protector: Simon Kenton's protégé, the great Kentucky scout of the frontier wars. The hosted pages carry the cover and the publisher's notice for the next number, The Lone Chief, a tale of the Saskatchewan trappers. A girl spy on the border, under Kenton's wing, is the whole promise of the number: scouts, danger, and a heroine in the fight.
56719-mimi-s-marriage:
Mimi’s Marriage is a Russian novel by Mikoulitch, turned into English by Hagberg Wright and issued at London in 1915. The author’s Russian name, Lidia Ivanovna Veselitskaya, stands on the title page. An introduction by the translator opens the book. The heroine is called Mimotchka in the tale itself.

Mimotchka is engaged, the first line announces to the reader. This time, it seems, she is engaged in earnest at last. Relations crowd in with congratulations, visits, and presents. Aunts question her on the details of her trousseau. Uncles tease her with their best wishes and their jokes. She blushes slightly and casts down her innocent looking eyes. The comedy of a Russian engagement fills the opening scene.
56819-the-babes-in-the-basket-or-daph-an:
A tale for the young fills this volume: The Babes in the Basket, or Daph and Her Charge. It was printed at New York in 1859, by the author of Timid Lucy and Heart and Hand. A frontispiece names its picture The Little Exiles. Fifteen chapters follow Daph's charge, from A Moonlight Visitor through strange proceedings and home scenes to a basket overturned and the end.

Chapter one sets the scene more than sixty years before, in a quiet room on a southern island. Moonlight pours through wide, shuttered windows onto a bare polished floor, where two fair children sleep in curtained beds like birds in cages. A cautious step sounds in the hall, and a short, strong woman with a black face and a gay turban stands in the moonlight. It is Daph, on a secret errand.
5706-time-and-change:
John Burroughs reflects on nature, science, and faith in Time and Change, published in Boston and New York in 1912. His preface warns readers plainly that the volume holds more hard science and scientific speculation than spiritual comfort, as if offering a stone where bread was asked. Essays that follow weigh what changing knowledge does to old beliefs about the natural world.

Burroughs writes as a field observer turned thinker, grounding large questions in birds, seasons, and country walks. Readers who enjoy nature writing with a philosophical edge will find calm, clear prose and honest doubt. The book appeals to those who want to see how a naturalist of his generation faced new science without giving up wonder at the living world.
57382-my-chinese-marriage:
My Chinese Marriage, by MTF, is the true story of an American woman who married a Chinese student and went to live in China. It was published in London in 1922 and is dedicated to her Chinese father and mother.

The narrator first sees Chan-King Liang on the opening day of college in her small American town. He is the new Chinese student, come to study international law and political science, and he lodges next door. Four long chapters carry the story: In America, In Shanghai, First Daughter-in-Law, and The Eternal Hills. The book follows the courtship, the voyage, and the wife's hard lessons in her new home. It stands as a rare plain account of such a marriage told from inside.
57592-love-and-marriage:
Love and Marriage is a treatise by Ellen Key, translated from the Swedish by Arthur Chater and published by Putnam of New York and London in 1911. Key had earlier written The Century of the Child. Havelock Ellis supplied a critical and biographical introduction, and the book reached a ninth printing.

The publishers' note frames the subject. The relations of the sexes, the state's control of them, and the family as the foundation of society have drawn Plato, Rousseau, Wollstonecraft, Mill, and Ibsen, among others. No writer, the note admits, has given solutions all can accept. Key, a veteran Swedish reformer, writes with her own conclusions plainly stated. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
57688-red-ben-the-fox-of-oak-ridge:
Joseph Wharton Lippincott wrote and drew a nature story in 1919 about a red fox called Red Ben. The setting is the pine barrens of New Jersey, where farms press deeper each year. Chapters follow the coming of the red fox, the den, and Ben learning to hunt. Other woodsfolk, from squirrels to a muskrat, share the pages.

A gray fox, a long chase, and Ben alone come in turn. Later chapters have Ben studying the enemy and travelling far. Blackie, another fox, enters late in the story. Freedom Is Sweet and Home Again close the book. Lippincott renders tracks and small beasts in his own drawings.
57812-scotland-in-pagan-times-the-iron-a:
The Rhind Lectures in Archaeology for 1881 take up Scotland in pagan times, and this set treats the Iron Age. David Douglas of Edinburgh published the lectures, with sellers in London, Cambridge, Glasgow, and Aberdeen. A plate of the Broch of Clickamin, near Lerwick in Shetland, fronts the book.

The lecturer says he took the post for two years so he could deal with the pagan past of Scotland in full. This series digs into the remains of the Iron Age alone. The Bronze Age and Stone Age wait for the next series. Brochs, forts, and buried goods supply the proof, read with care. The lectures give a first map of a Scotland before written records.
58035-andrew-jackson-s-hermitage:
Mary French Caldwell wrote the tale of Andrew Jackson's home, the Hermitage, in a form dated 1949. The Ladies Hermitage Association of Nashville put out the book, first in 1933, to guard the famed house. A first note by jurist John DeWitt praises her search of old deeds and home records.

From first log cabin to grand house of the old South, the home frames the wild career of Old Hickory. Kin by blood and by wedlock, close friends, land deals, and builds and rebuilds all get fresh light. Warmth of home life with Rachel at his side is the heart of the small, fond book.
58199-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
An index volume gathering the tables of contents of Charlotte Yonge's works as issued by Project Gutenberg, compiled by David Widger. More than sixty titles are listed, from The Heir of Redclyffe and The Daisy Chain to A Book of Golden Deeds.

The contents are reproduced volume by volume. Heartsease shows its three parts; The Pillars of the House takes two volumes; Dynevor Terrace likewise. Histories stand beside the novels: Young Folks' History of Rome, a history of France, and Cameos from English History. There are storybooks for the young, like Little Lucy's Wonderful Globe, and a life of Bishop Patteson. Readers get the whole shelf of the great Victorian family novelist mapped at once.
58650-introduction-to-the-study-of-the-h:
Introduction to the Study of the History of Language is a textbook by Strong, Logeman, and Wheeler, printed at London and New York in 1891. Strong taught Latin at University College, Liverpool. Logeman headed a school at Rock Ferry, and Wheeler taught Greek at Cornell. Twenty-three chapters map the science of language.

The book opens with how language grows, then how it splits into kinds. Sound change, shifts in word meaning, and analogy follow. Later chapters treat syntax, word formation, and the parts of speech. The final chapters cover mixture of languages and the standard language. Strong states the field's task: to explain how language moves from its earliest stage to its latest.
58660-pussy-and-her-language:
Pussy and Her Language is a study of cats and their speech by Marvin Clark. A bound in essay claims a great find in the tongue of cats by a French man. Rights date the work to the year eighteen ninety five. Parts open with a bold claim: it was the cat that did the deed.

Tales of cats who know house secrets and keep long recall fill first parts. Signs, sounds, and the roots of speech earn their own heads in the list. A Paris home for stray cats gets a warm part of its own in the book. The close claims the cat tops all four foot beasts in keen mind. Fond lore and bold claims mix in this odd cat shelf book.
58909-the-hastings-road-and-the-happy-sp:
The Hastings Road and the Happy Springs of Tunbridge belongs to a long series of English road histories by the same author. Earlier volumes traced the Portsmouth, Dover, Bath, Exeter, and Brighton roads, and the Great North Road to Scotland. Each book follows one old highway through its history, fashion, and folly.

This volume takes the road from London to Hastings, with the spa town of Tunbridge Wells on the way. A frontispiece shows the entrance to Hastings by Minnis Rock and the old London road. In the age of the stage-coach and mail, such roads carried trade, news, and pleasure seekers to the springs. The series, part history and part travel book, records coaching England just as the motor car began to end it.
58953-heritage:
Sackville West published Heritage with the Doran Company of New York in 1919, dedicating the novel to her mother. An epigraph from Caxton, about learning his English in the Weald of Kent, stands at the front.

The narrator spent two years in a rough gray village of the Apennines, Sampiero della Vigna Vecchia, tilted up a hillside around a little piazza with its civic palace and church. There, to study Italian, he lodged in the same house as a man named Malory. The two were companions but never friends, each sure their last day in the village would part them for good. Yet a story Malory told one evening under the stone-pines linked their lives, at long intervals, for many years. The novel unfolds from that telling.
59042-the-stock-exchange:
Charles Duguid, city editor of the Daily Mail, wrote a short guide to the London Stock Exchange, first issued in 1904. The copy here is the third edition, from 1913, in a series of books on business. Duguid sets out to show what the Exchange is and how its work gets done.

Chapters treat the market place, the members and their clerks, and the rule of the committee. He goes on to brokers and jobbers, the settling of accounts, option dealing, and the goods the market trades. A sketch of its past and a broker's day close the book. Plain readers and new clerks alike can follow his clear steps.
59386-the-history-of-human-marriage:
Edward Westermarck, lecturer on sociology at the University of Finland at Helsingfors, wrote The History of Human Marriage. Macmillan printed the third edition at London in 1901; the first had come in 1891. Alfred Wallace wrote a short note of introduction.

Wallace calls the book a thorough and philosophic treatment of hard problems in anthropology. Darwin, Spencer, Morgan, and Lubbock had agreed on many points, he notes, and students took their accord for settled science. Westermarck reached opposite conclusions on several of them after full study of the facts. His account of the widespread bar on marriage between near kin wins Wallace's special praise.
59616-a-little-knowledge:
Russ Winterbotham wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Worlds of If in December 1956. Its head note says Earthmen were considered stupid, but they knew something the alien did not, about his own planet. Even with modern conveniences, the tale opens, Caesar could never have staged such a triumph as Olbu's visit to Earth. The visit is a bigger deal for the archives than anything Caesar did.

Ralph Rodkey of the Interstate Broadcasting Network commends the visitor for being a good sport. Winterbotham wrote pulp science fiction and newspaper comics. The title's proverb warns both sides. A little knowledge, in his tale, cuts against the smug alien as much as the Earthmen.
59902-natalie-page:
Katharine Haviland Taylor wrote Natalie Page, a girl's novel copyrighted in 1921. Natalie tells her own story, and the first chapter explains her memory. The scenes around great events, she says, stay clearer with the years than the events themselves.

She remembers a big four-posted bed and a room of crying people. Someone lifted her up to kiss the woman on the bed. She does not remember how the woman looked, and the woman was her mother. The contents carry her forward: good-byes, and New York and a new home. A second bracelet and strange noises build the mystery. Evelyn blames her, and heart affairs follow Christmas fun. Late chapters turn to detective work. Girls of 1921 got a motherless heroine and a puzzle in bracelets.
60044-against-this-age:
Maxwell Bodenheim gathered these poems under a fighting title, Against This Age. Boni and Liveright printed the book at New York in 1923. Bodenheim gave it to Fedya and Minna, whom he calls four eyes within a blind world.

Some poems had run in The Century, The Dial, The Nation, and Harper's Magazine before this. Baby opens the list, then Nightmare and Something Delicate. Titles run short and sharp, in the new manner of the 1920s. Bodenheim was a loud voice of the Greenwich Village set, and his verse here takes aim at the age itself, as the title swears. Small magazines of the day gave him his first stage.
60195-the-coming-ice-age:
C A M Taber wrote The Coming Ice Age, a short work put out at Boston in 1896. Two maps front the book. They show how ice sheets and bergs spread in a past ice age, and how they lie now. Winds and the great flows of the sea are marked on both maps.

Taber says the book grows from a small work of 1894 on the cause of warm and cold spans. That work won the praise of men of rock lore and of teachers. He then gave the theme a year of fresh study. New finds, he says, bore out his views. Age and weak health kept him to the main lines of the case. He casts himself as a scout on a new road, not as its last guide.
6030-the-iron-star-and-what-it-saw-on-it:
John Preston True invites girls and boys and their elders to follow an Iron Star across the ages, from myth to history. His preface calls the world a wonderful place, grown day by day and century by century a little better worth living in, like a fairy story with the advantage of being true.

None of us saw the world's beginning, True admits, but scholars have worked the problem backward through the years. Starting from a good dry spot and following the star's wanderings, readers stay near the truth of how people lived long ago. The book teaches history as a journey, not a list.
60303-the-bridge:
Revelle's short story comes from Worlds of If Science Fiction for August 1957, and it puts Captain Alfred Lowary in charge of a great steel bridge in wartime. Jets scream overhead as his convoy halts beside the six-lane span. He posts his three platoons with care: one across the river, one in reserve, and one in defense on his own side. Machine guns cover a bend in the road with cross-fire.

His orders, read four times from a yellow sheet, never change, and they leave him sick at the stomach. No one gets on the bridge, he tells his officers, and Lieutenant Meyers asks the question the others avoid. Are they supposed to shoot their own people? Lowary answers that they are, if they have to. The tale hangs on that order and on the frightened souls who will test it.
6055-the-bobbsey-twins-at-snow-lodge:
Laura Lee Hope sends the Bobbsey twins to Snow Lodge for winter holidays, opening with runaways and a question from little Flossie: will Snap pull them, and give a good ride? Freddie, fastening the big shaggy dog to his sled with a homemade harness, answers with wisdom that Snap pulled fine on trial.

Chapters follow old Mr. Carford, a big snowball, an accusation, the story of Snow Lodge, unwelcome news, a snow slide, and lost children in the woods. Snap goes missing, a big storm hits, a tree falls, and missing money appears. The twins' winter adventure mixes snow play with a small mystery.
60608-satellite-passage:
Satellite Passage is a tale by Theodore Thomas from Worlds of If magazine. The tale ran in the October 1958 issue of that science sheet. Three men bend over a chart and compute an orbit once more. Their satellite will pass within fifty feet of the other satellite. Too close, Morgan judges, and the question is whether to move.

Kaufman says nothing and McNary snorts at the thought of moving aside. If moving is to be done, let them do it, Morgan agrees. A curious blend of anger and exhilaration stirs faint in him then. His pencil snaps in his fingers as he stares at the chart. They plan to take fresh readings as the other satellite nears. Five minutes would serve for the new reckoning before the pass. The Russians would milk any retreat dry, Morgan says at last.
61263-cultural-exchange:
Keith Laumer wrote Cultural Exchange, printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction for September 1962. Second Secretary Magnan is leaving Retief in charge of the office for two weeks. He takes his green-lined cape and orange-feathered beret from the clothes tree. He hopes Retief can run the routine without unfortunate incidents. When Magnan first came, the libraries and education division was a shambles, he says. He questions the wisdom of leaving so sensitive a desk to Retief.

The business at hand is a student exchange with the Bogans. Two thousand Bogan students are going to the industrial world of d'Land. The Bogans, hoodlums of the Nicodemean Cluster, have launched four military campaigns in twenty years. The exchange may channel their aggressions into culture, Magnan hopes. Breaking and entering, Retief answers.
61424-the-customs-lounge:
The Customs Lounge is a science fiction story by Proulx. It first appeared in Worlds of If in September 1963. The scene is a lounge for customs inspectors of many worlds. Inspectors trade tales while waiting for their shifts. Bad lukewarm kasser is the standing joke of the service. Old Grag tells of a find from his young days.

Venus travellers once carried sweets stuffed with contraband. The young one chewed too much and too loud, Grag says. He took a sweet and made a fine seizure. A promotion came out of that small catch. Inspector Flimp then tops the tale with one of his own. Shiploads of bewildered Earth folk crowd his memory. The story plays border control for comedy. Alien manners meet a very human office humour.
61507-ukridge:
Ukridge, issued by Herbert Jenkins at London in 1924, collects Wodehouse's tales of Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, a man for ever on the edge of a fortune. Wodehouse dedicates the book to Bill Townend, who first brought the two together. The contents also hold Ukridge's Accident Syndicate and No Wedding Bells for Him.

Ukridge counts his thousands before they are made. One scheme is a dog college; another backs Battling Billson, the tender-hearted pugilist, through his début, his return and his exit. Hope and his friend George Tupper keep him afloat between ventures. In the first tale he urges the narrator to write his life, promising they will clean up at least fifty thousand pounds apiece.
61908-scott-burton-in-the-blue-ridge:
Edward Cheyney wrote this forestry adventure. Appleton published it at New York and London under a 1924 copyright, as the fifth of his Scott Burton stories, after Scott Burton, Forester, and Scott Burton, Logger. A frontispiece shows a driver struggling desperately to hold his team.

Chapter one opens in a quiet New England house, where Scott sits absorbed in thought while his father asks about his new assignment. Scott has his sailing orders, but he frowns over them: a timber sales job far from home, in the Blue Ridge country. Twenty-nine chapters follow him into an old feud's rumblings, with characters named Old Jarred and Hopwood, a mystery of two stores, bids for a contract, and a trip to Washington. A moonshine still, an attempt at arson, and a ride after the marshal build to the end of the feud.
61925-challenge:
Sackville-West wrote the novel Challenge, published in New York by George Doran. The book opens with a ball in a London house, watched from a balustrade by a man and a woman in her forties. Diamonds sit in her hair and pearls hang over her shoulders. He points out the famous guests on the staircase and flatters himself that she might grace his own house.

Among the guests climbs a tall, dark man with his wife. He tells her the man's record: under-secretary at thirty-five, in the Cabinet before forty, tipped by many as the next Viceroy. Yet when the man looks up, the woman is startled by his face, which seems to have learnt all the sorrow of the world. Her companion shrugs: the man has power, wealth, and an admirable wife. Readers get a society novel that opens by asking what success costs.
62050-foreign-exchange:
Robert Owen, a United States senator from Oklahoma, wrote Foreign Exchange in nineteen nineteen. Owen led the Senate group on banks and money, and his short book says war has left the American dollar cheap in lands that took no side in the fight. Yet the United States sold far more than it bought in those years.

Owen gives a case from Spain, where the dollar buys far fewer pesetas than its gold worth, and he blames high charges by banks that lend and swap funds in war time. His fix is a Federal Reserve foreign bank to keep the dollar at par. He aims the book at bankers and at firms that buy and sell across seas.
62224-the-great-thames-barrage: The Great Thames Barrage sets out a plan to dam the river Thames with a great barrier. A drawing at the front shows the proposed work as it would look from the Gravesend bank. The book came out in the orbit of Public Works, a London magazine on government and town projects, run by the editor of The Surveyor and Municipal and County Engineer. Readers get the case for a huge river work, shown in print and pictures, from the age when such schemes filled the press.
62278-a-son-of-courage:
Archie McKishnie wrote A Son of Courage, published at Chicago with copyright in 1920. McKishnie also wrote Love of the Wild and Willow, the Wisp. He dedicates the book to his sister Jean Blewitt, who knew and loved its characters. A frontispiece shows a girl exclaiming over something lovely.

Twenty-six chapters open with Billy Wilson's strategy and a shower of fish. A new teacher is appraised, a message arrives by a bird called Croaker, and a wilderness merchant appears. A rabbit foot charm, a menagerie moved, and Lost Man's Swamp follow. Erie of the lighthouse and Billy to the rescue build the close. Readers get a Canadian backwoods boy's book.
62336-master-rockafellar-s-voyage:
Master Rockafellar's Voyage is a sea tale for boys by Clark Russell, first published in 1890 and given here in its fifth edition of 1913. Gordon Browne drew its twenty-seven illustrations. The chapter heads tell the tale in the boy's own voice. He begs to go to sea. He spends his first day on board ship. He sails from Gravesend, goes aloft, and sights a ship. In time he is struck by lightning. The form is a first-person log of a lad's first voyage.

The Rockafellars are an old sea family, the boy tells us. A portrait of Ebenezer Rockafellar, a rear admiral of the age of George the Second, hung in the dining room at home. The boy's birth and blood call him to the sea. Russell was the great sea writer of his age for boys and men alike. His tales mix true seamanship with high adventure.
62978-neighbourhood-a-year-s-life-in-and:
Neighbourhood traces a year's life in and about an English village. Tickner Edwardes wrote the book after The Lore of the Honey-Bee. Dutton of New York brought this copy out in the year 1912. Eight pictures stand through the month-by-month account of village days. The year opens with January frost, wild life, and a late thaw.

Shepherd families, dew-ponds, and the starling host fill the winter part. February brings the village green at daybreak and the coming lambs. March adds the woodland clearing, the rain bird, and the old ferryman. April sings with the first cuckoo, bluebells, swallows, and nightingales. Bees and primroses share that spring chapter with rain and shine. Edwardes watches downs, rivers, and lanes as the seasons turn round. Church feasts and cottage nights mark the high points of the year.
63502-torn-sails-a-tale-of-a-welsh-villa:
Torn Sails is a tale of a Welsh village by Allen Raine. Appleton of New York held the rights and printed it in 1898. Raine had writ Mifanwy and A Welsh Singer before this village tale. Seventeen chapters run from Mwntseison to the mill in the moonlight. A Welsh verse heads the book, turned into English below it.

I love her golden shores, her mountains bare, the verse sings out. Hugh Morgan, Mari Vone, and Owen's bidding fill the early chapters. Traeth-y-daran, changes, and a wedding call carry the village year on. Gwen's rebellion and Hugh's suspicions darken the mid part of it. The storm and torn sails give the book its title and crisis. Peace and the mill in moonlight close the Welsh tale out. The Gwendraeth river runs through the village to Cardigan Bay.
63813-in-his-image:
In His Image, by Bryce Walton, ran in Planet Stories in the winter of 1948. Its tag sets the scene: vast forms stand on the hills, proof against all harm, and slay the vermin that crawl below. Jon runs down a long hall and falls at the feet of the Old Man, in one cave of a vast hid warren. He has seen them: the Mechs. The Old Man warns that if the Mechs find the caves, they will probe men out like grubs and burn them with red-ray eyes.

Jon has been up top twice and will not grub in the dark any more. The Old Man lets him go on one term: never come back. As far as he knows, this cave holds the last men alive. Space fans get a grim tale of man's heirs.
63898-women-children-love-and-marriage:
Women, Children, Love and Marriage is a set of essays by Hartley, author of past books on the truth about woman and on mothers and sons. It came out at London in the mid nineteen twenties. A quote at its head, from a famed novel of the age, frames its blunt stance.

We will not face the world as we have made it, that quote says. We will not face our own souls as we find them, nor take the blame that is ours. We will get no where, it holds, till we stand man to man and face all out, break the old forms, and keep our pride and nerve whole. The essays then take women first: their ways, a land of the south, a hard age of life, and a mothers place in law.
63980-1970-a-vision-of-the-coming-age:
John Collins wrote this poem of a vision of the year 1970. The poem was printed at Burlington, New Jersey, in 1870. The speaker muses alone on a hot June afternoon in shade. Bees hum, crickets tire, and flowers lose scent in fierce sun.

He fancies he hears all words sent along the telegraph wires near him. Stock prices, wrongs, weddings, and death bed calls stream past in verse. A Japan merchant orders teas and asks for Bibles in return. A Boston lady orders oranges from a Cuban friend by wire. John Collins set his dream tale in rhymed verse.
64167-a-sentimental-practical-guide-to-a:
A Sentimental and Practical Guide to Amesbury and Stonehenge was compiled by Lady Antrobus and issued from the estate office at Amesbury. Its preface, signed at Amesbury Abbey in 1900, admits a departure from ordinary guide book lines. Photographs by Clarisse Miles illustrate the book, and this copy belongs to the tenth thousand.

The route leaves Salisbury by the upper road across bleak downs. Old Sarum stands two miles out: a bare hill ringed with entrenchments, once crowded with buildings and among the most important places in the island. Amesbury itself, eight miles from Salisbury, boasts shops, the telegraph, and a coming railway station. In earlier times it was celebrated for tobacco pipes marked with a gauntlet, specimens of which rest in the Salisbury museum.
64827-yesterday-s-revenge:
Yesterday's Revenge is a science fiction story by Nichols, taken from Comet magazine for January 1941. It opens with a roll of future wars. Years and decades of slaughter, hate, and retrogression pass: the World War, the War of the Wings, the War of the Rockets. Then came the Pacifist War, and the World Revolution drowning in its own blood. At last comes peace, the Peace of Fear.

In that peace cities rose again and great ships plied the seas, but the ground was soaked with the blood of lost generations. Bitter hate lived in the hearts of the men who rebuilt civilization's forms without its spirit, driven by the lash, the torture chamber, and the purge. The focus of all this hatred was the Master, Protector of the Peace, betrayer and dictator of the world. A passage preserved in the copy tells his rise.
64857-the-old-mill-and-the-covered-bridg:
Two landmarks of early American life, the water-powered grist mill and the covered bridge, are the subjects of the hosted text. Photos show an overshot wheel at Carillon Park and a bridge once used daily near Dayton, Ohio. That bridge spanned Little Sugar Creek, ran fifty-five feet long, and was fourteen feet wide.

Inside, the text argues that the grist mill marched with the pioneer and may have come before the saw mill in new settlements. Covered bridges carried troops in wartime and wagon trains moving west and south. Readers get a fond, plain account of how both structures were built, how they worked, and why the few that survive still matter.
66341-the-mystery-of-the-deserted-villag:
Elbert M Hoppenstedt wrote a boys' mystery novel in 1960 for Franklin Watts, dedicated to Richard. Ronnie is sliding down hay piles in the barn loft when a big black sedan arrives. A man in a business suit carries a briefcase to the farmhouse door. Ronnie knows why he has come, and his heart sinks.

The St Lawrence Seaway needs part of the Rorth farm land. Worse, it needs the part where a deserted village lies. Once the dam is built, river water will pile up over that low ground. The novel runs to eighteen chapters. It sets a boy's attachment to a lost village against a great public work.
66565-child-life-and-sex-hygiene-a-remar:
Child Life and Sex Hygiene, A Remarkable Message, by Otterbein Smith, copyright 1912, is an address by a pastor and lecturer on modern psychics. A section of the Women's Club of Pierre, South Dakota, first heard it and asked that it be printed. Smith dedicates the book to his mother.

His foreword says twenty years of study stand behind his striking claims about the sex life of children and young people. He defines sex hygiene as sex health and urges parents to wake to hidden dangers. The book is a period piece of the purity movement, earnest, alarmed, and sure that plain talk protects the young.
66613-the-last-plunge:
Sackett wrote The Last Plunge, a science fiction tale first printed in Imagination in October 1955. A headnote states the theme: grant the need for money, and a man will do any dangerous job; Borgmann was such a man. The opening sets the riddle. At about ninety degrees from absolute zero it is not hot, even with the sun shining all day. The place is Uranus, in its arctic circle.

Nils Borgmann, however, is sweating, for the heating unit on his space suit works badly. He needs money badly; he has a wife and seven children. Lowered by cable from a raft over the murk, he asks to be let down a little farther. A big white shape moves dimly below, an air lion. He fires, but the hide is so tough that a shot must land under the ribs or through the eye to kill.
66794-the-heritage:
The Heritage, a novel by Sydney Grier in the Balkan series, had reached a fourth edition by 1908. Blackwood published it at Edinburgh and London in that year. A prologue opens at nightfall in a leafless beech forest on a spur of the Balkans. Thin snow lies frozen on the rocky ground as the scene sets.

Chapter heads promise practical politics, revolution, and a rival heir at the start. A stern parent, two diplomatists, and the call of the red gods raise the heat. Later come a baptism of fire, a tower, and consuls to the rescue in haste. A contested election and the wages of unrighteousness close the list of turns. Grier wrote many tales of Balkan courts and British agents in that restless region.
6695-tales-of-the-jazz-age:
F. Scott Fitzgerald gathers his Jazz Age tales in a 1922 Scribner volume, with a table that groups them as My Last Flappers and other sets. The Jelly-Bean, a Southern story set in Tarleton, Georgia, drew scolding letters from all over the South, Fitzgerald notes with affection for his town. Each tale first ran in magazines like Vanity Fair, Metropolitan, and Smart Set.

Flappers, jelly-beans, and bright young folk move through parties, love affairs, and sudden falls. Fitzgerald writes with a lyric ease that made his name. Tales of the Jazz Age is a sparkling, bittersweet set, capturing the 1920s at their gayest and most hollow.
66958-the-last-fight-of-the-revenge:
Last Fight of the Revenge retells a sea battle of the year 1591. Sir Walter Raleigh wrote the core account of that fight in his age. Henry Newbolt adds an introduction to frame the tale for readers. Frank Brangwyn drew the illustrations for the 1908 London edition. A Bacon quote on the command of the sea fronts the book.

One English ship, the Revenge, fought a vast Spanish fleet alone. Sir Richard Grenville commanded her in that last, hopeless stand. Early pages give praise from past writers for Raleigh's prose. Plates show Queen Elizabeth on the Golden Hind and galleons in port. The text itself starts at page 61, after facsimile and preface.
67088-why-go-to-college:
Clayton Sedgwick Cooper asked Why Go to College in a book published in nineteen twelve. Cooper had earlier written College Men and the Bible. He gave this book to his college teacher and friend, E Benjamin Andrews.

Chapters weigh the general traits of colleges and a pick-and-mix style of study. The campus itself gets a full chapter, then the reasons for going. A last chapter sets the college man in the wider world. Pictures show the chapel at West Point, gates at Harvard, and halls at Yale and Princeton. Student waiters, stage plays, and the Lampoon staff add life.
67229-an-art-shop-in-greenwich-village:
An Art Shop in Greenwich Village is a short story by Ray Cummings. A narrator steps into a dim little shop lit by a lurid red glow on one side and a faint amber light above. Slovenly display cases, unframed paintings, and shelves crowded with curios fill the room.

A little old man greets him with offers. An ivory chess figure, carved by the Moors, is dusted on a coat sleeve and praised. The visitor says he lived a year in Spain, and the shopkeeper's dragged foot follows him down the room. Granada, the old man's birthplace, comes up at once. Cummings, a pulp writer, builds his tale on the shop's buried secret. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
67472-how-to-pick-a-mate-the-guide-to-a-:
Dr Clifford R Adams and Vance O Packard wrote a guide to picking a mate. E P Dutton and Company issued How to Pick a Mate in New York in 1946. Adams taught psychology and ran a marriage counsel service at Pennsylvania State College. The authors gave the book to their two daughters and two sons.

Twenty chapters ask why marry, how to tell love from a passing fire, and what traits count. Tests let readers rate charm, calm, and trust in a mate and in the self. Warnings name nine risky types and folk who should not wed at all. Couples of the time got blunt, test-based counsel.
67517-apes-and-monkeys-their-life-and-la:
Apes and Monkeys: Their Life and Language is a work of natural study by Garner, with an introduction by Edward Everett Hale. Ginn and Company published it in Boston and London in 1900. Garner spent years among monkeys and apes in the African jungle, testing whether their cries amount to speech.

Early chapters compare the skulls of monkeys, apes, and men, then turn to the phonograph, with which Garner took the first records of monkey speech. Named animals fill the middle of the book: Jennie, Pedro, and five little brown monkeys, then Nellie, who was his guest. Long sections follow his chimpanzees Moses, Aaron, and Elisheba, their characters, illnesses, and deaths. The book ends with the gorilla, its habits, its rule of its troop, and famed captives such as Othello. A new set of signs for writing ape sounds runs through the work.
67765-fighting-king-george:
John McIntyre wrote this boys' tale of the Revolution, copyrighted by Penn at Philadelphia in 1905. Graeber illustrated Tom Deering's adventures against King George for the publisher. How Fort Johnson fell opens the contents at page seven of the tale.

How Tom Deering made a name follows, and how the British ships ran from Charleston. Two men bury a chest of gold, and Tom joins Marion's brigade in the list. Tom fights with Gates at Camden, braves the Tories and holds a staircase, in a Carolina war story of the Swamp Fox's men told for boys.
68280-latent-image:
Wesley Long's story, printed in Astounding Science-Fiction in May 1944, is set on Pluto, where men have built cities with names borrowed from the old underworld. John McBride stands on the roof garden of Satan's Hotel in Hell, looking across the River Styx at Sharon, while the uranium smelters flare over Mephisto. Hell is warm and pleasant, but McBride's wife Enid is nineteen hundred million miles away, at a lens station in deep space.

Enid is expecting their child within the month, and Doctor Caldwell has forbidden the journey: the gravity of the run to Pluto would endanger her and the baby. McBride must wait out the week alone. Long builds a quiet story of distance and worry inside the hard machinery of his future.
68396-dr-courtney-s-guide-to-happy-marri:
Doctor Courtney's Guide to Happy Marriage is a tiny magazine article of advice. Courtney published it himself at Boston in the Multum in Parvo Library. The issue is volume one, number six, dated June of 1894. Five cents bought a copy of the smallest magazine in the world. Fifty cents took it for a year by post to any reader.

The Newly Wed opens the guide for those just set sail on matrimony. That sea proves troublous for those who embark unprepared, it warns. Marriage is far more than a civil contract or religious ceremony. Much lies behind those outward marks that couples ought to know well. Marriage should rest on mutual love and esteem, the guide insists. Marriages made to gratify the lower nature cannot hope to be happy. Practical advice for the wedded fills the rest of the small pages.
68471-tom-the-telephone-boy-or-the-myste:
Tom the Telephone Boy, or The Mystery of a Message, by Frank Webster, is a tale for boys. Cupples and Leon published it at New York in a thirty five cent cloth series. Webster also wrote Bob the Castaway and The Newsboy Partners, the front list notes. A plate shows Mr Cutter coming into a room and turning on the light.

Only a Farm Boy and The Boy from the Ranch stand in the same series list. The Young Treasure Hunter and Bob the Castaway fill out that row of titles. The Young Firemen of Lakeville and The Boy Pilot of the Lakes follow in print. Two Boy Gold Miners closes the advertisement of tales for boys in the front. A working lad and a strange message give this volume its plot and pull.
6858-grace-harlowe-s-second-year-at-over:
Jessie Graham Flower brings Grace Harlowe back for a second year at Overton College in 1914. Overton claims her own, the unforeseen strikes, Mrs. Elwood comes to the rescue, and a belated freshman arrives. An anarchist chooses a roommate, Elfreda makes a rash promise, and girls and their ideals fill the early chapters.

An offended freshman, a finger of suspicion, a summons, and Grace holding court lead to mercy, reform, and Christmas children. Grace makes a resolution and confesses a fault before the close. Grace Harlowe's Second Year is a warm, old-style college tale of friendship, honor, and growth.
68837-elsie-lindtner-a-sequel-to-the-dan:
Karin Michaëlis wrote a second book on Elsie Lindtner, in an authorized English version by Beatrice Marshall. John Lane of New York copyrighted it in 1912. A long summary at the front retells the first book, The Dangerous Age, in which Elsie wrote her life in a letter to a young architect who loved her. Her mother died at her birth and her bankrupt father lived in disgrace.

Elsie learned as a child that lack of money made their life sordid, and she worshipped money from that hour. She guarded her beauty like a fortune, shunning the sun and saving rain water for her face. She wed Richard Lindtner, a wealthy Dane, and for twenty two years in Copenhagen she seemed a happy wife. Inwardly, she says, her mind stayed cold. This volume takes up her diary and letters where the first left off.
6897-the-little-savage:
Captain Marryat left this adventure tale unfinished at his death, and the introduction explains how it reached print. Marryat wrote the first part and two chapters of the second, carrying the story to chapter twenty four. His son Frank Marryat then edited the volume and supplied a short preface to the second part.

The book stands as the last work of a popular sea writer, sent to press while its author lay in long illness. Readers meet a tale cut short by death and finished by a son's care, rather than a smooth whole. That broken history gives the volume its special interest for lovers of Marryat's sea stories.
6899-the-children-s-pilgrimage:
Two children sit on a doorstep on an autumn Sunday evening in a quiet old court behind Bloomsbury, with a mongrel dog gazing at them with hungry, loving eyes. The elder, a girl of ten, and her brother of eight look clean and respectable, not like waifs of the East End. Their street is a cul de sac leading nowhere, and at that hour it seems quite deserted.

Mrs Meade calls the first part Looking for the Guide, and the hymn line at its head sets the tone of a search. The children are alone in the world in a way the opening makes plain, and the tale follows their pilgrimage step by step. It is a story of trust, care, and a long road walked by small feet.
69042-potemkin-village:
Fletcher Pratt wrote this novelet for Startling Stories in February 1953. Director Unterbaum of the Intercolonial Office rises to greet his visitors as it opens. A recorder named Starnes and a writer named Heidekopfer are the pair he welcomes to his office in the first scene.

The Council wants three of the group to undertake a mission, Unterbaum says plainly. Lanzerotti already knows something of it, he adds, nodding toward the dark head in the room. A Potemkin village, in the old phrase, is a false front built to fool inspectors, and Pratt's space colonies hide their own secrets behind a show settlement.
69105-the-path-of-honor-a-tale-of-the-wa:
Burton Stevenson wrote this tale of the war in the Bocage, published by Lippincott in 1910, third in his Bastille series of French romances. Shakespeare's line on honor's narrow path stands as motto.

The contents open with the trap of Sergeant Dubosq, an enemy found a friend, and a pleasant bondage. A confession, a serpent in the garden, and Gabrielle's tower follow; then a tragedy, a vow, and the dragon's den. The narrator rides out of Tours at dawn, crossing the shallow river southward to Poitiers. The frontispiece catches a lady's scarlet face and startled eyes. Stevenson, author of Cadets of Gascony, writes the Vendée war as first-person romance. Readers get royalist France at swordpoint.
69142-given-in-marriage:
B M Croker wrote Given in Marriage, issued in London by Hutchinson and Company. Croker had earlier written In Old Madras and Lismoyle. Chapter one is A Stranger in the Land. I say, did you hear old pensioner Jones, jawing away to Haji Aboo about the gold reefs that lie round Tappah, an eager young planter asks to open it.

And what did you think, Ted, he asks. That the old boy was drunk as usual, was the uncompromising rejoinder. Filthy bazaar liquor, some of these days he will snuff out, Ted says. Well, of course it is shandy, but I have a notion there is something in his story, the first man urges. He swore one or two of the estates were chock full of gold, he adds. Novel readers get a Malaya planting tale of gold rumors.
6916-english-men-of-letters-coleridge:
H D Traill writes the life of Coleridge for the English Men of Letters series, facing a subject of many sides. His preface quotes De Quincey on Coleridge's multiform attainments and powers, and on the many demands they make on any biographer. De Quincey's praise is touched with humor, Traill admits, but in substance it is just, and it excuses the shortcomings of a short volume.

No complete life of Coleridge on any large scale then existed, and no full critical account of his work stood ready to hand. Traill therefore works within narrow limits, sketching the poet, thinker, and talker in brief compass. The book serves as a compact guide to a man whose genius spilled across poetry, thought, and talk.
69198-a-bird-of-passage:
Croker wrote this novel, published by Ward and Downey in London in 1887. Lines from 'The Tempest' stand at the front, about wind that scatters young men through the world to seek their fortunes. Port Blair opens the contents, and expectation and first impressions follow as the scene is set.

Denis has visitors, and a chapter asks what she is like in plain terms. A queen of the Cannibal Islands, Quentin's piano and a damsel in distress fill the middle. A wreck, a room named for Blue Beard and a ring from Lisle carry the tale of a wandering heroine in imperial settings.
70457-tumbling-river-range:
Tumbling River Range is a western novel by Tuttle, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1935. The contents open with Wedding Night and a grim second chapter, Hanging Is Too Good. The New Sheriff, Range Funeral, and Hashknife and Sleepy follow. Hashknife Smells a Rat, City against Range, Clues, and The Inquest show the book's double nature: a cattle-country mystery worked by Tuttle's recurring range detectives.

The first chapter lights up the Flying H ranch-house of Uncle Hozie Wheeler. Lanterns hang on the wide veranda, from the corral fence, and within the big stable. One stall is piled with empty five-gallon cans, cow-bells, and shotguns. Every noise-maker common to the cattle country is ready for the minister's final words. This is to be the biggest shivaree ever pulled off on the Tumbling River range. A passage preserved in the copy crowds the house with guests.
70656-chronicles-and-characters-of-the-s:
John Francis wrote Chronicles and Characters of the Stock Exchange, first contained in the Bankers' Magazine for 1850 and issued in a first American edition at Boston that year. Francis also wrote a history of the Bank of England. The volume adds stock tables from 1732 to 1846 and Bank dividend records.

His preface lists his aims: to gather remarkable incidents tied to the National Debt, sketch the causes that necessitated it and the corruptions that increased it, and reproduce its principal characters. Lotteries, early railways, and loans such as the Poyais scheme follow. Readers get an anecdotal history of the London money market by a City insider.
70732-the-old-vicarage:
The Old Vicarage, a novel by Mrs Hubback, authoress of The Wife Sister and May and December, was published in New York and Boston in 1856. Chapter one opens with verse from the Forsaken Merman: children voices should be dear to a mother ear.

It was a summer evening. The yellow sunshine streamed through the boles of the forest trees, tinting them with purple, vermilion, gold, or the richest brown. It gave a metallic lustre to the tops of the giant oaks. Beneath the trees lay a terrace commanding a forest glade. Readers get a mid Victorian domestic novel opening in a woodland set piece.
70874-knotting-and-splicing-ropes-and-co:
Knotting and Splicing Ropes and Cordage, one of the Work handbooks edited by Paul N Hasluck, was published by David McKay at Philadelphia in 1907, with numerous engravings and diagrams. Hasluck's preface calls the book a digest of information scattered over more than twenty thousand columns of the journals he edits.

Chapters move from rope formation to simple and useful knots, eye knots, hitches, and bends. Ring knots, rope shortenings, ties and lashings, and fancy knots follow. Rope splicing, working cordage, hammock making, scaffolding lashings, and splicing and socketing wire ropes complete the manual.
71596-whittier-at-close-range:
Whittier at Close Range is a near view of the poet Whittier by Frances Campbell Sparhawk. It came out at Boston in nineteen twenty-five. Sparhawk was known for tales and a set of girls books. The book is given to the name of her father. Its first scene is set in the poets yard room, a fit name for his study.

A young friend of the poet waits there and takes in the room. His chair stands past shelves he could reach, with books strewn past the whole house. A paint of a west sun set, a gift from a friend, hangs by a cut of ice fields sent by a far north man. The poet had cast out a paint of his own young face from that room. Talk of the Scots bard and of heather bells fills the first part.
72304-world-edge:
World Edge is a science fiction story by Jack Egan. The tale appeared in Amazing Stories in November 1962, with pictures by Finlay. A blurb above the story shows a man beneath a thousand moons of many colours. A girl stands beside him, a dragon glares across the room, and something waits outside.

Harvey Crane wakes flat on his back under a pink half dome of sky. Blue and yellow trees of triangular shape block one view. A tapered cylinder stands balanced on its nose nearby. To his right there is no horizon at all, only the edge of the world. He crawls to that edge and looks down into swirling rose depths. A girl then appears, scolds him for landing the ship badly again, and lifts the great rocket by a wingtip with ease.
72559-life-s-little-stage:
Life's Little Stage, a novel by Agnes Giberne, was printed in London in 1913. Giberne also wrote Sun, Moon and Stars and other books for young readers. The story opens as Magda Royston leaves school for good. She begs to stay two years more, or even one. Her teacher, Miss Mordaunt, urges her to make the best of the change.

Chapter heads promise Swiss scenes, a night in a mountain hut, and an avalanche. Names that recur include Patricia and Virginia. Later heads speak of lost chances, true service, and hard tests. The tale follows a girl into adult life, where small chances matter. Its frame verse asks how great trials can be met if small ones are thrown away.
72752-rose-cottage:
Eleanora Stooke wrote this story, Rose Cottage, printed in London and Edinburgh. Stooke also wrote Polly's Father and Little Gem. A frontispiece shows a boy handing his mother his first week's earnings with pride. Eight chapters carry the tale: the new arrivals, a chapter of excuses, Jim gets work, the good shepherd, a request, a Sunday-school treat, an accident, and a great change.

Chapter one paints the village of Sunleigh in March, between two hills, with a stream running by meadows gold with daffodils. Marian Morris, the vicar's only daughter, walks up the street to the baker's and then to Mrs Mugford's shop, which sells nearly everything. There she hears the news: Rose Cottage has been taken by a family called Lethbridge, in only yesterday.
72944-school-life-at-winchester-college:
Robert Blachford Mansfield wrote of his school days at Winchester College under the old system of 1835 to 1840. The third edition came out at London in 1893, the five hundredth year since the school's founding. A glossary explains words and customs found only at Winchester.

Mansfield calls his book a true record of a system long since swept away. He recalls the games, the dress, and the daily round of a Winchester junior. Changes begun in his time by Charles Wordsworth, second master and a fine sportsman, get their due. The last chapter was rewritten for this edition. Old boys of the school would find much to stir their own memories in these pages.
73015-anne-page:
Netta Syrett's Anne Page was published by the John Lane Company in 1909. Syrett had written The Child of Promise before it. The novel opens not with a person but with a place and an hour: at the time between sunset and twilight, Miss Page is generally to be found in her garden.

Fairholme Court, her house, faces west with a long irregular front. So the garden takes the pageant of the sunset, the glory of the after-glow, and the slide from daylight into purple night. The house itself is a medley: begun in the last years of Elizabeth, enlarged under later reigns, its newest wing Georgian, the red brick mellowed. Roses wreath the latticed windows of the older part; clematis riots over the roof and climbs the chimney-stacks. Below the hall a smooth lawn runs, unspoilt by flower-beds, to a sunk fence and meadowland dotted with elms.
73115-the-house-of-bondage:
The House of Bondage is a novel by Reginald Wright Kauffman, author of What is Socialism, issued in New York with a copyright of 1910. The front pages list printing after printing: a second in November 1910, a ninth by April 1911, a sixteenth by April 1912.

Kauffman opens with a Caveat Emptor, a warning to the buyer. The story, he says, is meant for three classes of readers only. It is for those who must bring up children, and those who must bring up themselves. It is also for those strong enough to think of bettering the weaker. The scene opens in a market town among cape-coated Mennonites and bearded Amishmen forecasting a parching summer. The novel is an exposure tale, written to make comfortable readers face a bondage practiced under their noses.
73244-salvage:
Roy Norton wrote Salvage, a sea tale of Captain Eli Drake and his hunt for cargo. The front blurb dubs Drake the Opportunist for his nose for a chance. His neat steam schooner Malabart lies idle at Piraeus in Greece. Trade sleeps and big lines squeeze small owners hard.

Drake eats his own funds to keep ship and crew whole. He wires agents and walks the docks of Athens in vain. Then a winch clanks on a rusty tramp near by. Cases marked as mining gear swing light as air in the slings. Bill Morris, a man who fled hot ports, stands on her bridge. Drake smells fraud and gain in one breath, and steps in to look close.
7353-birds-in-town-village:
W. H. Hudson's Birds in Town and Village reworks his first book about bird life, Birds in a Village from 1893, with affection and a critic's hand. Hudson explains in his preface that the reissue let him mend faults in the portions he kept and throw out a good deal of matter not worth keeping. The first portion, Birds in a Village, was mostly rewritten with fresh matter added.

The book joins town and village birds with impressions of rural scenes in England, written by an author who cherished his first book above others. Hudson watches sparrows, songbirds, and village life with a naturalist's patience and a poet's ear. Readers get a revised classic of English bird writing, kept and improved by its author.
73643-cambridge:
Noel Barwell described Cambridge in words and Haslehust pictured it, in this volume of the Beautiful England series from Blackie and Son of London and Glasgow. Sister volumes treated Oxford, Canterbury, Bath and Wells, and the Thames. A view of the Great Court of Trinity College serves as frontispiece.

The picture list walks the reader through the colleges. Byron's Pool, the kitchen wall of Peterhouse, the old hall of Corpus Christi, and Erasmus' Tower at Queens' College all appear. Other plates show the gateway and Wren's Bridge at Saint John's, the market place, and the library staircase. Clare College from the Backs and the Fellows' Garden at Christ's close the set. Barwell opens by praising the diversity of England's landscape and the spirit of each place. Lovers of the university towns get Cambridge in prose and plate together.
73932-bodily-changes-in-pain-hunger-fear:
Walter B Cannon sums up his lab's work on what strong feeling does to the body. He held the George Higginson chair of physiology at Harvard. D Appleton and Company published the book in 1915.

Cannon starts with digestion: the feelings that help the stomach's juices flow, and the fear and pain that stop them. He then lays out the visceral nerves, with the broad sympathetic system built for wide action and the cranial and sacral branches built for narrow tasks. Later matter, flagged in the contents, covers the adrenal glands and the changes that fit an animal to fight or flee. The book made Cannon's name with general readers and still anchors talks on stress, since it first tied emotion to clear changes in blood, gut, and glands.
7401-a-crystal-age:
W. H. Hudson's romance of the future begins with a feeling most readers know: dissatisfaction with the present order, joined to a vague hope that something better may come. His preface warns that any picture of the future must be false, since we cannot imagine what we have never known. Yet the attempt itself, he argues, has a perennial interest.

The story that follows imagines a future people living in pastoral simplicity, far from the noise and machinery of Hudson's own age. A traveler finds their world and learns its customs, its loves, and its limits. The novel is less a blueprint than a dream: a quiet, beautiful society held up as a mirror to the restless nineteenth century that produced it.
74074-the-cottage:
Frank Belknap Long wrote The Cottage, a story printed in Fantastic Universe in September 1954. The blurb gives its turn in advance. There was a savage cruelty in Durkin's hatred of his children, and little did he know that on other worlds cruelty boomeranged. Long's stories had appeared in twenty-seven anthologies by then, from Hammett's Creeps by Night to Derleth's Sleep No More.

Will Durkin drives home from town over a rutted dirt road. He stares at his bony knuckles and slashes at the empty air, equipped and ready for a cruel duel with another man's offspring. The narrator wonders whether the cruelty was in him at birth. The stony soil of his childhood helped make him: a gaunt, restless-eyed man who could find no pleasure in merriment. Long builds a dark tale on that drive home.
74148-metipom-s-hostage:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote Metipom Hostage, a narrative of adventures befalling David Lindall in King Philip War. Houghton Mifflin Company in Boston and New York issued the book in nineteen twenty one. Copyright rests with the Boy Scouts of America and with Barbour. A King Philip portrait is the frontispiece. Twenty three chapters fill the book. Chapter one is The Red Omen.

The Meeting in the Woods, Down the Winding River, and The Spotted Arrow follow. David Visits the Praying Village and What Happened at the Pool come next. Captured and Metipom Questions bring the hero into the sachem hands. The Village of the Wahoo setts and Sequanawah Pledges Friendship fill the middle. The Cave in the Forest and David Faces Death raise the stakes. In King Philip Power closes the peril. Boys get a colonial war tale from a famed school story writer.
7433-the-awkward-age:
Henry James's novel of 1899 is an experiment in pure talk. Almost the whole book is dialogue, with hardly any narration to explain what the speakers mean. The awkward age of the title is the age of Nanda Brookenham. She is a young woman in London society, no longer a child and not yet safely married. She stands caught between her mother's fashionable circle and her own conscience.

Around Nanda gather her mother, Mrs. Brookenham, the faithful Mr. Longdon, and the charming Vanderbank, all talking brilliantly and revealing themselves by what they say and withhold. James's preface calls the book's germ small beside the mass it grew into, and the growth is all in conversation. It is a demanding, dazzling novel of manners, best read slowly, listening hard.
74669-the-twelve-best-short-stories-in-t:
Auguste Dorchain chose The Twelve Best Short Stories in the French Language for Gowans and Gray in 1915. The book is number five in a cosmopolitan library from London and Glasgow. All twelve tales stand in English dress, by a team of hands. The first is The Adventures of the Last of the Abencerrages, by Chateaubriand, from 1806. Xavier de Maistre gives prisoners in the Caucasus, and Balzac gives El Verdugo.

De Vigny, Merimee, and Musset add a red seal tale, the Venus of Ille, and a white blackbird. Stendhal, Gautier, Daudet, and Flaubert fill the next span, with Vanina Vanini and Saint Julian. Coppee gives a gate-keeper, and a last tale of Mademoiselle Perle closes the set. Readers get a short, rich tour of French tale craft across one century.
75467-sweated-industry-and-the-minimum-w:
Sweated Industry and the Minimum Wage is a reform study by Clementina Black, published by Duckworth in London in 1907. Gardiner, chairman of the National Anti-Sweating League's executive, wrote the introduction. The book opens with a sentence from Howells: the whole spectacle of poverty is incredible, and people deny it exists because they cannot believe it even when they see it.

Black first explains the term sweating and the work done in workers' homes. She reports special investigations into the character of home work. Her cases include match-box making, with the process, the payment, and the history of one Jarvis family. Shirt making and paper-bag making follow, each with individual cases. Some men home workers, racquet balls, and other trades are also treated. The evidence builds toward her remedy of a legal minimum wage.
75618-the-wonders-of-salvage:
The Wonders of Salvage, by David Masters, was first printed in London in 1924, with forty eight plates from photos. Masters had also written The Romance of Excavation. He gives the book to his wife.

A front plate shows the steamer Devona in a hopeless spot on September 15, 1917. Salvors raised her in four days by rigging wire mattresses and pumping her wheat cargo to drain the water. Other plates show divers at work in Tobermory Bay, sand washed for signs of treasure, and the gold of the Lutine sifted from the sea bed. One set shows the battleship Leonardo da Vinci brought into dock upside down. Sea fans get the wild craft of saving ships and goods from the deep.
75944-the-royal-exchange:
A E W Mason wrote The Royal Exchange, a note on the occasion of the bicentenary of the Royal Exchange Assurance. The Royal Exchange in London issued the book in nineteen twenty. Seven chapters in two parts fill the volume. Part one treats the house, and part two treats the business. Plates show the first, second, and third Royal Exchange buildings.

Chapter one opens on January twenty third, fifteen seventy one, when Queen Elizabeth dined with Sir Thomas Gresham at Austin Friars. Gresham founded the first Royal Exchange, and the queen came in state with trumpeters and halberdiers. Later chapters treat the Great Fire and the second Exchange, then the third. The South Sea Bubble and the birth of the Assurance Corporation open part two. A chapter on assurance and a chapter on the corporation close the tale. City readers get trade history in elegant prose.
76049-dancing-devil-range:
W C Tuttle wrote Dancing Devil Range as a western tale of Hashknife Hartley and his partner Sleepy Stevens. A long freight train rattles through desert hills at dusk, and the two drifters ride the caboose. Hashknife stands inches over six feet, lean and steel-muscled, with grey eyes under a low sombrero.
