Sleepy is shorter, broad, and bow-legged, with an innocent grin and blue eyes. Both wear worn Stetsons, faded overalls, and home-made gun-belts with plain wooden-butted Colts. A brakeman warns that they are pulling into Northgate, the rail point for the Dancing Devil range. Loading corrals line the tracks. A headnote warns that peace on earth was far from Dancing Devil Valley that season.
76100-odeyne-s-marriage:
Evelyn Everett-Green wrote Odeyne's Marriage, in a new edition from John Shaw of London, one of a set of uniform story books. The tale opens with a dainty invalid in bed, putting on a becoming cap. She asks whether this is truly Desmond's wedding day, and settles on her pillows to hear the news. Chapter heads then take the reader to Odeyne's home and through farewells and greetings.

The Ritchies and Beatrice appear at home, and an adventurous drive and new friendships follow. A shock, a child named Little Guy, and a homecoming fill the middle parts. Later heads darken, with the pace that kills, a crash, and a strange Christmas. A part named the two wives and a close on husband and wife end the tale.
76649-the-autobiography-of-calvin-coolid:
The Autobiography of Calvin Coolidge was printed by the Cosmopolitan Book Corporation in New York in 1929. Seven chapters divide the life. Scenes of my childhood, seeking an education, the law and politics, and in national politics come first. On entering and leaving the presidency, some of the duties of the president, and why I did not choose to run follow.

Chapter one sets Plymouth on the easterly slope of the Green Mountains, twenty miles west of the Connecticut River, in a country of narrow valleys and hills. A military road cut in the French and Indian War ran through it, from Charlestown in New Hampshire to Fort Ticonderoga. Near the height of land along that road, the grandfather of Coolidge's grandfather, Captain John Coolidge, located a farm and settled in about 1780. Portraits show him at three and at seven, and at Amherst College.
76827-us-and-our-charge:
"Us, and Our Charge" is a children's story by Amy Le Feuvre. The Religious Tract Society published it in London. Le Feuvre had written a shelf of kindred tales, Us and Our Donkey among them. The tale is told as a diary by one of the children.

The narrator marvels that only a year has passed since the diary began. Things happening, she reflects, make people old faster than weeks do. A bomb-shell opens the story, and a new home follows it. The children explore, perform a rescue, and suffer a loss in turn. A long Sunday, a governess, and a godmother fill the quieter chapters. Then the beginning of war enters the household's small world. A first recruit, an aunt's hospital, and a search follow in the contents. The find and sad news close a story of home-front childhood.
77128-ten-years-experience-in-raising-ca:
Ten Years Experience in Raising Carrots and Cabbage is a farm guide by H Cook. The author farmed in Columbia County in the state of New York. Soil, sowing, tilling, and storing of roots fill the first half. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

Short parts give rules for hoe work, weed work, and seed choice for both crops. A part weighs roots against roots as feed for stock in hard coin terms. Fat hog tales back the claim that roots pay the small farm well. Five acres is held up as stock enough for a good home farm. Weather signs and a home rain gauge close the plain spoken book.
77531-midsummer-at-hay-lodge:
Midsummer at Hay-Lodge is a children's story book by Ruth Buck, writing as Lamb, published by Chambers in 1870 in the Chambers's Library for Young People. The frame story follows a widowed mother and her daughters Marian and Kate, who wait at the window for the postman. Their brother Bernard has been six months away at school, his first half-year from home.

The first letter brings the news that Bernard comes tomorrow, and little Kate dances round the room. Each chapter of the holiday carries a tale told within it, from the parrot and the magpie to Maggie's daisies. The conclusion sends Bernard back to school. The book is Victorian children's fiction in its family form: a holiday, a fault, and stories as the medicine.
77562-facing-old-age:
Abraham Epstein wrote a study of want in old age in the United States. The book came out in New York in March 1922. Epstein had led a state probe of old age grant plans. His theme is how the old come to lean on kin or state. Grant schemes in far lands stand next to home facts in it.

Counts of the poor old and tales of their last years ground him. Poor houses, kin aid, and small rents each take their due. He asks what a rich land owes those past work years. Grave, sourced prose makes his case step by step. Reform men of that age took the book up fast.
78220-murder-at-the-vicarage:
Agatha Christie wrote Murder at the Vicarage, copyrighted in 1930 and dedicated to Rosalind. The vicar himself tells the tale. It begins at a Wednesday luncheon at the vicarage, over remarkably tough boiled beef.

The vicar remarks, most unbecoming to his cloth, that anyone who murdered Colonel Protheroe would do the world a service. His nephew Dennis warns him the words will be remembered when the colonel is found bathed in blood. Griselda, the vicar's young and distracting wife, treats the parish as a huge joke. The stage is set for the murder the title promises.
7832-the-deluge:
David Graham Phillips's The Deluge opens with Mr. Blacklock, then moves through kings arising, a woman's arrival, a candidate for respectability, danger signals, and gentlemen in quotes. Blacklock goes into training, trails Langdon, and meets pillars of society who prove hollow.

Later chapters bring Anita, a genteel hold-up, a windfall from Gentleman Joe, a conspiracy against Anita, and Black Matt's triumph. The novel opens with a jest on Napoleon and a faked royal genealogy, then turns to American finance, politics, and love, where money floods like a deluge over old morals.
78416-on-the-dodge:
Will James wrote and illustrated On the Dodge, a Western tale told by a cowboy in his own speech. Its motto warns that when the law is a bullet, it does not indulge in delays.

The narrator finds his big buckskin horse stolen one morning, led through a gate by a man in spike-heeled boots. The print of the rounded shoe is one he would know anywhere, for he shod the horse himself. He guesses some hunted man needed a fresh horse badly and borrowed his. He snares the best company horse and rides the trail like a comet. A worn brown saddle horse stands abandoned a mile on. Then a voice orders him to hold them up.
78727-tramps-of-the-range:
Tramps of the Range is a western tale by Tuttle of the cow country. Tuttle also wrote Flames of the Storm and Ranch of the Tombstones. The first faint flush of dawn creeps over the Mission River hills. The Overland train draws to a stop at little Moon Flats then. In that moment's pause a man drops off the baggage car rods.

He creeps between the trucks and walks slowly down the main street. The town lies deserted, and he studies its false fronted buildings closely. He seems to have been there before, the narrator marks in quiet. Moon Flats was a cow town, a shipping point for the ranges. One street, wooden sidewalks, hitch racks, and deep dust describe it.
78780-the-marriage:
Ann Bannon's The Marriage is an original Gold Medal novel, printed by Fawcett in December 1960 and marked as no reprint. The cover copy tells of Page and his wife Sunny, who is expecting a baby. A long-distance call from Page's stepfather brings word that shakes the marriage to its roots.

The first chapter, though, opens in a quiet Chicago home, where Jack Mann takes a phone call after supper. His wife Laura is combing their daughter Betsy's hair for bed. The caller is a stranger named Winkler, shy and well-spoken, who says friends of Jack's asked him to call. Two homes, two calls, and the fear that a marriage may not be what it seemed.
79117-a-literary-history-of-rome-in-the-: A Literary History of Rome in the Silver Age, by J Wight Duff, stands in the Library of Literary History. Its twin in the set covers Rome to the close of the Golden Age. Bound in front are the great journals' words on that first book. They call it full and deep, yet human. They praise a style that compels the ear. On that proof, this volume takes the tale past the gold age, with the same wide reading at its back.
79172-the-stone-age:
Clement Wood explains deep time in The Stone Age, Little Blue Book number 481, edited by E Haldeman-Julius and copyrighted in 1923 at Girard, Kansas. The first chapter is called The Record of the Rocks. Wood walks a field behind his house at Hastings-on-Hudson with the naturalist J Otis Swift, who picks up a fragment of quartz.

Swift says a volume could be written about that stone: weathered from granite, rounded by water, scratched by a glacier. Its chipped places, though, were made by the hand of man, an Indian hammer stone. Wood has handled over five hundred such worked stones nearby.
79290-the-fatal-marriage:
The Fatal Marriage; or, Orville Deville is a novel by Mrs. Southworth, published at Philadelphia by Peterson. Southworth was among the most popular American novelists of her century. The title page lists her shelf of tales: Ishmael, Self-Raised, The Missing Bride, Retribution, A Beautiful Fiend, and dozens more.

A motto from Scott heads the tale: it is an old tale, and often told, but no maiden true, betrayed for gold, loved or was avenged like this one. That is the book in a couplet. Southworth's heroines suffer betrayal, hidden marriages, and lost inheritances, and win through by constancy. The Fatal Marriage ran in the story papers and then between covers, as her books did for forty years. Her readers, mostly women, made her the best-selling American novelist of the eighteen hundreds.
79501-the-electronic-siege:
The Electronic Siege is a science fiction story by John Campbell. The tale appeared in Wonder Stories in April 1932. A note from the editor praises Campbell's earlier comic story and promises serious work of equal skill. The blurb sets a mystery on an inhabited asteroid, with vanishings in space.

The story opens at the customs dock of the space liner Vega. Scientists of Earth and Venus board all afternoon for a great meeting on Mars in the year 2374. One late comer stands out from the pale and tanned scholars. He is a short, hugely fat man in a riot of colours. Green silk trousers, a red shirt, and lavender braces top his outfit. He waddles like an old steam engine, puffing as he comes. His odd figure hides more than the dock guard guesses.
79530-the-prophetic-marriage:
The Prophetic Marriage is a novel by Warwick Deeping, printed at New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Deeping also wrote Sorrell and Son and Roper's Row. He dedicates the book to Lieutenant-Colonel Andrew Baxter, in memory of happy days they spent together in France. The story opens on Spaniards Row in Pentworth.

Tod Western, a combative and clannish child, plays a jungle game under the laurels at Number 13. He hears two loiterers judge his father: that silly fool Western will never make any money. Tod pushes his round head through the leaves and fires back that only a silly fool wants to make money. Joab Twain of Twain's Stores turns an enormous angry face on him. Tod answers that three of yesterday's eggs from Twain's were rotten. Deeping builds his tale on a dreamer's household.
79626-a-social-mirage:
A Social Mirage is a book of essays on love, marriage and society by Mrs Frank Leslie. It came out in 1899. Short, titled chapters run from love's torments to the social slang of Paris.

Leslie writes on friendship between man and woman, and on love weighed against money. American husbands and the rights of American girls each get a chapter. She pleads for good manners and treats old maids with respect. The society girl as a wife is drawn with a shrewd eye. Her tone is bright, worldly and frank. The book is a sharp tour of her social world. Her own portrait faces the title page of the book.
7972-homer-and-his-age:
Andrew Lang wrote this study as a follow-up to his earlier Homer and the Epic, taking up the critics who doubted that one poet made the Iliad and Odyssey. He examines the alleged discrepancies in the poems, the case for Homeric unity, and what the epics reveal about the age that produced them. An editor's note warns that unclear typesetting in the original left some passages marked with gaps.

Lang argues from the poems themselves, testing whether one mind could hold their world together. His prose is clear and combative, aimed at general readers as well as scholars. The book still serves as a spirited defence of Homer as a poet rather than a committee, and as an introduction to the long debate over who wrote the epics.
8208-poems-of-coleridge:
Arthur Symons selected and arranged these poems of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, with an introduction and notes. His contents span the poet's career: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, Christabel, Kubla Khan, Lewti, The Ballad of the Dark Ladie, Love, Dejection: An Ode, France: An Ode. Fears in Solitude, This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison, Frost at Midnight, The Nightingale, The Eolian Harp, Hymn Before Sun-Rise, Youth and Age, and Work Without Hope, among many others.

Symons's selection gives the essential Coleridge in one volume, from supernatural ballads to meditative conversation poems. His introduction places the poet among the Romantics and explains his uneven, brilliant career. For readers new to Coleridge, this is the ideal starting point, and for old readers, a well-chosen companion.
8489-specimens-of-the-table-talk-of-samu:
This volume gathers specimens of the table talk of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, dedicated to James Gillman of the Grove, Highgate, and to Mrs. Gillman, who housed the poet in his later years. Coleridge's talk, recorded by listeners, ranges over poetry, philosophy, religion, and politics, in the brilliant, digressive style that made his conversation famous.

A note warns that Greek transliterations in the file are missing or suspect, but the English talk survives in full. Readers meet Coleridge the talker, not only the poet of the Ancient Mariner, thinking aloud at table. The book is a primary source for Romantic conversation, and for Coleridge's mind in its freest form.
8668-revenge:
Robert Barr packs twenty-one tales of payback into this collection, from An Alpine Divorce and Which Was the Murderer? to A Dynamite Explosion, An Electrical Slip, and The Vengeance of the Dead. Illustrations promise a safe blown open, a cord dangling above a policeman's head, and a bomb launched outward, and the stories deliver on that melodramatic billing. Over the Stelvio Pass, a deal on change, a modern Samson, and the exposure of Lord Stansford keep the settings shifting.

Barr writes with a journalist's briskness and a showman's sense of the twist, letting revenge arrive by law, by accident, by science, or by sheer nerve. The tales are short, sharp, and built for a single sitting each. Fans of Victorian sensation fiction will enjoy the variety, and the collection shows how the revenge plot, old as drama itself, adapted to dynamite, electricity, and the modern city.
9194-the-second-deluge:
Garrett Serviss wrote this science romance in 1912 about a second deluge drowning the world. Cosmo Versál mocks fate, then watches the first drops fall and the world swept with terror. A third sign leads to selecting the flower of mankind, and waters rise as crowds storm the ark. New York faces its last day, and a billion is bid for a share.

The ark sails over drowned Europe, to Paris under the sea and adventures in Colorado, as a terrible nucleus nears. Serviss mixes astronomy with adventure. The novel remains a lively early disaster tale, vast in scale and Victorian in wonder.
94-alexander-s-bridge:
Bartley Alexander builds great bridges and a great reputation, then risks both for an old love. Willa Cather's Alexander's Bridge, her first novel, follows the engineer between Boston, London, and the Canadian west. Professor Wilson watches his friend's rise with quiet doubt.

Alexander's marriage to Winifred steadies him, while Hilda Burgoyne, an actress from his youth, unsettles him. The bridge he designs becomes a test of nerve and character. An epilogue closes the story after disaster. The short novel shows Cather finding her voice. Cather later called it a study in divided loyalty, and critics still debate its hero.
9415-olaf-the-glorious-a-story-of-the-vi:
Robert Leighton wrote this Viking age story around Olaf the Glorious, opening with the finding of Olaf. In early summer, Sigurd Erikson journeys north into Esthonia to gather the king's taxes. In a seaport on the Gulf of Finland, tall, strong, and fair-haired, with armed servants in train, he rides across the marketplace toward the sea.

Fishing boats put out with the tide, merchant vessels lie at anchor, and a long dragonship waits near the strand. Leighton fills the tale with voyages, battles, and Norse honor. The book remains a rousing boys' adventure of the Viking world, vivid and swift.
a-crystal-age:
W. H. Hudson framed A Crystal Age as a romance of the future. his preface admits every such dream is built from the dreamer's own age — in his case, the cults and crazes of the 1880s. His narrator, out botanizing, falls into a ravine, is buried by falling earth, and wakes after a long unconsciousness in a changed world.

The future he finds is a quiet, communal household in a great house amid rich country, where people live close to nature and find his modern habits strange. Love in that ordered world follows rules he cannot accept, and his feeling for a daughter of the house drives the story to its close. Hudson's utopia is pastoral rather than mechanical, a dream of life returned to the soil.
a-straight-deal-or-the-ancient-grudge:
Owen Wister, the novelist of the American West, turns to public argument in nineteen chapters about England and America after the First World War. He begins with the flood of angry letters that any printed opinion now brings. His own opinion is plain: the old grudge between the two peoples should end.

Chapter by chapter he takes up wartime complaints, old history taught badly in schools, Irish questions, and slights remembered on both sides of the Atlantic. He grants faults to each country and asks readers to weigh the record fairly. The book is a plea for friendship between the English-speaking peoples, written in a plain, combative style.
a-treatise-concerning-the-principles-of-:
George Berkeley's Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge inquires into the causes of error in the sciences. Its title page adds the grounds of scepticism, atheism, and irreligion to the charge sheet. Berkeley dedicates the work to the Earl of Pembroke. His preface asks the reader to suspend judgment until the whole is read through once.

Berkeley argues that things exist only as they are perceived by a mind. Matter, as philosophers imagined it, is an empty abstraction behind our ideas. From this he builds proofs of God's existence and the soul's immateriality. An introduction attacks abstract ideas before the principles begin. The treatise made its young Irish author a founder of idealism, the doctrine that reality is mental. Few philosophy books so short have argued so long.
alexander-s-bridge:
Willa Cather's first novel centers on Bartley Alexander, a celebrated bridge builder at the height of his fame. The story opens with Professor Lucius Wilson, who taught Alexander, arriving in Boston and looking up his former student. Wilson's visit frames the portrait of a man whose public triumph rests on a strained marriage and an old love not fully buried.

In ten chapters and an epilogue, Alexander moves between Boston, London, and the great bridge he is building in Canada. A chance reunion with Hilda Burgoyne, the actress he loved before his marriage, reopens what his success had closed. Cather keeps the scale small and the prose exact. This printing also includes Alfred Noyes's poem The Barrel Organ after the novel.
ammianus-marcellinus-roman-history-yonge:
Ammianus Marcellinus, a retired Roman officer, wrote his history of the empire in the late fourth century. C. D. Yonge translated the surviving books into English. Much of the full work is lost, but the remainder is rich.

The surviving books run from Constantius through the reign of Valens. Emperor Julian's Persian campaign receives a long, admiring account from a near witness. Ammianus writes with a soldier's eye for terrain, weather, and morale. Historians rank him as the last great historian of Rome. His pages remain a prime source for the late empire.
among-the-trees-at-elmridge: Ella Rodman Church takes young readers among the trees at Elmridge, opening with a spring opening and moving to maples, elms, and old acquaintances. Each chapter introduces a tree by its leaves, bark, and habits, in talk suited to children. The book makes botany a friendly outdoor lesson, learned tree by tree.
amours-de-voyage:
Arthur Hugh Clough wrote his verse tale as a set of letters in English hexameters, and this text follows the 1903 Macmillan edition. The speaker, Claude, travels in Italy while Rome is in turmoil, and writes to his friend Eustace about sights, doubts, and a young woman he keeps meeting. He is clever, restless, and unable to commit to anything.

Across five cantos the letters move from Rome to Florence and the hills, mixing travel notes with shy courtship. Claude questions faith, duty, love, and his own hesitation, often with dry humor. The poem is prized for sounding like real modern thought, unsure and self-mocking, inside old verse forms.
an-inland-voyage:
Robert Louis Stevenson's first book recounts a canoe trip through Belgium and France. His friend Walter Simpson went with him. The dedication addresses Simpson as the Cigarette. The contents chart the route. It runs from Antwerp to Boom, then down the Willebroek Canal. It passes the Royal Sport Nautique and the canalized Sambre, past Maubeuge and Landrecies. At last it follows the Oise in flood, through Compiègne to Précy.

Two young men in canoes are taken for pedlars. Rain soaks them again and again. Innkeepers and canal folk feed and amuse them. Stevenson turns discomfort into comedy. He watches bargemen, lock-keepers, and the flat green country with care. Travel for its own sake is the subject. The book sets out the wandering voice that runs through all his later work.
an-occurrence-at-owl-creek-bridge:
Ambrose Bierce wrote this short story of the Civil War, told in three numbered parts. It opens on a railroad bridge in northern Alabama, where a man stands with a rope around his neck, hands bound, watched by Federal soldiers and a captain. The drop is about to be taken from under his feet. Bierce stays close to the physical facts: the boards, the sentinels, the cannon on the slope.

The condemned man is Peyton Farquhar, a planter who tried to burn the bridge for the Confederacy. As the plank tips, the story follows his sharpening senses and what seems to be an escape through the creek and the woods home. Bierce's ending reframes everything before it, and the tale has become the classic example of the tricked point of view in short fiction.
at-large:
E. W. Hornung published this novel with Scribner's in 1902, between his famous Raffles stories of the amateur cracksman. Hornung here leaves burglary aside for a drama of suspicion inside respectable English life. A colonel, a forceful lady visitor, and a man named Dick drive the early tension, as an identification at a doorway stops a door mid-swing.

Dialogue carries the book: interviews, challenges, and guarded answers slowly expose what each person knows. The colonel's cry of recognition, and the lady's anger on the other side of the door, show Hornung's method of letting manners crack under pressure. Readers who know Raffles will find the same crisp scenes and reversals, turned toward reputation and doubt rather than crime for sport.
at-whispering-pine-lodge:
Lawrence J. Leslie published this boys' adventure in 1919, sending four chums into the Adirondacks for a stay at a fur farmer's lodge. Max leads the party; Touch-and-Go Steve slips off with his steel-jointed fishing rod whenever work calls. Bandy-legs and the others complete the team of outdoor boys.

Their host Obed Grimes keeps a lodge of many wonders, stocked with the products of his fur farm. Night prowlers threaten the stock, so traps, taps on the cabin wall, and a tree bearing strange fruit supply the mysteries. Steve's dream comes true before the fur farmer's triumph closes the tale. Leslie writes brisk series fiction: camping craft, animal lore, and small dangers solved by plucky teamwork.
birds-in-town-village:
W. H. Hudson's Birds in Town and Village revises and enlarges his first book about bird life, Birds in a Village, first published in 1893. Hudson rewrote the first portion with fresh observations, threw out matter he judged unworthy, and added an entirely new part on birds in a Cornish village.

Five shorter essays between the two long parts are retained with little alteration, in one or two instances covering the same ground as the new matter. Hudson writes of English rural scenes with the affection of a first book's author, mending faults where he found them. Bird lovers and readers of English nature writing will find this a mellow, observant volume.
britannica-1911-acropolita-george:
George Acropolita (1217-1282) was a Byzantine historian and statesman. He was born at Constantinople. His father sent him young to the Nicaean court. John Vatatzes ruled that exiled empire. Successive emperors trusted Acropolita with state missions. The office of great logothete, or chancellor, came in 1244. He commanded troops in 1257 without much capacity. Enemies captured him and held him two years.

Diplomacy gave him his greatest task. Michael Palaeologus sent him to Pope Gregory X. At Lyons he accepted Rome's supremacy for the emperor. His chronicle covers the years 1204 to 1261. It continues the work of Nicetas Acominatus. A contemporary in high office wrote it. The entry rates him trustworthy on facts.
britannica-1911-adam-s-bridge:
Adam's Bridge is a chain of sandbanks. It is also called Rama's Bridge. The shoal runs from Ceylon's island of Manaar. It reaches to Rameswaram off the Indian coast. The Gulf of Manaar lies to its south-west. Palk Strait lies to its north-east. The chain runs more than thirty miles. It seriously impedes navigation between the coasts. Some banks stand dry at all tides. Most water over it measures only three or four feet.

Engineering has cut passages through it. Three tortuous channels were dredged for vessels. Ships now avoid the long Ceylon circumnavigation. Temple records blame a storm of 1480. Geology shows an isthmus once stood there. Steamers of the British India company use the passage.
britannica-1911-age:
Age, a word with four chief uses, is set out in a word and history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It can mean a great span of past time, such as the Bronze Age. It can mean a famed epoch or a generation. It can mean a stage in the life of a person or thing. In law it means the point at which a person bears full blame for acts.

The longest part deals with the old belief that human history falls into ages. Hesiod, in his poem Works and Days, tells of five races in turn. A golden race lived in ease and became kind spirits after death. A silver race sank lower and was buried by Jove. A bronze race was harsh and warlike and fell by its own strife. A heroic race, the men of Troy and Thebes, broke the trend.
britannica-1911-alger-of-liege:
Alger of Liège, who died near 1131, turned down offers from German bishops again and again, preferring a quiet learned life. Men also called him Alger of Cluny and Algerus Magister. The French priest began as a deacon at St Bartholomew's in Liège, his home town, and moved near 1100 to the city's cathedral church of St Lambert.

His last years passed as a monk at Cluny, where he died old and well thought of for holiness and sharp mind. Much of his writing is gone, his history of the Liège church among it. Four works remain. De Misericordia et Justitia, a set of Bible and Fathers passages with notes, matters much for church law. A second work, in three books, treats the sacraments of the Lord's body and blood and answers the Berengarian heresy. Peter of Cluny praised it, and so did Erasmus.
britannica-1911-alkan-charles-henri-vale:
Piano studies of extreme hardness are Alkan's claim on notice. His invention struck judges as less modern than it might have been, yet his piano technique and feel for effect ran in some ways ahead of even Liszt's. Beside Liszt, what he lacked was economy and tact in spending those gifts.

Charles Henri Valentin Morhange Alkan (1813–1888) was a French composer, born and dead in Paris. Alkan was his taken name, a nom de guerre. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in his sixth year and shone there until 1830. A London visit came in 1833; after it he settled in Paris as a piano teacher for the rest of his life.
britannica-1911-alnage:
Alnage, or aulnage, was the official supervision of woollen cloth in England. It covered both the shape and the quality of the cloth. The system began under Richard I. An ordinance required woollen cloths everywhere to share one width. That width was two ells within the lists. The cloth had to be of equal goodness in middle and sides. The rule is usually known as the Assize of Measures, or Assize of Cloth. Magna Carta re-enacted it.

Under Edward I, an official called an alnager enforced the system. He measured each piece of cloth. He stamped it to show it met the standard. Imported cloths of varied sizes forced repeal of the width rules in 1353. New, lighter drapery under Elizabeth brought fresh standards. A statute of 1665 created an alnager of the new drapery, against fraud. Alnage duties and the office itself were abolished in 1699.
britannica-1911-appanage:
Appanage is the subject of an entry on royal custom in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The French word comes from a Latin phrase meaning to give bread. In its first sense it meant the support given by parents to younger children. That support stood apart from the rights of the eldest child under the custom of the first born.

In later use the term narrowed to money grants for younger children of ruling houses. The entry ties it chiefly to Germany and Austria. Such a grant went back to the state or the head of the family when the line died out. In English history, the entry notes, the system never played a large part.
britannica-1911-arbitrage:
Arbitrage is the trade that evens out prices between markets. A dealer buys where a thing is cheap. He sells where it is dear. Stocks and shares are the chief field for this work. Foreign exchange and gold bars come next. Most deals run between London and other large money centres. New York is the other main pole. London leads because it is the world's chief banking centre. A move in London prices soon moves prices elsewhere.

A local shock can also start the flow. A crisis in France would first push down French stocks. Fear would then drive funds out of the country. That flow would move the exchanges against France. In calm times the profit on each deal is very small. Fast posts, wires, and phones let dealers close deals at great speed. Keen rivalry cuts the gain to the bone. Samuel Montagu signs the piece.
britannica-1911-ariege:
Ariege, an inland department of southern France, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Spain bounds it on the south, and three French departments on its other sides. It takes in the old countship of Foix and parts of two old provinces. It covers 1,893 square miles and held 205,684 people in 1906.

The article stresses how much of it is mountain. Its southern border is held by the snow-clad peaks of the eastern Pyrenees, the highest rising past ten thousand feet. Many passes cross into Spain, but most are hard paths open only a few months of the year. Two lesser ranges run across the centre of the department. South of them lies high ground, and north of them the rich plains of river soil. The entry gives the lay of a land that falls from ice to farmland.
britannica-1911-ayscue-sir-george:
Ayscue, Sir George (d. 1671), was a British admiral from an old Lincolnshire family, knighted by Charles I, of whom little is known before a naval command in 1646. In 1648 his influence kept much of the fleet loyal to Parliament when Batten defected to Holland.

Rewarded as admiral of the Irish Seas, Ayscue won Parliament's thanks at the relief of Dublin, helped Blake reduce Scilly, and conquered Barbados and other royalist islands. The drawn battle off Plymouth in 1652 cost him his command. After years advising Sweden for Cromwell, he returned at the Restoration. He fought at Lowestoft. In the Four Days' Battle of 1666 he lost his flagship and his liberty. He stayed a prisoner in Holland until the peace.
britannica-1911-bage:
Bagé is a town and municipality of the state of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil, about 176 miles by rail west-north-west of the city of Rio Grande. The municipality counted 22,692 people in 1890. The town stands 774 feet up in a hilly region near the Uruguayan border.

Bagé trades for a wide district where cattle work rules. Its region forms the watershed of southern Rio Grande do Sul, streams running east to the Atlantic and north-west to the Uruguay river. Dating from colonial times, the town has always mattered militarily, lying only twenty-five miles from the frontier. An Argentine general captured it in 1827, it figured in most of Argentina's civil wars, and Uruguayan revolutionists often frequent it.
britannica-1911-balfour-sir-james-judge:
Sir James Balfour of Pittendreich (died 1583 or 1584) was a Scottish judge and politician. Trained for the legal side of the Scottish church, he was taken at St Andrews in 1547 and sent to the French galleys with John Knox and others. Freed in 1549, he changed sides more than once.

Balfour served Mary of Guise, then the lords of the congregation, whose plans he betrayed. Under Queen Mary he rose fast: lord of session, privy councillor, and lord clerk register. The 1911 Britannica entry ties him closely to Bothwell and to the plot against Darnley. He is said to have drawn up the Craigmillar bond and to have lodged Darnley at Kirk o' Field.
britannica-1911-banbridge:
Banbridge is a town of County Down, Ireland, on the river Bann, 23 miles south-west of Belfast on a branch of the Great Northern railway. It stands on a rise, and its urban district held 5,006 people in 1901. The town is entirely modern, the entry stresses.

One odd work marks its main street. To ease a steep climb, a central carriageway 200 yards long is cut fifteen feet deep along the street. Bridges join the terraces on each side. Banbridge is the chief seat of the linen trade in the county, with cloth and thread factories, bleachfields, and chemical works. The 1911 Britannica entry also notes a memorial in Church Square to the Franklin expedition and to Captain Francis Crozier, born in the town.
britannica-1911-bancroft-george:
George Bancroft (1800–1891) was an American historian and statesman, born at Worcester, Massachusetts, on 3 October 1800. His family had been in America since 1632, and his father Aaron was a revolutionary soldier, clergyman, and author. The son studied at Phillips Academy, Harvard, and then at Heidelberg, Göttingen, and Berlin.

At Göttingen, Bancroft learned Plato from Heeren, the great historical critic, and caught from him a zeal for minute, painstaking study. A tour of Europe brought him wide notice. Goethe, Humboldt, Hegel, and Byron were among those who received him. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, follows his turn from the ministry his father planned for him. It traces his move toward history and public life, and on to his great history of the United States.
britannica-1911-barge:
Barge, from a medieval Latin word for a boat, once named a small sailing vessel. By 1911 it generally meant a flat-bottomed boat for carrying goods on inland waters. Canal barges were usually towed, though some had engines, and the men in charge of them were called bargees.

On tidal rivers, barges often carried masts and sails, or drifted with the current steered by long oars, when they were called dumb-barges. Harbour barges that load and unload ships are called lighters. The 1911 Britannica entry adds grander and odder uses. There is the ornamented state barge for ceremonies. There are the Oxford college barges, houseboats for rowing clubs. In New England, a covered passenger vehicle is called a barge.
britannica-1911-barrington-george:
George Barrington (born 1755), an Irish pickpocket whose life took him to Australia, is the subject of a curious 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Born at Maynooth under the name Waldron, son of a working silversmith, he robbed his schoolmaster, ran away, and joined a touring theatre company as Barrington. At Limerick races he took up pocket-picking with the company manager, then fled to London and kept stealing, once robbing Prince Orlov of a costly snuff-box at Covent Garden.

Punishments did not stop him. After terms of hard labour and a release granted on condition he leave England, he was caught again and sentenced in 1790 to seven years' transportation to Botany Bay. On the voyage he revealed a convict plot to seize the ship, won freedom in 1792, and became superintendent of convicts and high constable at Parramatta. Books on Botany Bay and New South Wales followed.
britannica-1911-baton-rouge:
Baton Rouge is the capital of Louisiana, in the United States, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the east bank of the Mississippi river, about seventy miles north-west of New Orleans, on a bluff safe from the highest floods. Its people numbered 14,897 in the 1910 count. Old houses in the Spanish style give the town a quaint look, and the state capitol of 1880–1882 replaced one burned in the Civil War year of 1862.

Learning fills much of the entry. The State University and Agricultural and Mechanical College stands there, grown from a seminary once led by W. T. Sherman. Its Audubon Sugar School trains men in cane growing and sugar making. The town also holds schools for the deaf and blind, and the state prison. Sugar, cotton, and fruit farms crowd the rich river lands, and factory output nearly doubled from 1900 to 1905.
britannica-1911-benson-george:
George Benson (1699–1762) was an English dissenting minister born at Great Salkeld in Cumberland. Whitehaven school and Glasgow University trained him, and in 1722, on Edmund Calamy’s word, an Abingdon congregation chose him as pastor. In 1729 his turn to Arminian views moved him to a Southwark pulpit.

At Crutched Friars from 1740 Benson worked beside the learned Nathaniel Lardner and succeeded him in 1749. His Defence of the Reasonableness of Prayer came in 1731, with notes on Paul’s shorter epistles after it. His History of the First Planting of the Christian Religion came out in three volumes in 1738. It showed great learning. It won him fame well beyond his own communion. His Socinian views later cost his books their readers, all the same.
britannica-1911-bentham-george:
George Bentham (1800–1884) was an English botanist born at Stoke near Portsmouth, nephew of Jeremy Bentham. His father, Sir Samuel, was a naval engineer of near-equal gifts in another line. George had no school or college training at all.

What Bentham had was a power of steady, close attention, held the key to his standing as perhaps the greatest systematic botanist of his century. Botany drew him because the logical methods he had taken from his uncle’s writings fitted plant study so well, not from any early love of natural history. In 1854 he gave his herbarium and library to Kew. His Genera Plantarum, finished with Hooker, was received as warmly as Linnaeus’s Species Plantarum in its day.
britannica-1911-berkeley-george:
George Berkeley (1685–1753) was an Irish bishop and philosopher, eldest son of a customs officer, born near Dysert Castle at Thomastown. Kilkenny school and Trinity College, Dublin, trained him. At Dublin his subtle mind refused every doctrine on mere authority. That marked him to some as a dunce and to others as a genius.

Berkeley’s Common Place Book, his private notebook, lets readers watch his ideas grow. In 1709 his New Theory of Vision first applied his new principle. Sight and touch, he argued, share no common element. Each must be learned by experience. His deeper claim is that matter, as an abstract unseen stuff, does not exist. The entry argues it at length. For all its defects, it judges the conception a clear step forward in human thought.
britannica-1911-berlin-carriage:
Berlin, as a carriage, is a four-wheeled vehicle with a separate hooded seat behind, detached from the main body. This short 1911 Britannica entry explains that the design took its name from the city of Berlin, where it was first used. It was designed about 1670 by a Piedmontese architect in the service of the Elector of Brandenburg, and it served as a travelling carriage.

The word carried other meanings too. As an adjective it marks goods first made in Berlin, of which the best known is Berlin wool, and a Berlin warehouse sells wools and fancy goods. Swift mentions authors who scribble in a berlin, and Scott uses the spelling for the birlinn, a large Gaelic rowing boat.
britannica-1911-bilge:
Bilge is a word drawn from bulge, through the French bouge and the Latin bulga, a bag. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the word three linked senses at sea and in the cooper's yard. First, it is the belly, or widest part, of a cask. Second, it is the broad, flattish part of a ship's bottom above the keel. Third, it is the lowest inside part of the hull itself.

From that last sense comes the term bilge-water. It is the foul water that gathers in the bilge of a ship. Bilge-keels are also defined in the entry. They are pieces of timber fixed to a ship's bottom to cut down rolling. The entry is a short glossary note of a few lines. It points readers to the article on shipbuilding for the keels in detail.
britannica-1911-birkbeck-george:
George Birkbeck (1776–1841) was an English physician and philanthropist, born at Settle in Yorkshire. He showed an early bent for science as a boy. In 1799, fresh from his medical degree, he took the natural philosophy chair at Glasgow's Andersonian Institution. The next year he gave a free course of science lectures for working people. Those lectures ran for three years and proved a great success. He moved to London in 1804 to push his schemes further.

In 1823 he helped found the London Mechanics' Institute, the 1911 Britannica entry records. The institute later took his name as Birkbeck Institution, or College. He endowed it with £3,700 at the start and directed it until his death. He died on 1 December 1841 with the work still growing. Buildings grew in 1883 to 1885 as its classes widened. Day and evening classes now cover sciences, literature, languages, and art.
britannica-1911-blackmore-richard-doddri:
Richard Doddridge Blackmore (1825–1900) was an English novelist best known for Lorna Doone. Born at Longworth in Berkshire, where his father was curate, he went to Blundell's School and Exeter College, Oxford, then trained for the bar and was called in 1852. Poor health later forced him out of London.

He settled at Teddington, worked as a market-gardener, and wrote on the side. Clara Vaughan (1864) was his first novel, and Lorna Doone (1869) made him famous at once as a leader of the romantic revival. Later novels named include The Maid of Sker and Christowell. The entry praises the book's outdoor air, its hero John Ridd, and the yearly visits readers make to the Doone Valley.
britannica-1911-bocage:
Bocage is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French landscape term. The word comes from an old French term for a wood. It is applied to several regions of France. Those regions share a set of common marks. A granite formation underlies them in most cases. Their surface is undulating or hilly in character. Much of the land is heath or reclaimed ground. Clumps of trees dot the fields and lanes.

The most important district is the Bocage of Normandy. It covers parts of three departments named in the text. Those are Calvados, Manche, and Orne in the north. A second district is the Bocage of Vendee. It sits in the departments of Vendee and Deux-Sevres. Maine-et-Loire and Loire-Inferieure also hold parts of it. The entry is brief, but it fixes the term well. Land, rock, and tree cover give the word its sense.
britannica-1911-bonney-thomas-george:
Thomas George Bonney (born 1833) was an English geologist who made the Alps and old rocks his study. Born at Rugeley, the grammar school master's son, he went to Uppingham and St John's College, Cambridge, and came out 12th wrangler in 1856. Ordained in 1857, he taught maths at Westminster school until 1861, pursuing geology as a pastime in the Alps.

In 1868 St John's made him tutor and geology lecturer. His field work centred on igneous and metamorphic rocks, in the Alps and across England and Scotland, from the Lizard and Salcombe to Charnwood Forest, Wales, and the Highlands. He took the geology chair at University College, London, in 1877. He led the Geological Society, the Mineralogical Society, and the Alpine Club, and his books include The Story of our Planet (1893).
britannica-1911-boole-george:
George Boole (1815–1864) was an English mathematician and logician who taught himself advanced maths while working as a schoolmaster. Born in Lincoln, a poor but studious tradesman's son, he first loved classics and came to higher mathematics only at seventeen, slowed by lack of good help. At sixteen he was already an assistant teacher at Doncaster.

He kept school at Lincoln, moved it to Waddington, and in 1849 became professor of mathematics at Queen's College, Cork. In 1855 he married Mary Everest. To the public he was known by his books on logic and maths. The entry's later pages set out his symbolic method, by which set premises yield their conclusions by rule, and its twin method for probabilities in the Laws of Thought.
britannica-1911-borage: Borage is a herb with bright blue flowers and hairy leaves and stem, known in the garden as Borago officinalis. The very short entry gives its sound, like courage, and guesses its name came from a Latin word for rough hair. In the entry's time the plant was valued as a cordial, a drink meant to lift the heart, and as a herb to bring down fever. Cooks used it too, the entry adds, putting it into salads and into claret-cup, a spiced wine drink.
britannica-1911-bordage: Bordage is a short entry with two senses, one from the sea and one from feudal land law. In sea language, from a French word for side, it is the planking on a ship's side. In feudal language, from a Latin word for a cottage, it is a kind of villein tenure. The services owed by such tenants took the same name. A bordar got his cottage from his lord in return for menial work. The entry sends readers to the article on villenage.
britannica-1911-brigandage:
Brigandage takes its name from the Italian brigante, an irregular or partisan soldier. Bandit, a word of the same sense, comes from a man declared outlaw by proclamation, the bando. Italy is treated as the classic home of the craft. The brigand so defined makes war by ambush and surprise, lives off plunder, blackmail and ransom, and kills prisoners who cannot pay.

Yet the long entry insists the label is not always just. Brigandage could be the last resort of a people under invasion. Calabrians who fought for Ferdinand of Naples and Spanish irregulars who resisted the French from 1808 to 1814 were called brigands by their foes. One Calabrian on trial before a French court under Murat turned the charge back, telling his judges that they were the thieves. History, custom and law across many lands fill out the survey that follows.
britannica-1911-brizeux-julien-auguste-p:
Julien Auguste Pelage Brizeux (1803–1858) was a French poet born at Lorient in Morbihan on 12 September 1803. His family was of Irish origin, long settled in Brittany, and he was trained for the law. In 1827 he instead reached the stage, with a one-act verse comedy, Racine, written with Philippe Busoni and staged at the Theatre Francais.

Travel in Italy with Auguste Barbier marked him deeply, and a second visit in 1834 led to a full translation of Dante's Divine Comedy in terza rima, printed in 1841. Yet Brittany gave him his true subjects: the rustic idyll Marie (1836), Les Bretons (1845) drawn from his native province's folklore and legends, and Telen-Aroor (1844) in Breton dialect. His Histoires poetiques (1855) was crowned by the French Academy. He died at Montpellier on 3 May 1858, leaving studies in Breton language and place-names behind him.
britannica-1911-bronze-age:
Bronze Age is the name archaeologists give to the stage of human culture between the Stone Age and the Iron Age. When weapons, tools and utensils were as a general rule made of bronze. The term carries no fixed dates. It marks a level of civilisation through which most races are believed to have passed at one time or another. Some lands passed through it earlier and others later.

Finds of stone with bronze, bronze with iron, and even stone with iron together in burial mounds suggest the three stages overlapped in many countries. Yet likeness of weapon and tool types across Europe has led most authorities to put a fairly shared start there between 2000 and 1800 BC. Mexicans and Peruvians were still in a bronze age in recent times. Some archaeologists have denied any distinct Bronze Age existed, a challenge the entry takes up from the mixed finds themselves.
britannica-1911-brown-george:
George Brown, a Canadian newsman and statesman who lived from 1818 to 1880, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born in Edinburgh on November 29, 1818. He moved with his father to New York in 1838, then to Toronto in 1843. There they started The Banner, and in 1844 he began the Toronto Globe on his own.

The Globe grew from a weekly to a daily in 1853 and swayed opinion across Ontario. Brown entered the Canadian parliament in 1851 and led the Clear Grit party. He pushed for seats by population count, a rule won in 1867. He also backed a union of the British colonies in North America.
britannica-1911-browne-william-george:
William George Browne (1768–1813) was an English traveller born at Great Tower Hill, London, on 25 July 1768. Sent at seventeen to Oriel College, Oxford, he left the university with a moderate competence from his father and gave himself to literary pursuits. The fame of James Bruce's travels and the African Association's first discoveries turned him into an explorer of Central Africa.

He reached Alexandria in January 1792, visited the oasis of Siwa, and spent the year studying Arabic and examining ancient Egypt's ruins. In spring 1793 he visited Sinai and in May set out for Darfur with the great yearly caravan by the desert route, his most important journey, rich in new information. The sultan of Darfur detained him by force and he endured much hardship, blocked from returning by Abyssinia, until allowed back to Egypt with the caravan in 1796. After a year in Syria he reached London in September of the next year.
britannica-1911-bryn-mawr-college:
Bryn Mawr College is a college for women in Pennsylvania. It stands at Bryn Mawr, five miles west of Philadelphia. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the school. The site covers 52 acres above rolling country. The buildings are grey stone in Jacobean Gothic style. They include lecture and science halls. The library held about 55,000 volumes in 1908. There are also a gymnasium, a hospital and six halls of residence.

Dr Joseph W. Taylor founded the college. He was a member of the Society of Orthodox Friends. The college was incorporated in 1880. It opened for instruction in 1885. In 1908 it had 419 students. Entrance demands are high. Students follow a group system for their studies. It lets them specialize in two or more subjects. Teaching is given largely by lectures. The college takes hearers, undergraduates, and graduate students. Graduates may work toward the M.A. or the Ph.D.
britannica-1911-buchanan-george:
George Buchanan (1506–1582) was a Scottish humanist and scholar. This long 1911 Britannica biography follows his career. He was born in February 1506 at the farm of Moss, in Killearn parish. His father died young and left the family poor. An uncle sent him to the university of Paris in 1520. When the uncle died, he came home. He studied at St Andrews and graduated in 1525. He followed his teacher John Major back to Paris.

At Paris he taught at the college of Sainte-Barbe. He later tutored the young earl of Cassilis. The article follows his church disputes and his time abroad. It covers his years in Portugal and his trial there. His satire Franciscanus is among the works named. His De Jure Regni set out his political thought. His Rerum Scoticarum Historia told Scotland's story in Latin. He died on 28 September 1582.
britannica-1911-bull-george:
George Bull was an English divine who lived from sixteen thirty four to seventeen ten. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Wells and schooled at Tiverton, he entered Exeter College, Oxford. He left in sixteen forty nine when he refused an oath to the Commonwealth.

Bull was ordained in secret in sixteen fifty five by Bishop Skinner. He rose through posts at Bristol, Suddington, Gloucester, and Llandaff over time. In seventeen o five he became bishop of Saint Davids in Wales. His chief work defends the Nicene faith from the early church fathers. He also wrote to show that Paul and James agree on justification.
britannica-1911-burges-george:
George Burges, English scholar of the old tongues, was born in India in 1786 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was schooled at Charterhouse and at Trinity College in Cambridge. He took his degree in 1807 and won a members prize in both 1808 and 1809. He stayed at Cambridge as a famed coach for students.

His name as a Greek scholar stood high, and he cut sharply at rival scholars in print. Bad ventures with money left him in straits in later years. In 1841 a civil list pension of one hundred pounds a year was granted to him. He died at Ramsgate in 1864. The entry faults his love of bold changes to old texts, yet grants his vast learning and hard work.
britannica-1911-burns-sir-george:
Sir George Burns lived from 1795 to 1890 and was an English ship owner. The Britannica life of 1911 opens in Glasgow, where he was born. His father was a clergyman named John Burns of that city. With his brother James he set up as a merchant about 1818. Six years later the pair ran small sailing ships to Liverpool.

Trade grew, and the ships soon sailed to Belfast as well. Steam craft in time took the place of sail on the route. In 1830 the firm joined hands with the McIver house of Liverpool. Burns took chief charge of the ships and their crews. In 1838 he helped found the Cunard line for Atlantic mails.
britannica-1911-butler-george:
George Butler is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Butler was an English schoolmaster and churchman who lived from 1774 to 1853. He was born in London and studied at Cambridge. He became a fellow there, first teaching maths and then Latin and Greek. He served as a public examiner and as a select preacher.

The article praises his time as head master of Harrow from 1805 to 1829. His wide knowledge, tact, and skill at sport made his rule both sound and liked. He later settled at Gayton and rose in the church. He became chancellor of Peterborough and then its dean in 1842. The text also gives short lives of two sons. One son's wife, Josephine Butler, won fame for rescue work among women.
britannica-1911-cabanis-pierre-jean-geor:
Pierre Jean George Cabanis, a French physiologist who lived from 1757 to 1808, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Cosnac, he was a lawyer's son sent to school at Brives at ten. Bright but headstrong, he warred with his teachers till he was dismissed. His father then left him to study as he liked at Paris for two years.

After travel in Poland and Germany he turned to verse, then, at his father's wish, to medicine. His work on hospitals won him charge of the Paris hospitals in 1789, and in 1795 he became professor of hygiene. He was close to Mirabeau in his last years. Cabanis backed the Revolution and sat in the Council of Five Hundred, but as a foe to tyranny he refused all posts under Bonaparte. His chief work ties mind to body.
britannica-1911-canning-george:
George Canning, who lived from 1770 to 1827, is the subject of a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a British statesman born in London to an Irish landed family. His father died on his first birthday, leaving the family with nothing. His mother went on the stage, and the boy grew up in a harsh household.

The article tells how an uncle, Stratford Canning, stepped in to save the boy. A small income was settled on him, and he was sent to Eton and then to Oxford. From that hard start he rose to high office in British public life. He led foreign policy for years and, near the end of his life, briefly headed the government. The life thus frames his rise as talent rescued by one timely act of family duty.
britannica-1911-carew-george:
George Carew (d. about 1613) was an English diplomatist and historian. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career in service. He was the second son of Sir Wymond Carew of Antony. He was educated at Oxford and at the Inns of Court. He then spent some years in travel on the continent. Queen Elizabeth knighted him in reward for merit. He became secretary to Sir Christopher Hatton.

Carew rose to a mastership in chancery in time. He was sent as ambassador to the king of Poland. Under King James he helped negotiate the union with Scotland. For several years he served as ambassador to France. On his return he wrote a Relation of the State of France. It sketches the leading persons at the court of Henry IV. The work is written in the classical Elizabethan style. Dr Birch later printed it with his own history of negotiations.
britannica-1911-carriage:
Carriage is a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on vehicles used to carry goods and people. In its widest sense the word covers any form of carrying, from a coster's barrow and a farm cart to railway sleeping-cars and royal state carriages. The entry narrows its scope to vehicles for carrying persons that are drawn by horses. Tramcars, railway carriages, and motor-cars are left to other articles.

A history opens the account. Wheeled carriages appear early in Egypt as the car or chariot, the word the Bible usually renders as chariot. These bodies were small and light, holding two people standing upright, and they could run at great speed. Their narrow build suited the tight streets of eastern cities and mountain roads sometimes only four feet wide. The entry builds from such beginnings toward the horse-drawn carriages of its own day, treating form, build, and use in detail.
britannica-1911-carteret-sir-george:
Sir George Carteret (c. 1610–1680) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English politician born on Jersey, where his family had long held land. Trained for the sea, he became comptroller of the navy in 1639. During the Civil War he served the king, succeeding his uncle as bailiff of Jersey in 1643 and becoming the island's lieutenant-governor the same year.

From Jersey, Carteret ran an active privateering campaign for the Royalist cause, and Parliament branded him a pirate and barred him from any amnesty. His rule was severe but profitable, and the island sheltered Royalist exiles, including Prince Charles, who made him a knight and baronet. In 1650 Charles granted him an island near Virginia to be called New Jersey, though no settlement followed then. After a seven weeks' siege he surrendered Jersey in 1651 and joined the exiles in France.
britannica-1911-cartilage: Cartilage is a very short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, a single sentence long. It defines cartilage, from the Latin cartilago, as the firm, elastic, and gristly connective tissue found in vertebrates. The entry gives no further detail of its own. Instead it sends the reader to the articles on Connective Tissues and on Joints for the fuller account of where this tissue sits in the body and how it works.
britannica-1911-cartridge: Cartridge is a very short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, a single sentence long. The word is a corruption of the French cartouche, and the entry defines a cartridge as a case of brass or other metal, cardboard, silk, or flannel. The case holds an explosive charge and, usually, the projectile as well, and it serves both small arms and ordnance. For the full treatment the entry points the reader to the article on Ammunition.
britannica-1911-cathcart-sir-george:
George Cathcart, who lived from 1794 to 1854, was an English soldier and son of an earl. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from Eton and Edinburgh into the army in 1810. As aide to his father he went to Russia and joined headquarters in 1813. He saw the great battles in Germany and France and the taking of Paris.

His close study of those wars bore fruit in a plain, soldierly history in 1850. After peace he went to the congress of Vienna with his father in train. He stood at Quatre Bras and Waterloo as aide to Wellington himself. Staff duty kept him in France until the army of occupation left.
britannica-1911-cattermole-george:
George Cattermole, an English painter chiefly in water colours, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Diss in Norfolk in August eighteen hundred, he began work at sixteen. He started as a draughtsman of buildings and views. He then made designs to be engraved for popular annuals.

From there he moved into water colour painting in his own right. He became an associate of the Water Colour Society in eighteen twenty two and a full member later. In eighteen fifty he withdrew from that society and took to painting in oil. His most fertile period fell between those years, the entry says.
britannica-1911-clinton-george:
George Clinton (1739-1812) was an American soldier and leader in affairs of state. He was born at Little Britain, in Ulster county, New York, on 26 July 1739. His father, Charles Clinton, was born in Ireland of English parents and came to America in 1729. The father led a regiment of local troops in the French and Indian War. The son went to sea at sixteen but found the sailor's life sour to his taste.

Clinton joined his father's regiment and went with him as lieutenant in the attack on Fort Frontenac in 1758. After the war he practised law in his home town and held minor posts in the county. From 1768 to 1775 he sat in the New York assembly. In the quarrels with Great Britain he backed the colonial cause with zeal. In 1775 he was chosen for the second Continental Congress.
britannica-1911-codinus-george:
George Codinus is the name borne by three works of the late Greek east, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out the doubt that hangs on that name. The tie of the works to him is a mere ease of use, the text holds. Two of the three are with no name in the hand copies. Of the man himself, no fact is known at all. He is thought to have lived toward the end of the fifteen hundreds.

The chief of the three works deals with the chief city of that east realm. It treats its past, its ground plan, and its marks of note. Its parts run from the found of the city to its bounds, its statues, its halls, and the build of its great church. The work was writ in one reign of the realm.
britannica-1911-college:
College in Roman law meant a body of men joined by shared work or shared rights. The 1911 Britannica article traces the word from that start. Such a body, called a collegium, held rights apart from those of each member, much like a modern corporation. At least three members were needed in law. Colleges served trade, faith, or public life, like the guilds of England or the priestly colleges of Rome.

The name now clings most to schools, above all the colleges of Oxford and Cambridge. In English law these are counted as charity corporations with a lay character. The article says they grew from free groups of teachers and scholars at the universities. Old tales speak of some three hundred halls at Oxford in early days. Rules in time bound scholars to licensed houses only.
britannica-1911-colman-george:
George Colman (1732–1794), called the Elder, was an English dramatist and essayist born at Florence. His father was resident at the court of the grand duke of Tuscany and died within a year of his birth. William Pulteney, later Lord Bath, took charge of the boy's schooling. Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, followed in turn.

At Oxford he joined with Bonnell Thornton to found The Connoisseur. That paper ran from 1754 to 1756 and reached its 140th number. Johnson judged that it wanted weight. Colman took his degree in 1755 and was called to the bar in 1757. Friendship with Garrick did the law no good. He kept at practice until Lord Bath died. The entry goes on to his theatre years. He ran Covent Garden as acting manager for seven years.
britannica-1911-combe-george:
George Combe, a Scots student of the mind who lived from 1788 to 1858, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born in Edinburgh on October 21, 1788. He went to Edinburgh high school and its university, then joined a law office in 1804. By 1812 he had his own law practice.

At first Combe laughed at phrenology, the claim that the brain's shape shows the mind. A brain cutting by Spurzheim changed his mind. He came to hold that the brain is the organ of mind, made of parts for each trait. His first essay on the topic came out in 1817. He helped found a group for it in 1820.
britannica-1911-concierge:
Concierge is a French word of unknown root, as a brief note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells. At first it named the guardian of a house or castle. In the middle ages it named a court officer who kept a royal palace.

In Paris the old palace on the island in the Seine left royal use about 1360 and became the seat of the courts of law. The part of it in the care of the concierge was then turned into a prison, the Conciergerie. In modern use the word names a hall porter or janitor.
britannica-1911-concubinage:
Concubinage, the state of a man and woman living as if wed without full legal marriage, is explained in a 1911 Britannica article. In early times a concubine was seen as a lower rank wife. She lacked firm rights and could be sent away at any time. Her children could lose their share to the wife's sons.

Roman law, the piece shows, treated it as a known legal status. A concubine did not rise to her partner's rank, and her children were not lawful heirs. Yet a father had to support them and leave them a share if no lawful children lived. Later wedlock between the parents could make the children lawful.
britannica-1911-cooperage:
Cooperage is the art of making casks, barrels and other round vessels. Their sides are built of split staves, held tight by hoops round them. The word runs back to Dutch and German terms for a cask maker, and to a Latin root of the same trade. Pliny gives the craft's birth to the folk of the Alpine valleys. Great age thus marks the trade.

Its branches split by the load the vessel must bear. Tight or wet cooperage makes casks for liquids. Dry or slack cooperage makes casks for dry goods. White cooperage makes tubs, pails and churns with even staves. Tight work calls for the most care and skill of the three. A liquid cask must stay tight when full, with no leak at any seam. The entry then walks through the making. A rope is passed round the staves and drawn tight by a windlass.
britannica-1911-crabbe-george:
George Crabbe (1754–1832) was an English poet born at Aldeburgh in Suffolk on 24 December 1754. His family came in part from Norfolk and in part from Suffolk. His grandfather was the first of the name to settle at Aldeburgh, as collector of customs there. The poet's father held a small post in the customs of the town in his turn. Six children were born to that house, and George was the eldest.

The sea has swept away the small cottage of his birth. The quay at Slaughden, half a mile off, still stands to be seen. His father worked there, and the son worked with him in later days. A dame's school in Aldeburgh gave him his first lessons. At nine or ten he went to a boarding school at Bungay. At twelve he moved to a school at Stowmarket and stayed there for years.
britannica-1911-cribbage:
Cribbage is a game of cards, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains its roots and its board. A much older game called Noddy came first, and cribbage seems to be a better form of it. John Aubrey credits its invention to Sir John Suckling, who lived from 1609 to 1642.

The entry describes a full pack of fifty-two cards and a board drilled with sixty holes for each player, plus a game hole at each end. Each player moves two pegs along the rows as scores grow. It sets out forms for two players, three players, and four players in pairs, with cards set aside to form the crib in each case.
britannica-1911-croly-george:
George Croly (1780–1860), a British divine and author, was born in Dublin on 17 August 1780, the son of a physician. Educated at Trinity College, Dublin, he took orders and held a small curacy in the north of Ireland. About 1810 he moved to London and lived by literary work. He wrote criticism for periodicals and gave poems, reviews, and essays to Blackwood's Magazine and the Literary Gazette.

Croly's chief works show a restless range. Paris in 1815 was a poem in the manner of Childe Harold, and Catiline a tragedy of 1822. Salathiel, a romance of the Wandering Jew kind, succeeded in 1829, and a life of George IV followed. He hoped long for preferment from Tory leaders his pen had served. A Whig patron, Lord Brougham, at last gave him the living of St Stephen's, Walbrook, in 1835. He died suddenly in London on 24 November 1860.
britannica-1911-cruikshank-george:
George Cruikshank is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English artist. He was a caricaturist and illustrator of his age. He lived from 1792 to 1878. He was born in London in September 1792. The entry accepts him as the type of the born humorous artist. His grandfather had taken up the arts before him. His father, Isaac Cruikshank, followed the painter's profession. The children were born amid those surroundings at home.

Their first playthings were the materials of their father's arts. George followed the family tradition with amazing facility. He easily surpassed his peers as an etcher in youth. His father died about the year 1811. George, still in his teens, was already a popular artist by then. All his acquisitions were native gifts of home growth. Outside training was dispensed with in his case.
britannica-1911-darley-george:
George Darley (1795-1846) was an Irish poet born in Dublin. His parents emigrated to America and left him with his grandfather at Springfield in County Dublin. He graduated from Trinity College, Dublin, in 1820, but a bad stammer barred the church and the bar, so he settled in London. His first poems, The Errors of Ecstasie, appeared in 1822, and he wrote steadily for The London Magazine.

Darley counted Cary, the translator of Dante, and Charles Lamb among his friends. Under the name Grey Penseval he published prose tales in 1826, and his fairy opera Sylvia met no success. About 1830 he became dramatic and art critic to the Athenaeum. His longest poem, Nepenthe, came in 1835, and he died in London in November 1846.
britannica-1911-decimal-coinage:
Decimal coinage sets coin values in tens around one standard unit. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes no real system keeps that strict pure form. France pairs its franc with ten and one hundred franc pieces above it. Half steps like twenty and five break the clean scale in practice there.

The United States led in 1786 and 1792 with the dollar unit. France came next, and the Latin Union spread her scheme in 1865. Germany, the north kingdoms, Austria Hungary, Russia, and Japan all joined in time. Britain and India stood out as the chief holdouts in that era. English plans split on keeping the pound or the farthing base.
britannica-1911-demiurge:
Demiurge, from Greek words for one who works for the people, means a handicraftsman or artisan. In Homer the word stretches wide, covering not only hand-workers but even heralds and physicians. In early Attica the demiurgi formed one of the three classes of the people, beside the Eupatridae and the land-working geomori. The entry weighs whether they were a class of the whole people or a kind of trading nobility.

Across the Peloponnese, Sparta excepted, and in many parts of Greece the word named a high magistrate. Elis and Mantineia sent demiurgi to the peace treaty of 420 B.C., and the Achaean League had ten such officers presiding over its assembly. In Plato the word names the creator of the world, and the Gnostics took it up from him.
britannica-1911-eliot-george:
George Eliot, the famed English novelist, opens a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. That pen name hid Mary Ann Evans, born in 1819. She was born at Arbury Farm in Warwickshire, her father's post. Her father ran the estate of a local landowner there. Her first twenty-one years passed on that Arbury estate. Schooling at plain, sound schools ran till she was seventeen.

Her mother's death called the young Eliot home as housekeeper. Freed from set lessons, she read widely by her own taste. She worked at German, Italian, and music on her own. A strict faith training in youth marked her mind for life. In 1841 the family moved to Coventry and a wider circle. New friends there, the entry shows, stirred her thought.
britannica-1911-erzgebirge:
Erzgebirge, a mountain chain of Germany, is mapped in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It runs from the Elbe to the Elstergebirge along the frontier between Saxony and Bohemia. Its length runs to about eighty miles, and its mean breadth to about twenty five. The south slope stands steep and rugged.

In places that south wall drops in a near straight fall of 2000 to 2500 feet. The north side splits into valleys and slopes gently to the great plain of north Germany. Some of those valleys are rich, and others wild and romantic. The core of the chain forms a plateau more than 3000 feet high on average. At its ends rise the highest peaks, the Keilberg at 4080 feet and the Fichtelberg at 3980 feet.
britannica-1911-eschwege:
Eschwege is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Eschwege is a town in the Prussian district of Hesse-Nassau in Germany. It stands on the river Werra, southeast of Cassel. By 1905 its people numbered just over eleven thousand. The town joins an old town, a new town, and a small island part by bridges.

The article calls it a busy making town. Its trades include leather work, yarn spinning, and cloth weaving. Other trades make cigars, brushes, drinks, oil, glue, and soap. Two old buildings are named, a tower from 1455 and the old castle. The history notes shifts between Thuringia and Hesse. It was home to a branch of the Hessian house until that line died out in 1655.
britannica-1911-etheredge-sir-george:
Sir George Etheredge, also spelled Etherege (about 1635–1691), was an English dramatist of the Restoration. He came from an Oxfordshire family and may have studied at Cambridge. Dennis insisted he knew neither Greek nor Latin. He travelled in France early and may have seen Molière's first comedies in Paris. Back in London he read law at an Inn of Court. His first comedy, The Comical Revenge or Love in a Tub, reached the Duke's theatre in 1664.

Its sparring between Sir Frederick and the Widow brought a new style of wit to the English stage. She Would If She Could followed in 1668, airy, busy and immoral. Etheredge moved among Sedley, Rochester and the court wits, and settled 6,000 pounds on his daughter by the actress Elizabeth Barry. The entry judges that his London men and women live vividly, though with less insight than Congreve's.
britannica-1911-fichtelgebirge:
Fichtelgebirge is a mountain group of Bavaria, treated in this 1911 Britannica article. It forms the centre from which several ranges run out: the Elstergebirge toward the Erzgebirge in the north-east, the Frankenwald in the north-west, and the Böhmerwald in the south-east. The streams it gives rise to flow toward the four chief points of the compass.

The Eger runs east and the Saale north, both to the Elbe, the Weisser Main runs west to the Rhine, and the Naab south to the Danube. The highest points of the mass are the Schneeberg at 3,448 feet and the Ochsenkopf at 3,356 feet. The district is fairly thickly peopled and rich in wood. It also holds iron, copper, lead, sulphur, and many kinds of marble, and its people work chiefly in the iron mines, at forges and blast furnaces, and in charcoal burning.
britannica-1911-findlay-sir-george:
Sir George Findlay, an English railway manager who lived from 1829 to 1893, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was of pure Scots descent and was born at Rainhill in Lancashire in May 1829. He went to school at Halifax but left at the age of fourteen. He then set to learn the mason's craft on the Halifax railway, where his father worked.

Two years on he got a place on the Trent Valley works, and when that line was done in 1847 he went to London. There he helped build engine sheds at Camden Town. Years later, as general manager of that same railway, he could point to stones he had dressed with his own hands. He rose through charge of tunnel work and of line building.
britannica-1911-frank-marriage:
Frank-marriage, in Latin liberum maritagium, was a form of estate in English land law, by then already obsolete. When a landowner gave land to a daughter on her marriage, she and her husband held it, with the heirs of their two bodies, free of all service except fealty. That freedom lasted until the fourth degree of descent from the giver had passed.

The right of a freeholder to settle land in this way was first recognised in the reign of Henry II. From then until the reign of Elizabeth it stayed the most usual kind of marriage settlement. The entry is short and purely legal, giving the term, its terms of tenure, and the span of its use.
britannica-1911-frankpledge:
Frankpledge was an early English system in which neighbours stood surety for one another. Groups of ten men, called tithings, were bound to produce any member accused of wrongdoing, or bear the loss themselves. Laws of Edgar and of Canute, the latter from about 1030, already required every man to have such a surety, called a borh.

After the Norman Conquest the system took the name frankpledge, and laws of Henry I ordered every person of substance over twelve to be enrolled.
