Sheriffs checked the rolls at their tourn, later limited to one view a year at Michaelmas. Many lords held the view in their own court leet. The system was still active in 1376 but faded under the Tudors, though a few courts leet survived to modern times.
britannica-1911-fraternities-college:
College fraternities are student societies found in the colleges of the United States and Canada, most named from Greek letters. They work on the lodge system, each body made of chapters, with only one chapter of a fraternity at any one college. All are nominally secret, Delta Upsilon excepted, and members join as freshmen and live together in chapter houses.

The first was Phi Beta Kappa, founded at William and Mary in 1776, which later turned purely honorary. Union College gave Kappa Alpha in 1825, Sigma Phi and Delta Phi in 1827, and Psi Upsilon in 1833, and the system spread from there. By 1910 there were 32 men general fraternities with 1068 chapters. Professional bodies began with Theta Xi in 1864, and women societies with Kappa Alpha Theta in 1870.
britannica-1911-fuller-george:
Fuller, George (1822–1884), an American painter, was born at Deerfield, Massachusetts. He spent time in the studio of the sculptor H. K. Brown at Albany. In 1857 he was elected to the National Academy of Design. For years his work attracted little notice, and he painted in obscurity at Deerfield.

From 1876 his pictures suddenly found favour, and his reputation rose quickly. His canvases are known for the brown mist that hangs over their figures. Among his best-known works are The Turkey Pasture, Romany Girl, and Nydia, the Blind Girl of Pompeii. He died at Boston on the 21st of March 1884.
britannica-1911-gage: Gage is a pledge, something handed over as security that an agreement will be kept, and forfeited if it is not. The word runs through engage, wage and wager, and comes from Old French, from the Latin vadium, a pledge. One special way of giving a gage was throwing down a glove or gauntlet as a challenge to judicial combat, the glove pledging that both parties would appear on the field. Hence the phrase to throw down the gage of defiance, for any challenge.
britannica-1911-gamboge:
Gamboge is a gum resin got from a tree of Cambodia and Siam. The 1911 Britannica entry takes its name from Camboja, its home district. The tree that yields it bears leathery leaves like laurel leaves. Its blooms are small and yellow, and its fruit holds four seeds. The juice that hardens into gamboge sits in ducts in the bark.

Men cut the bark and catch the juice in bamboo joints set below. In trade it comes in round pipes or rolls of that juice. Poorer grades come in cakes or in loose, shapeless masses instead. It looks a dirty orange outside, hard and brittle to the touch. Ground down, it yields a bright yellow powder for paint.
britannica-1911-gauge:
Gauge, in the 1911 Britannica, is a word for a standard of measurement, and for the tools that measure against it. The entry starts with wine casks: gauging first meant finding what a cask holds, and gauger still names certain American custom-house officials, and in Scotland an exciseman. From casks the word spread to all kinds of measure.

Workshop gauges check that work matches set sizes, and set sizes are used for wire and screws. The entry then explains single gauges in detail: the rain gauge, the wind gauge, and the water and steam gauges on a boiler. The Bourdon steam gauge gets a full account of its curved tube and pointer. Railway gauge, the distance between the rails, and the sailor's weather gage close the survey.
britannica-1911-german-language:
German is a language of the West Germanic group, and a long entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out its kin and its scope. Together with English and Frisian it forms that group. The group also once held Langobardian, a tongue that died out by the ninth or tenth century. Burgundian is classed with the East Germanic group instead.

The entry defines the German tongue as the speech of tribes who spoke it at their first look in history and speak it still. It names Saxons, Franks, Hessians, Thuringians, Alemannians, and Bavarians. Dutch and Flemish spring from the same stock but are left out, as their later growth ran apart from German.
britannica-1911-gerry-elbridge:
Elbridge Gerry, an American statesman who lived from 1744 to 1814, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Marblehead, Massachusetts, the son of a rich merchant from England. He graduated at Harvard in 1762 and joined his father's trade. By 1772 he sat in the Massachusetts General Court with the patriot party.

Gerry served on the Committee of Correspondence, a key tool of joint resistance by the colonies. In 1775 he backed a bill to arm ships against British trade and set up a prize court. From 1776 to 1781 he sat in the Continental Congress, where he urged independence early. He signed the Declaration of Independence after its formal signing, since he was away at the time. He also led the committee that watched over the treasury.
britannica-1911-gillespie-george:
George Gillespie, a Scottish divine who lived from 1613 to 1648, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Kirkcaldy in January 1613, where his father was parish minister, he entered St Andrews as a presbytery bursar in 1629. After a brilliant student career he became chaplain to Lord Kenmure and then to the earl of Cassillis. His conscience would not let him accept the episcopal ordination then required for a parish.

While with Cassillis, Gillespie wrote a dispute against English popish ceremonies imposed on the Church of Scotland. Published without his name in 1637, it drew wide notice. The privy council found it so harmful that copies were called in and burnt. In 1638 he was ordained minister of Wemyss and sat in the famous Glasgow Assembly. There he preached against royal interference in church matters.
britannica-1911-glas-george:
George Glas (1725-1765) was a Scottish seaman and merchant adventurer in West Africa, son of John Glas the divine. The 1911 Britannica entry has him born at Dundee in 1725 and brought up as a surgeon. He commanded a ship trading between Brazil, the north-west African coast and the Canary Islands.

On the Saharan coast he found a river navigable some way inland, and proposed a trading station there. The Lords of Trade promised 15,000 pounds if he won free cession of the port to the British crown. In 1764 he sailed with his wife and daughter, made a treaty with the local Moors, and named the place Port Hillsborough. The Spaniards seized and imprisoned him at Teneriffe. His shore party was attacked and several killed. Released in 1765, he sailed for England on the Earl of Sandwich. The crew mutinied for the ship's treasure, stabbed Glas, and threw his wife and daughter overboard.
britannica-1911-gleig-george:
George Gleig was a Scottish churchman who lived from the mid seventeen hundreds into the next age. Born on a farm, he went to college in Aberdeen at age thirteen and took first prizes there in maths and in moral thought. He took church orders young, held a charge in Fife, and later moved to Stirling, where he stayed for the rest of his life.

The 1911 Britannica entry stresses his work as a writer and editor. He wrote for leading reviews, gave key pieces to an early Britannica, and edited its last parts when its first editor died. Twice picked as bishop but blocked, he rose at last to head the church in Scotland, and pushed mild reform and closer ties with the church in England.
britannica-1911-gordon-cumming-roualeyn-:
Roualeyn George Gordon Cumming, a Scottish traveller and sportsman, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Known as the lion hunter, he was born in eighteen twenty. He was the second son of a baronet of Altyre and Gordonstown. From his early years he showed a strong passion for sport.

He was educated at Eton and at eighteen joined the East India Company service in India. He served as a cornet in the Madras Light Cavalry. The climate of India did not suit him, and he left after two years. In the East he had begun the hunting trophy collection for which he became known.
britannica-1911-gorge:
Gorge, a word whose strict sense is the throat seen from outside, is traced in a word study entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. From that base sense it spread in many ways. In falconry it names the crop of a hawk. It then came to mean the food fed to a hawk and what the crop holds.

From the sense of greed came the phrase about ones gorge rising at a thing one loathes. By likeness to a throat, gorge also names a narrow pass or ravine. In fort building it is the neck of a work or bastion. In building craft it is the narrow part of a Roman Doric column. The entry also sorts out gorget, a small form of the word. Gorgeous, the entry notes, may not come from gorge at all.
britannica-1911-gouge:
Gouge is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a tool of the chisel type. The word was adopted from the French gouge. The New English Dictionary makes it probably Celtic in origin. Welsh has gylf, a beak, and Cornish has gilb. A gouge has a curved blade in its build. It is used for scraping a groove or channel in wood. 

A similar instrument is used in surgery by doctors. It serves in operations for cutting out portions of bone. Gouge is also the name of a bookbinder's tool. That tool impresses a curved line on leather covers. In mining, a gouge is a layer of soft rock. It is sometimes found at the side of a coal vein. The miner can scoop it out with his pick. That lets him attack the vein more easily from the side.
britannica-1911-graham-sir-james-robert-:
James Robert George Graham was a British statesman born in Cumberland in the late seventeen hundreds. Schooled at Westminster and Oxford, he went abroad on the grand tour and served as aide to a British envoy in Sicily. Back in England he won a seat in the Commons for Hull as a Whig, then lost it at the next vote.

The 1911 Britannica entry follows his climb as a voice for change. A pamphlet on corn and cash made his name as a man of new views, and he backed the great Reform Bill with force. He rose to head the navy in the cabinet of Earl Grey. Quarrels over the Irish Church then split him from his party, and he crossed in time to the other side.
britannica-1911-grange:
A grange, in its first sense, is a granary or barn for storing grain. The word comes through French from a Latin term for a grain store. In the middle ages a grange was a cut off part of a manor. It had farm houses and barns and belonged to a lord or a religious house. Crops were stored there so rent or tithe could be gathered in.

Such barns are often called tithe barns, and a chapel was often among the buildings. The word now also names a fine farm house or a country house with farm land. In form a grange was a long building with a high wood roof. Posts or columns could split it into a nave and aisles. Some were huge, more than three hundred feet long.
britannica-1911-grenville-george:
George Grenville (1712-1770) was an English statesman, born on 14 October 1712, second son of Richard Grenville and Hester Temple. The 1911 Britannica entry has him educated at Eton and Christ Church, Oxford, and called to the bar in 1735. He entered parliament in 1741 for Buckingham, and held the seat until his death.

He began among the Boy Patriots who opposed Walpole. Office came in steps: lord of the admiralty in 1744, lord of the treasury in 1747, treasurer of the navy in 1754. In that post he carried a fairer system for paying seamen's wages. He stayed in office when his brother Temple and Pitt resigned in 1761, and led the Commons under Bute. The long article follows his rise to the premiership and the American taxation that made his name a byword across the Atlantic.
britannica-1911-grey-sir-george:
Sir George Grey (1812-1898) was a British colonial governor and statesman, born in Lisbon on 14 April 1812. The 1911 Britannica entry notes he was born eight days after his father, a lieutenant-colonel, fell at the storming of Badajoz. He passed through Sandhurst with credit and took his commission in 1829. In 1839 he sold out and left the army.

Stationed in Ireland in the early thirties, he saw poverty that left a deep mark on him. In 1836 the Royal Geographical Society accepted his offer to explore north-west Australia. He landed at Hanover Bay late in 1837, and was speared near the hip in a skirmish, shooting the chief who wounded him. His wound forced retreat, but he tried again the next year around Shark's Bay, through a series of disasters. The long article follows the governorships, in South Australia, New Zealand and the Cape, that made his name.
britannica-1911-guillaume-d-orange:
Guillaume d'Orange (d. 812) is a hero of French romance. He is also called Guillaume Fierabrace. Other names are St Guillaume de Gellone and Marquis au court nez. He stands at the centre of the southern cycle of romance. The trouvères called that cycle the geste of Garin de Monglane. Its poems form branches of one main story. That gives the cycle unusual unity.

Other great cycles treat Charlemagne or Doon de Mayence. The Guillaume poems instead hang together as one poetic history. Many cyclic manuscripts try to present that history whole. The account works through the poems branch by branch. It weighs their heroes, ladies and Saracen wars. It also asks what history lies behind the legend. The saint of Gellone and the courtier of Charlemagne merge in the figure. The result is a map of a whole epic family.
britannica-1911-harvey-sir-george:
Sir George Harvey, Scottish painter born at St Ninians near Stirling in February 1806, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a watchmaker. Soon after his birth the family moved to Stirling, where he was placed with a bookseller. Love of art grew too strong to deny.

At age eighteen he entered the Trustees Academy at Edinburgh. He shone there so fast that Scottish artists founding a new academy called him in as an associate in 1826. His first picture, A Village School, was shown that same year. From then on he showed work each year. His best known pictures treat scenes from faith history in a Puritan light. Works on Covenanters preaching and at communion lead that list.
britannica-1911-hay-george:
George Hay (1729–1811) was a Scottish Roman Catholic divine. He was born at Edinburgh on 24 August 1729. Accused of sympathising with the 1745 rebellion, he was imprisoned. His imprisonment ran from 1746 to 1747. He then entered the Roman Catholic Church. The Scots College at Rome trained him. In 1759 he joined a Scottish mission with John Geddes. Ten years later he became bishop of Daulis in partibus.

In 1778 he became vicar apostolic of the lowland district. Protestant riots in 1779 destroyed his furniture and library by fire. He ran the Scalan seminary from 1788 to 1793. In 1799 he founded the Aquhorties seminary near Inverury. He retired there in 1802 and died there in 1811. His theological works fill several devotional titles. The Sincere Christian and The Devout Christian lead them. Bishop Strain edited his works in 1871–1873.
britannica-1911-hayter-sir-george:
Sir George Hayter (1792–1871) was an English painter born in London. His father was a popular drawing-master and perspective teacher. The boy went to sea in early youth. Then he studied at the Royal Academy. Miniature painting was his first specialty. In 1816 he became miniature-painter to Princess Charlotte. Italy, especially Rome, held him for years between 1816 and 1831.

Back in London he turned to portraiture in oils. Royal likenesses multiplied from his hand. Victoria made him her principal painter. He also taught drawing to the princesses. A knighthood came in 1842. His large public canvases are essentially portrait groups. The Trial of Queen Caroline holds 189 likenesses. Queen Victoria taking the Coronation Oath is accounted his finest. Posterity, the verdict runs, will not keep the prestige court patronage gave him.
britannica-1911-hepplewhite-george:
George Hepplewhite (d. 1786) was one of the most famous English cabinet-makers of the 18th century, yet almost nothing is known of his life. He was apprenticed to Gillow at Lancaster and traded in the parish of Saint Giles, Cripplegate. His widow Alice took charge of his estate in June 1786 and traded on as A. Hepplewhite and Co. His work is known from The Cabinet-Maker and Upholsterer's Guide, first printed in 1788.

The name stands for a fashion more than a man, so no piece can be pinned to his hand. Lightness, delicacy and grace mark the style. Carving gave way to inlay, and chairs grew smaller. Its best-known form is the shield back, used in many designs. Legs grew slight and tapering, ending in a spade foot that often became a thin spider leg. Most modern chairs owe something to this school of makers.
britannica-1911-herbert-george:
George Herbert (1593–1633) was an English poet, born at Montgomery Castle on the 3rd of April 1593. He was a son of Sir Richard Herbert and brother of Lord Herbert of Cherbury. His mother Magdalen, a friend of John Donne, shaped him strongly. Schooled at Westminster, he went to Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1609, took his B.A. in 1613, and became a fellow in 1616. He was Reader in Rhetoric in 1618 and orator in 1619.

A sinecure rectory from King James in 1623 raised court hopes, but his patrons and the king soon died. Guided by his mother and by Nicholas Ferrar of Little Gidding, he took holy orders. He became prebendary of Layton Ecclesia in 1626 and rebuilt its church. In 1630 he was given the living of Fugglestone with Bemerton, near Salisbury, and ordained priest that September. He had married Jane Danvers in 1629, after three days' acquaintance. Izaak Walton's Life of him (1670) stays the standard account.
britannica-1911-hickes-george:
George Hickes (1642–1715) was an English divine and scholar, born at Newsham near Thirsk on the 20th of June 1642. He became a fellow of Lincoln College, Oxford, in 1664, and rector of St Ebbe's in 1675. After service as chaplain to the duke of Lauderdale in Scotland, he became dean of Worcester in 1683.

Hickes opposed James II's declaration of indulgence and Monmouth's rising, and tried to save his brother John, a Sedgemoor refugee. In 1688 he refused the oath of allegiance, lost his deanery, and fixed a protest to the cathedral doors. The nonjurors sent him to James II in France, and in 1694 he was consecrated suffragan bishop of Thetford. His great works are a grammar of Anglo-Saxon (1689) and the Thesaurus of the old northern languages (1703–1705).
britannica-1911-hitchcock-george:
George Hitchcock is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an American painter born in Rhode Island in eighteen fifty. He first trained for the law at two famed schools. He then gave up law and learned art in Paris instead.

The entry notes the Dutch garden scene that first won him notice in Paris. He kept a work room in Holland for years and painted Dutch scenes. French and German honours came to him in time. His works are held in large museums in Europe and America. The entry is brief, but it fixes his odd path from law books to paint and fame.
britannica-1911-horne-george: George Horne's entry survives only as a fragment. The hosted text opens mid-article, in the middle of a sentence about a series of expositions built on the Messianic idea; the opening of the article is missing. What remains is plain. In 1776 Horne was chosen vice-chancellor of his university. In 1781 he was made dean of Canterbury. In 1790 he was raised to the see of Norwich. He died at Bath on the 17th of January 1792. His collected Works, with a memoir by William Jones, appeared in 1799.
britannica-1911-hostage:
A hostage is a person handed over by one belligerent to another, or seized, as security for carrying out an agreement, or to prevent certain acts of war. The practice is very old, used again and again in dealings with conquered nations. The word comes through French from the late Latin for the state of being an obses, a hostage.

Rome took the sons of tributary princes and educated them in the city. That held a pledge for the nation's loyalty, and steeped a possible future ruler in Roman ways. Britain in her early occupation of India, and France among the Arab tribes of North Africa, copied the practice. The account follows hostages through later wars, down to the hostages of the Paris Commune in 1871, among them Archbishop Darboy and the judge Bonjean, shot in batches.
britannica-1911-jessel-sir-george:
George Jessel is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Jessel was an English judge who lived from 1824 to 1883. He was born in London, son of a Jewish coral merchant. Barriers of faith kept him from Oxford and Cambridge, so he went to University College in London. He gained high honours in maths and natural philosophy in 1844.

The article follows his rapid rise at the bar after 1847. His pay grew fast in his first three years, though his work lay mainly in property transfers. In 1868 he entered parliament as a Liberal for Dover. Two learned speeches on a bankruptcy bill won Gladstone's notice. In 1871 he was made solicitor general. His forceful, direct way with the bench drew wide respect. In 1873 he succeeded to the post of master of the rolls.
britannica-1911-keith-george:
George Keith (c. 1639–1716) was a British divine, born at Aberdeen about 1639 and trained for the Presbyterian ministry at Marischal College. In 1662 he became a Quaker and worked with Robert Barclay. After a term in prison for preaching in 1676, he toured Holland and Germany on a preaching mission with George Fox and William Penn.

Two more spells in prison in England drove him in 1684 to emigrate to America. There he was surveyor general in East New Jersey and then a schoolmaster at Philadelphia. He travelled in New England defending Quaker teaching against Increase and Cotton Mather. Then he fell out with his own people over the atonement, charged them with deist views, and formed a body of his own, the Christian Quakers, or Keithians. Back in London he pressed his case, but the Yearly Meeting of 1694 disowned him, and he set up a society of his own at Turner's Hall.
britannica-1911-kerguelen-s-land-cabbage:
Kerguelen's Land Cabbage is a plant of the cabbage family, in botany Pringlea antiscorbutica. It looks much like the common cabbage and belongs to the same family. Its cabbage like heads of leaves are rich in a pale yellow, highly pungent essential oil. The oil gives the plant a strong flavour but makes it very wholesome.

Captain Cook found it on his first voyage. The first account of it was printed by Joseph Hooker, in the botany of the Antarctic voyage of the Erebus and Terror. During that expedition's stay on the island the plant was eaten daily, cooked alone or boiled with the ship's beef, pork, or pea soup. Hooker called it perhaps the most interesting plant found on the whole voyage in the Antarctic Sea.
britannica-1911-kingsbridge:
Kingsbridge, a market town in Devonshire in England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies forty eight miles south south west of Exeter on a branch rail line. The urban district held 3025 people in 1901. The town sits six miles from the English Channel, at the head of an inlet.

That inlet takes in only small streams along its course. The town climbs a sharply sloping site above the water. Its church of St Edmund is mainly in the Perpendicular style of building. Parts of it reach back to Norman and Early English times in their form. The town hall holds a museum of natural history for the public. A house called Pindar Lodge stands where John Wolcot, the famed Peter Pindar, was born. Iron founding, ship building, and a coasting trade give the town its work.
britannica-1911-landor-walter-savage:
Walter Savage Landor, an English writer, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Warwick in seventeen seventy five, he was the eldest son of his parents. He was sent to Rugby school but was removed at the headmaster's request. He then studied in private with a vicar.

In seventeen ninety three he entered Trinity College, Cambridge, the entry tells. He took up republican views while there. In a famed incident he fired a gun at the windows of a Tory he disliked. He was sent down for a year and refused to return. That act also led to a sharp quarrel with his father.
britannica-1911-liddell-henry-george:
Henry George Liddell, an English scholar and church man born in eighteen eleven, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Binchester near Bishop Auckland, he was the eldest son of a church man of a noble house. He was schooled at Charterhouse and at Christ Church, Oxford.

He won top marks in two fields in eighteen thirty three. He then taught at his college and was ordained five years later. He served as Greek reader and then as head of Westminster School. His life work was a great word book of Greek and English. He and Robert Scott began that work in eighteen thirty four. The first form came out in eighteen forty three. It at once became the set book of its kind. The entry holds that it kept that rank for years, with much new matter added in time.
britannica-1911-lillo-george:
George Lillo (1693-1739) was an English playwright who worked by day in trade. London was his birthplace, on 4 February 1693. His Dutch father kept a jeweller's shop, and Lillo stayed a partner in it for years. A ballad opera, Silvia, opened his stage path in 1730.

Fame came on 22 June 1731 at Drury Lane. The London Merchant told of George Barnwell, a London apprentice who robbed his master and killed his uncle. Prose carried the tale. Low rank had long been barred from grave drama. Lillo broke that rule and went back to old English home tragedy. Moral aim was plain, and scoffers called it a Newgate tragedy. Crowds loved it all the same. Holiday shows for apprentices kept it alive for years. The Christian Hero followed in 1735.
britannica-1911-lockhart-george:
George Lockhart (1673-1731), of Carnwath, was a Scottish writer and man of politics. His Lanarkshire house traced its line to Sir Simon Locard. Tale links Locard to the heart of Bruce, borne east with Douglas. A heart in a lock on the shield keeps that tale. The strange surname grew from it, men hold.

Grandfather James held a judge's seat as Lord Lee. Uncle William fought for the king, then served Cromwell. He wed Cromwell's niece and sat as envoy at the French court. A second uncle, George, shone as a pleader in state trials. He rose to head the court of session in 1685. A wronged suitor shot him dead in Edinburgh in 1689. The Carnwath estates of the old earls came to that uncle by purchase. George took them up in his turn.
britannica-1911-macdonald-george:
George Macdonald, a Scottish novelist and poet who lived from 1824 to 1905, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Huntly in Aberdeenshire, he was the son of a farmer of Glencoe stock. His family line went back to families that suffered in the massacre of Glencoe. His youth passed under the strong influence of the Congregational Church and of Calvinism. He took his degree at Aberdeen University.

Macdonald then studied in London for the Congregational ministry. In 1850 he became pastor of a church at Arundel, and later did ministerial work in Manchester. Poor health forced a change, and after a stay in Algiers he settled in London as a writer. His first book, a dramatic poem, came out in 1856. The faerie romance Phantastes followed in 1858. His first clear success was David Elginbrod in 1862, the first of many popular novels.
britannica-1911-mackenzie-sir-george:
George Mackenzie of Rosehaugh, who lived from 1636 to 1691, was a Scots lawyer in a 1911 Britannica life. He was born at Dundee, schooled there and at Aberdeen, and took a degree at age sixteen. Three years of civil law study at Bourges in France followed. He joined the Scots bar in 1659 and rose fast in practice.

After the Restoration he held court posts and sat for the county of Ross in parliament. In 1677 he became king advocate under Charles the Second. In that post he took part in harsh acts of rule that stained his name for good. The entry is candid about both his talent and the dark mark his later office left.
britannica-1911-manrique-jorge:
Jorge Manrique is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Manrique was a Spanish poet and soldier who lived from about 1440 to 1478. He was born probably at Paredes de Nava. He was a son of a count of that place. Like his family he backed Queen Isabel with zeal. He served with honour in many fights and gained a post in the order of Santiago.

The article says he was killed in a skirmish near a fortress in 1478. His love songs and satires are called clever works in the taste of his age. His lasting fame rests on one poem alone. It is an elegy in forty stanzas on the death of his father. Great common thoughts on death gain new weight from his own grief in it. That single moment of high expression has kept his name bright for four centuries.
britannica-1911-marriage:
Marriage is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on the union of husband and wife. The text gives the roots of the word in French and Latin. It sets out two views of the term. One is the act or rite that makes the legal bond. The other is the shared life of the pair and their kin.

The entry then lays out three stages in the growth of the bond. The first is a loose stage with few rules. The next gives the husband a property right in his wife. The last treats the pair as more and more equal in law. The text notes that these stages did not fall in a neat line in each life.
britannica-1911-martin-homer-dodge:
Homer Dodge Martin, an American painter of land views, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life note. Born at Albany, New York, in eighteen thirty six, he trained for a short time with William Hart. His first work kept to the Hudson River School line. He joined the National Academy of Design as a full member in eighteen seventy four.

A trip to Europe in eighteen seventy six won him to the Barbizon school of France. He lived in France for four years and painted in Normandy. Named works span Westchester hills, the Adirondacks, and Newport views. Critics rank him with Inness and Wyant as a top trio in his field. He died at Saint Paul in eighteen ninety seven.
britannica-1911-mason-george:
George Mason lived from 1725 to 1792 and was an American statesman. The 1911 Britannica life opens in Stafford county, Virginia, his birth place. His family was of Royalist stock and came after Charles the First fell. Kin of his held posts in the civil and army service of Virginia. Mason was a near neighbour and lifelong friend of George Washington.

In later years the two friends split on points of politics. Vast estates and high rank gave Mason great sway with planters. He helped found the Ohio Company and the town of Alexandria. In 1759 he sat in the Virginia House of Burgesses for a term. In 1769 he drew up non importation resolves for Washington's use.
britannica-1911-matheson-george:
George Matheson is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a Scot who preached and wrote on faith from 1842 to 1906. He was born in Glasgow, the son of a merchant. He did well at the school in Glasgow in the old tongues and in thought. At age twenty he lost his sight in full. He still chose to join the church and study.

His first post began in 1868 at Innellan on the coast. Books on faith in Germany and on old and new belief made his name. Queen Victoria asked him to preach at Balmoral. In 1886 he moved to a church in Edinburgh. There he did his chief work as a preacher. One hymn of his is still sung in many churches.
britannica-1911-maubeuge:
Maubeuge is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a town of northern France in the department of Nord, on both banks of the Sambre river. It lay close to the Belgian frontier, east of Valenciennes by rail. Population figures for town and commune in nineteen hundred six are both given.

As a fortress it had an old ring of bastions at its centre. Around that lay a large entrenched camp built after the war of eighteen seventy. The town had a trade board, a college, and a commercial school. Foundries, forges, and blast furnaces gave it a strong industrial base.
britannica-1911-mcduffie-george:
George McDuffie was a statesman of the south in the United States, who lived from seventeen eighty-eight to eighteen fifty-one. He was born in Georgia and took to the bar past youth. He sat in the state house of the south land, then in the chief house of the land for past ten years. At first he wrote past lax reads of the state pact.

In time he swung to the most stern stand for state rights, past the sway of a great south chief. He helped draft his states defy note to the land. He served as state chief, then as a chief house man. His case that the maker pays the tax on goods from past seas was called the base of that stand.
britannica-1911-messuage: Messuage, in law, is a term equal in meaning to a dwelling house for legal purposes. Its brief entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica states that the term also covers outbuildings, an orchard, a court yard, and a garden that belong with the house. The word comes from Anglo French forms linked to words for a household and for dwelling. A wider sense beyond house may once have existed, but no such split in meaning survives in law today.
britannica-1911-monk-george:
George Monk, first Duke of Albemarle, who lived from 1608 to 1660, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the second son of a Devon gentleman of good family and poor means. He was born at Potheridge in December 1608. A thrashing given to a county under-sheriff drove him from home.

Monk took naturally to the career of arms after that flight. He served as a volunteer in the expedition to Cadiz. The next year he did good service at the Isle of Rhé. In 1629 he went to the Low Countries, then the school of war. There he won a high name as a leader and a disciplinarian. A quarrel with the civil powers at Dordrecht made him throw up his commission. Back in England he gained a lieutenant-colonelcy of foot. On the Scottish border he saved the English guns at Newburn by cool handling.
britannica-1911-morland-george:
English painter George Morland, born in London in seventeen sixty three, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He painted animals and rustic scenes. His grandfather was a subject painter whose popular pictures were engraved. His father was also an artist and engraver, and a picture restorer.

His father was at one time rich, but later fell into reduced means. His pictures of laundry maids were very popular in their day. Morland's mother was a Frenchwoman with a small property of her own. The boy showed sketches of remarkable promise at a very early age. He showed works at the Royal Academy in seventeen seventy three, at age ten. He kept showing at art societies through his teens. His father kept a drawing the boy had made even earlier.
britannica-1911-mortgage:
Mortgage is an old French legal word that means dead pledge in sense. Its law entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. A mortgage secures money by making it a charge on property goods. If the debt is not paid by the set time, sale can follow.

In English law the property passes to the lender by a deed form. That deed fails if the debt is paid on the fixed day. Roman law shows three clear stages in the growth of such deals. First the land passed whole, with a pledge to give it back. Next the lender held the goods but not the title to them.
britannica-1911-mount-holyoke-college:
Mount Holyoke College is a school for the higher study of women in South Hadley, Massachusetts. It stands near Mount Holyoke and was the first school of its kind in America. Mary Lyon founded it, and it was chartered as Mount Holyoke Female Seminary in 1836. It opened in 1837 and took the name of college in 1893. Its grounds hold halls for class work and labs, an art block, a library, and seven homes for students.

For the first two years, students take set courses in Latin, Greek, French, German, English, and history. They also study the Bible, physics, and chemistry. The last two years are spent on courses they choose. A year of higher work is open to those who have finished. Each student helps with house work or school tasks to keep costs down.
britannica-1911-old-forge:
Old Forge is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a borough in Pennsylvania. It lies in Lackawanna county on the Lackawanna river. Scranton stands about six miles to the north east. A count from 1900 gives the borough 5630 people. Of those, 2494 were born in foreign lands. Most of that group were Italians, the text says. Two railways serve the borough for travel and trade.

The town hall and the high school are its chief public buildings. The borough sits in the anthracite coal region. Coal mining is the main work of its people. Other manufactures add to the local trade base. Old Forge was first settled in the year 1830. It was made a borough much later, in 1899. The entry is short, but it fixes the place well. Coal, rail lines, and new comers mark its character.
britannica-1911-page:
Page, the word for a serving boy, is traced in a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. No one root for the word is sure, the entry warns. Kindred forms run through the Romance tongues of Europe. Some link it to a Greek word for a small boy. Others link it to slave youths trained as tutors in Rome.

Such youths served in the palace of the Roman emperors. They stood at state rites much like pages of later kings. One French scholar ties the word to folk of the country side. That tie would mean pages were not always boys at all. In English the word first named a boy who helped a head servant. Royal and noble houses then gave the post its shine.
britannica-1911-palladium-image:
Palladium was an archaic wooden image of Pallas Athena kept at Troy. Its myth entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The image stood in the citadel as a pledge of city safety. It showed the goddess stiff in old style, spear in her right hand.

Tale says Athena ordered the image made for Pallas, Triton daughter. Athena had slain Pallas by chance, and the image honoured her name. Zeus cast it down from heaven as Ilus founded Ilium city. Odysseus and Diomedes stole it from her temple in the war. That theft, men said, made the capture of Troy at last possible.
britannica-1911-patteson-john-coleridge:
John Coleridge Patteson was an English missionary and bishop of Melanesia. He lived from eighteen twenty seven to eighteen seventy one. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London, the eldest son of a King Bench judge, he shone at Eton.

Patteson studied at Balliol College, Oxford, and became a fellow of Merton. In eighteen fifty four he joined Bishop Selwyn on a mission to Melanesia. He sailed the isles in the ship Southern Cross and won deep trust. He spoke twenty three tongues with ease, a rare gift noted here. Traders who posed as missionaries to kidnap labour led to his death.
britannica-1911-peacock-george:
George Peacock was an English man of sums who lived from seventeen ninety-one to eighteen fifty-eight. He was born near Darlington and went to a chief school at Cambridge in eighteen nine. He came out near the top of his year in sums. With two friends he then led a famed fight of marks.

That fight brought the marks of the main land to Cambridge in place of the marks of Newton. It threw open a vast store of new finds past the sea. He printed sets of tasks and sat on boards that probed his school. He rose to a chair of stars and to head a great church.
britannica-1911-peele-george:
George Peele was born in 1558 and died about 1598, an English dramatist. The 1911 Britannica life opens in London, where he was born and schooled. His father was clerk of Christ's Hospital and wrote on book keeping. George was schooled at that same hospital in his boyhood years. In 1571 he entered Broadgates Hall at Oxford for his studies.

In 1574 he moved to Christ Church and took degrees in 1577 and 1579. That year the hospital asked his father to make him earn his bread. He went up to London about 1580 to seek his fortune there. In 1583 he staged two Latin plays for a Polish guest at Oxford. Praise came too for his English verse rendering of Euripides.
britannica-1911-petrie-george:
George Petrie lived from 1790 to 1866 and was an Irish scholar of old things. The 1911 Britannica life opens in Dublin, where he was born in January 1790. His father James was a painter of portraits from Aberdeen in Scotland. George trained as an artist and won fame for Irish landscape views. Yet his heart lay with the old remains of his native land.

In 1828 he took charge of the survey work on Irish antiquities. That state survey mapped and logged the old sites of Ireland. In 1832 he took the helm of the Dublin Penny Journal. That cheap journal spread facts to the common reader each week. His essay on round towers won a prize in 1830 and still stands.
britannica-1911-pocock-sir-george:
George Pocock was a British admiral, son of a navy chaplain, who entered the sea service as a boy of twelve. He sailed under the shield of an uncle who was a captain in the fleet. He rose by clean steps: lieutenant, commander, then post captain in his early thirties.

After service in the West Indies he was sent to the East Indies as captain of a war ship in a fleet bound for India. That fleet worked with a famed soldier to win Bengal for Britain, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Pocock rose to flag rank in quick time. On his chiefs death he took command of all sea forces in the east. A fresh fleet joined him, yet his whole force stood at a mere seven small ships of the line as war with France broke out.
britannica-1911-porridge:
Porridge is a short word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a soft cooked food and the history of its name. The word is an altered form of pottage, from the French potage, soup or what is cooked in a pot. Porridge is made by stirring meal, above all oatmeal, in boiling water and cooking it slowly until the mass turns soft. The dish and its name belong most of all to Scotland; in Ireland the same food is commonly called stir-about.

The article notes that the older use of the word has died out. That use meant a broth of vegetables, or of meat and vegetables, thickened with barley or other meal, and pottage is now the usual term for that dish. The form porridge itself seems to date from the sixteenth century.
britannica-1911-powell-george:
George Powell (about 1658-1714), an English actor and playwright, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of an actor of the same name. He first appeared in 1687, playing a king's son in a version by Tate of a play by Fletcher. He wrote or reshaped several plays of his own and acted in them.

The article says he performed in a long list of plays of his day almost until his death. As a tragic actor he took over many of the parts of Betterton, the great actor of the age. The entry adds a dry verdict: he gained the roles, but not the genius that went with them. Short as it is, the piece preserves the shape of a working stage career of the time.
britannica-1911-privilege:
Privilege in law means a special right or freedom granted apart from common right. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the word to privilegium, a law made for one person. In Roman use such a law more often worked against a person. In modern use it works in favor of the holder alone.

English law sorts privilege as personal or tied to a place. Peers and universities hold forms of it by that split. Parliamentary privilege and clergy relief from some duties are key cases. The entry then turns to the United States. Two clauses in its founding text on citizen rights are quoted and glossed at length.
britannica-1911-renouf-sir-peter-le-page:
Sir Peter le Page Renouf (1822-1897) was an Egyptologist, and this 1911 Britannica entry stresses the church quarrels that marked his life. He was born in Guernsey and schooled at Elizabeth College there. He went on to Oxford but left without a degree after becoming a Roman Catholic under the sway of Dr Newman. Like many converts of the time, he proved a thorn to the strict party in his new church.

He fought against the teaching of papal infallibility, and his 1868 treatise on the old case of Pope Honorius was placed on the list of banned books. From 1855 to 1864 he taught ancient history and eastern tongues at the Catholic university Newman tried to build in Dublin. He also edited journals there, one of which was shut down under pressure from the church rulers. In 1864 he became a government inspector of schools.
britannica-1911-richardson-george:
Richardson, George is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English architect and designer of the eighteenth century. His birth and death dates are not fixed; men guess his birth about 1736 and his death in 1817. He stood as a noted rival of the brothers Adam. From 1760 to 1763 he travelled in Italy and the south of France and took in the inspiration of a lifetime.

Richardson showed a rare skill at fitting classical ideals to the needs of his day. In 1765 he won a Society of Arts premium for a street design in the classical manner. He was above all a designer of ceilings and chimneypieces: his Book of Ceilings came in 1776 and his Collection of Chimneypieces in 1781. His marble fireplaces, rich in coloured stone, still stand in many houses.
britannica-1911-ridding-george:
George Ridding, an English headmaster and bishop who lived from 1828 to 1904, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Winchester College on 16 March 1828, he was the son of a fellow of that college. He was educated at Winchester and at Balliol College, Oxford. He became a fellow of Exeter College and a tutor from 1853 to 1863.

In 1863 Ridding was appointed second master of Winchester College in the same year. On the retirement of his father in law he succeeded to the headmastership of the school. In that office, from 1867 to 1884, he carried out a series of radical reforms. Those reforms raised both the reputation and the numbers of the school in great measure. In 1884 he became the first bishop of Southwell, a new diocese.
britannica-1911-ridge: Ridge is a word for the line of a back, used for many things that share that shape, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. It covers the strip of soil a plough throws up between furrows on a farm. It covers the raised lines on bones where muscles or ligaments attach in the body. In building, the ridge is the highest part of a roof, covered with lead, slate, or tiles.
britannica-1911-riesengebirge:
Rising on the line between Silesia and Bohemia, the Riesengebirge form a high and rugged range. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls them the Giant Mountains in English. They are the highest part of the Sudetic system. Peaks such as Schneekoppe rise above five thousand feet.

A main crest runs along the north side, with a lower chain to the south. Deep valleys, steep north slopes, and more gentle south slopes shape the land. Views stretch from Breslau toward Prague on clear days. A chapel to Saint Lawrence crowns the top peak, with a hotel for travelers close by.
britannica-1911-romney-george:
George Romney, an English painter of history and portraits who lived from 1734 to 1802, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Dalton in Furness in Lancashire, he was the son of a builder and cabinet maker. The boy showed a turn for making things, carving figures in wood and building a violin he played for hours.

His sketches of the rustics near home drew notice, and at nineteen he was apprenticed to Steele, a travelling painter who had studied in Paris. That master's erratic habits held the pupil back. In 1756 Romney wed a young woman who had nursed him through a fever. He then set up as a portrait painter on his own, moving through the northern counties and painting likenesses for a couple of guineas each. By twenty seven he had saved about a hundred pounds to seek his fortune in London.
britannica-1911-rooke-sir-george:
Sir George Rooke, English naval commander who lived from 1650 to 1709, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born near Canterbury in 1650. Entering the navy as a volunteer, he served in the Dutch Wars. By 1673 he had risen to post captain in the service.

After the Revolution of 1688 he led the squadron that raised the siege of Londonderry in 1689. Rear admiral rank came in 1690, and he fought at Beachy Head that year. At Barfleur in 1692 he served under Russell with note. A night attack at La Hogue, where he burned six French ships, won him a knighthood. A gift of one thousand pounds came with that honour as a reward. In 1702 he led the attack on Cadiz and wrecked the Plate fleet at Vigo on the way home.
britannica-1911-rose-george:
George Rose, a British politician who lived from 1744 to 1818, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born on June 17, 1744, and schooled at Westminster. He joined the navy, fought in the West Indies, and left the service in 1762. He then took civil posts, keeping records and tax work.

Rose rose as a secretary to the treasury under Lord Shelburne and then under Pitt. He entered parliament in 1784 and stayed loyal to Pitt for years. Pitt gave him rich posts in return. Rose left office with Pitt, came back with him in 1804, and held trade and navy pay posts. He died still a member in 1818.
britannica-1911-routledge-george:
George Routledge (1812-1888) was an English publisher of cheap books, and his career is told in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Brampton in Cumberland, he learned the trade with a bookseller at Carlisle. He came to London in 1833, opened as a bookseller in 1836, and began publishing in 1843.

The entry says his fame rests on the vast number of cheap books he issued. His shilling series, the Railway Library, was a huge success, carrying works such as Uncle Tom's Cabin to a wide public. He also issued popular editions of Irving, Cooper, Bulwer Lytton, and Disraeli. His firm became George Routledge and Sons, with a New York branch from 1854.
britannica-1911-sacrilege:
Sacrilege is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a crime against holy things. It means the breach or fouling of things held as sacred. Its scope shifts much from one faith and age to the next. Where cult objects loom large, the crime is held in more dread.

The Latin root word at first meant just theft of holy things. By Cicero's time it took in any insult or harm to them. The entry traces how the crime's scope shrank over time. In early faiths near all grave wrongs fell under the name. As the sense of the holy grew more inward, the scope narrowed. The old guard against it was the curse held in the things.
britannica-1911-salt-range:
Salt Range, a system of hills in the Punjab and the North-West Frontier Province of India, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It takes its name from its vast stores of rock salt. The range begins with a lofty hill on the right bank of the river Jhelum. It crosses the Indus, and a southern branch then forms a border between two districts before it merges in the Waziristan hills.

The range holds the great mines of Mayo, Warcha, and Kalabagh. They yield a supply of salt that cannot be used up and serve the wants of all northern India. Coal of an inferior quality is also found in the range.
britannica-1911-sand-george:
George Sand is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French novelist. That name was the pen name of Madame Dudevant, nee Dupin. She lived from 1804 to 1876. The entry calls her the most prolific authoress in literary history. Among the women novelists of France, she stands unapproached. Her life was as strange and adventurous as her novels. Her books are mostly idealized versions of her own life.

In her self revelations she followed Rousseau, her first master. But the entry draws a sharp contrast between them. Rousseau darkened all the shadows in his Confessions. Sand is the heroine of her own story throughout. She is often frail and faulty in that telling. Yet she comes out as more sinned against than sinning. Her huge correspondence has recently been published in full. Family documents have also come to light for scholars. Those give full materials for tracing her career.
britannica-1911-sandys-george:
George Sandys (1578–1644) was an English traveller, colonist, and poet. He was the seventh and youngest son of Edwin Sandys, archbishop of York. He was born on 2 March 1578 and studied at St Mary Hall, Oxford, but took no degree. His travels began in 1610, when he first went to France. From north Italy he passed by Venice to Constantinople, and from there to Egypt and Mount Sinai. He went on to Palestine, Cyprus, Sicily, Naples, and Rome.

Sandys put out the tale of those travels in 1615, a work that added much to the knowledge of lands and peoples. He also took a great part in the first English settlement of America. In April 1621 he became the treasurer of the Virginia Company and sailed to Virginia. When Virginia became a crown colony, he was made a member of its council in 1624.
britannica-1911-scone-village:
Scone, a parish in Perthshire, Scotland, is described in a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It holds Old Scone, site of an old abbey and palace, and New Scone, a small modern village north of Perth near the Tay. The parish held a little over two thousand people in 1901.

Scone was once the chief place of the northern Pictish realm. Councils met on the Moot Hill, and the first such meet on record was held there in 906. Its abbey was founded in 1115, though monks had been there long before. Kings of Scots were crowned at Scone on the Stone of Destiny, till Edward the First took that stone to Westminster in 1296. The last crowning there was that of Charles the Second in 1651. The entry ends with the later palace and a bed said to bear work sewn by Mary Queen of Scots.
britannica-1911-scutage:
Scutage was the money payment that stood in for knight service under the feudal system. A 1911 Britannica entry names its source as the shield, scutum in Latin tongue. Holders of a knight fee owed war service, and scutage let them pay cash instead. The term at times loosely covers other levies charged on the same fee base.

Scholars once dated its start to 1156 or to the Toulouse campaign of 1159. Proof now shows it in use under Henry the First and Stephen as well. Split fees and paid troops both pushed kings to take cash over service. Each levy took the name of the campaign it was raised to fund.
britannica-1911-siege:
Siege is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes through French from a root meaning to sit. A siege is the sitting down of an army before a fortified place to take it, either by direct attack or by starving those inside into surrender. The entry sends readers to other articles for the craft of fort building and siege work.

A second part of the entry treats a special kind of coin. A siege piece is money struck during a siege, when the usual mints were shut or their coins could not be had. Such pieces were often made in special shapes to set them apart from normal coinage, and their workmanship was rough. The diamond shape was common in the Great Rebellion in England. A shilling struck at Newark in 1645 is named as a prime example.
britannica-1911-sion-college:
Sion College is a London body for city clergy with a famed library. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells its founding by will. Doctor Thomas White left the plan in his will of 1623. It joined a college, a clergy guild, and an almshouse in one.

Clergy of city parishes and their offshoots gain by the fund. Old buildings stood on the site of a blind hospital. That hospital dated from 1329, and a nunnery stood there before. A hall, a chapel, and a library filled the first site. In 1884 the almshouses shut and their folk took pensions. Their count then grew from twenty to forty in all. New buildings on the Victoria Embankment opened in 1886. The theology library now lends to members and the public.
britannica-1911-smalridge-george:
George Smalridge was an English bishop who lived from sixteen sixty three to seventeen nineteen. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Lichfield, he studied at Westminster school and at Christ Church, Oxford. His views were shaped by his friend Francis Atterbury at Oxford and beyond.

Smalridge taught at Christ Church and served two chapels in London. He became dean of Carlisle in seventeen eleven and dean of Christ Church later. In seventeen fourteen he was made bishop of Bristol as well. His Jacobite views kept him from a top Oxford post in seventeen o seven. Swift, Steele, and Doctor Johnson all praised his sermons and his mind.
britannica-1911-smollett-tobias-george:
Tobias George Smollett was a British writer of tales who lived from seventeen twenty-one to seventeen seventy-one. He was born in a vale in Dumbartonshire and named in March of that year. His father died young, and his grand sire did what he could for the brood. The boy was sent to a famed school, then to Glasgow to learn a trade.

He was bound to a bone man for five years, a slight that fed his sharp and keen bent for life. At age eighteen he crossed south to win London with a sad play. That play failed, and want drove him to sea as a healers mate.
britannica-1911-south-orange:
South Orange is a township and village in Essex county, New Jersey. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it some 15 miles west of New York City. The village held 4,608 souls in 1900 and 6,014 in 1910. The township apart from the village held 2,979 souls by 1910. A rail line and electric cars link it with Newark and Orange.

Most folk there live in homes and work in the great cities. It is first of all a suburb for New York and Newark. On Orange mountain lies a county park of wild woods and roads. Seton Hall College, a Roman Catholic school, has its seat there. The school was founded at Madison in 1856 and moved in 1860.
britannica-1911-spalatin-george:
George Spalatin, the name taken by George Burkhardt (1484–1545), was a key figure in the Reformation. He was born on 17 January 1484 at Spalt, near Nuremberg, where his father was a tanner. From that town he took his new name. He went to Nuremberg for his schooling at the age of thirteen. Soon after, he went to the university of Erfurt, where he took his first degree in 1499. There he drew the eye of Nikolaus Marschalk, the most strong of the masters.

Marschalk made Spalatin his scribe and took him to the new university of Wittenberg in 1502. In 1505 Spalatin came back to Erfurt to study law. He was put in the way of Conrad Mutianus and was met with a warm welcome by the small band of German scholars of whom Mutianus was chief.
britannica-1911-spratt-thomas-abel-brima:
Thomas Abel Brimage Spratt (1811-1888) was an English naval officer and scholar of land and sea. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his survey work in the Mediterranean until 1863. He served with honor in the Black Sea during the Crimean War. Work with Edward Forbes drew him toward natural history and geology as well.

With Forbes he wrote Travels in Lycia from their joint field work. He found remains of a pygmy elephant in caves at Malta. His two volume work on Crete covered its land, rocks, old sites, and wildlife. Later posts covered fisheries and care of the Mersey river.
britannica-1911-stalybridge:
Stalybridge is a borough of Cheshire in England, with its parliamentary area reaching into Lancashire. It lies on the river Tame in a hilly district, six miles east of Manchester. Its people numbered twenty seven thousand six hundred seventy three in nineteen o one. Three rail lines serve the town from different companies. Towns lie close on all sides, so the district is densely filled with people.

Stalybridge is one of the oldest seats of cotton making in its locality. The first cotton mill there was built in seventeen seventy six. The first steam engine followed in seventeen ninety five, the entry says. Machine works, nail works, and paper mills also stand in the town. Iron and brass foundries add to its trades in heavy goods. The town became a market town in eighteen twenty eight and a borough in eighteen fifty seven.
britannica-1911-stephenson-george:
George Stephenson was an English builder of engines who lived from seventeen eighty-one to eighteen forty-eight. He was born near Newcastle, the son of a coal pit fire man. As a boy he kept cows, then drove a pit horse. He could not read till past youth, when night school gave him fast ground.

He rose to chief engine wright at a great pit. There he built a safe lamp for miners, at the same time as a famed knight built his own. He then built a steam engine for pit tram roads that ran with good proof. His work led to the first rail line to haul both folk and goods by steam power.
britannica-1911-stepney-george:
George Stepney, who lived from 1663 to 1707, was an English poet and envoy, as a 1911 Britannica life records. He was born at Westminster and schooled there before going to Trinity College at Cambridge. A friend in high office helped him into state service abroad. In 1692 he went as envoy to Brandenburg and then to other German courts.

He also served at Vienna and later at The Hague, and he knew German affairs in depth. Marlborough held him in high trust when others sought his recall. His letters survive in large sets and show a clear, exact hand. He died at Chelsea in 1707 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
britannica-1911-stock-exchange:
Stock Exchange is a market where men buy and sell securities. The 1911 Britannica entry defines those goods as negotiable papers of value. Most trade runs in stocks, bonds, and shares of firms, it says. Gains on them are paid as interest or as dividend when earned. Bills of governments and of towns also pass through such markets at times.

In old days the British state issued exchequer bills of that kind. Those bills sat in truth closer to bonds with shifting rates. The rate was fixed half yearly ahead by the treasury in London. Flaws in that plan led the state to drop the form in time. Markets for such papers have lived for some hundreds of years.
britannica-1911-stockbridge:
Stockbridge is a township of Berkshire county in western Massachusetts, with about nineteen hundred people in nineteen ten. It covers twenty four square miles of hill country. A lake called Stockbridge Bowl lies two miles north of the village. South of the village a cleft in Bear Mountain holds Ice Glen. Its caves stay lined with ice even in midsummer. Monument Mountain rises in the south of the township.

The village stands on the Housatonic river and is known as a summer resort. It has a casino, golf links, a public library, and an academy. A bell tower marks the old Indian mission there. Jonathan Edwards was pastor at Stockbridge in the seventeen fifties. He wrote his work on freedom of the will while living in the town.
britannica-1911-stone-age: Stone Age is the term for the first stage of human life, when folk knew no metals. Their arms and tools were made of stone, horn, or bone. The term holds no fixed span of years, since that age came first in some lands and late in a few. It splits in two parts, one of rough stone and one of stone ground smooth.
britannica-1911-stone-george:
George Stone, archbishop of Armagh who lived from 1708 to 1764, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Andrew Stone, a London banker. Westminster School and Christ Church at Oxford gave him his schooling. Once he took holy orders, his rise in the church ran very fast.

That speed owed much to the sway of his elder brother Andrew. Andrew became private secretary to the duke of Newcastle at about 1729. For years he stood in close trust with the duke and with Henry Pelham as well. In 1734 he became under secretary of state. He won great personal sway with George the Second, who made him tutor to Prince George. On that prince rise to the throne, Andrew served Queen Charlotte as treasurer. The entry uses the brother to frame the archbishop path.
britannica-1911-strossmayer-joseph-georg:
Joseph George Strossmayer is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a Croatian bishop and leader born in eighteen fifteen. His parents had moved from Austria, and he was of German stock. He was trained for the church in his home land and in Hungary.

The entry tells how he rose from priest to teacher to court chaplain in ten years. In eighteen forty nine he was made bishop of his home see. He drove the growth of Slav pride in lands ruled from Hungary. Schools, a learned house, and a new church seat rose by his hand. He led the fight against Magyar rule of his folk for years.
britannica-1911-swanage:
Swanage is a seaside resort and small port in Dorsetshire, England, on the east coast of the Isle of Purbeck. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 3,408 in 1901. The town lies on Swanage Bay, south of Poole Harbour. Its shore is wild and steep, with caves cut in the cliffs. Open high downs lie inland from the town. The bay has a fine sandy beach, good for bathing.

The church of Saint Mary has a massive tower that may predate the Norman age. The town also has a town hall and a hall with a library. Stones mark two events: a sea win by King Alfred over the Danes in the bay in 877, and the late Prince Consort. A large trade ships stone out from the Purbeck quarries near the town.
britannica-1911-syringe:
A syringe is a tool for drawing up and squirting out liquids. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes its name from the Greek for a reed or pipe. It works on the principle of the pump. The common form is a glass or metal tube with a pointed nozzle. A tight piston rod runs inside it. Dip the nozzle, pull the rod, and air pressure fills the tube. Push the rod back and the fluid jets out.

Sizes run from the needle pointed shot giver to the large belly syringe. Doctors use them to inject fluids and to wash wounds. Small ones are made of glass, larger ones of metal. A common kind uses a rubber tube with a bulb at its centre. Squeezing that bulb draws liquid up the tube. A flat holed nozzle on a metal body makes a garden kind for watering plants.
britannica-1911-tallage:
Tallage, a past tax in England, is traced in a law and past entry in the 1911 Britannica. Towns, boroughs, and crown lands paid the tax to king or lord. The word may rest on a root for a cut off part, or on the tally stick. It first shows in the reign of Henry the Second. In that age it stood in for an old town aid paid past the set rent.

Kings levied it oft, and lords lost the right to levy it on their own. Town folk raised their share most oft by a head tax at home. Use of the tax died out by twelve eighty three as grants in the diet took its place. Three late levies are named, the last in thirteen thirty two. That last try met such heat that the king dropped it for a set grant.
britannica-1911-tas-de-charge:
Tas de Charge is a French term of building for which English has no one word, and a brief entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out what it names. It names the low runs of stone in a Gothic vault. Those runs are laid in flat rows, not on the curve. They are bound fast into the wall and form one solid mass.

In most vaults those runs rise to about a third of the height of the vault. As they climb, they push out toward the room. That push cuts down the span that must still be vaulted on the curve. The trick gives the vault a firm base and a short free arch. The note is tiny, but a reader of church build terms will fix the part at once. It is the spring base from which the true vault ribs take off.
britannica-1911-ticknor-george:
George Ticknor, an American teacher and writer, fills a long life in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Boston in seventeen ninety one, he learned first from his father, a school head. He took his degree at Dartmouth while still in his teens. Law came next, but he gave up his Boston law work in a year. Study at Gottingen in Germany turned him to tongues and books.

Harvard made him its chair for French and Spanish in eighteen seventeen. He pushed for class groups by skill and for free choice of studies. His great work was a full past of Spanish books and life, out in eighteen forty nine. It gave long quotes and full book lists. Tongues soon carried it to Spain and France.
britannica-1911-tonbridge:
Tonbridge, also spelt Tunbridge, is a market town in Kent, in the south west part of the county. It stands on rising ground above the river Medway, about thirty miles from London. A stone bridge of seventeen seventy five crosses the river there. Its people numbered about twelve thousand seven hundred in nineteen o one. The church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul was fully restored in eighteen seventy nine.

Ruins of an old castle stand in the town, chiefly a fine gateway with two round towers. The castle was once guarded by three moats, one formed by the Medway itself. Tonbridge School was founded by Sir Andrew Judd, a lord mayor of London. Inlaid wood goods called Tonbridge ware are made there in large amounts. Gunpowder mills stand on the banks of the Medway.
britannica-1911-tonnage:
Tonnage is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on how ships are measured. The way merchant ship tonnage is found is set by law. Those laws are the Merchant Shipping Acts named in the text. The entry notes that several kinds of tonnage exist. Displacement tonnage is the kind used for warships. It is the true weight of water a ship pushes aside.

Warships are built to carry all their loads at a set depth. Coal, guns, stores, and water all count in that load. Their tonnage is the weight of water displaced at that depth. So the figure joins the weight of the ship's own frame. It adds all that sits on board her as well. The value can be found from the space sunk below water. That space counts the rudder and screws too.
britannica-1911-tonnage-and-poundage:
Tonnage and Poundage were old port taxes in England in this 1911 Britannica tax entry. Tonnage fell on wine brought in by ship, past two older wine dues. Poundage fell on all goods in or out at twelve pence in the pound. At first traders agreed to the dues by pact with the crown. The diet first granted them in thirteen seventy three, for set terms at first.

Kings came to hold the grants for life in most reigns. Charles the First was not granted them, yet took them on his own word in sixteen twenty eight. That act was called a breach of right by law in sixteen forty. In time the dues were pledged to the state debt. They were wiped out for good in seventeen eighty seven.
britannica-1911-turberville-george:
George Turberville is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English poet born near fifteen forty in Dorset. His house was an old one that a famed novel later borrowed for its name. He was schooled at Winchester and then held a fellowship at Oxford.

The entry tells how he went to Moscow as aide on a royal mission. Verse letters on the ways of Russia from that trip still live in print. Books of songs, sonnets, and verse tales came from his pen for years. He also turned old Latin love tales into English verse for home readers. Works on hawks and the hunt are laid to his name as well.
britannica-1911-villenage:
Villenage was a medieval condition of men between freedom and slavery, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica treats its name and history. The term points to serfdom, and it occurs in France as well as in England. It came into English speech through Norman French. Its root lies in Latin words for a farm and a farm worker.

The earliest uses of the word show up in documents of the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Domesday Book is among the sources named for those early uses. The entry calls the history of the word and of the state alike instructive in English usage. The stuff from which the villein class was formed already existed in Anglo Saxon times. On the one hand stood the Saxon orders of men, as the entry goes on to show.
britannica-1911-wantage:
Wantage, a market town in Berkshire, England, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The hosted text opens with entries on other towns, then gives Wantage's own article in full. The town lies in the Vale of White Horse, in a hollow at the foot of steep hills. Its urban district held 3,766 people in 1901. A steam tramway links it to Wantage Road station on the Great Western railway.

The church of St Peter and St Paul is cross-shaped and looks Perpendicular in style. It keeps an early nave arcade and ornate tower arches from an older period. The article places the town in the Abingdon parliamentary division. Readers get a short gazetteer sketch of the town's site, church, and rail links as they stood at the start of the twentieth century.
britannica-1911-warburton-bartholomew-el:
Warburton, Bartholomew Elliott George is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a British traveller and novelist. Known as Eliot Warburton, he was born in 1810 near Tullamore, in Ireland, and died in 1852. He was schooled at Trinity College, Cambridge, and called to the Irish bar in 1837. He gave up law for travel and letters.

His first book, The Crescent and the Cross, made his name. It told of his travels in 1843 in Turkey, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt. It split public attention with Kinglake's Eothen, printed in the same year, 1844. The East held men's minds at the time, and Warburton wrote with force for the taking of Egypt. The article says his lively tale of adventures and his bright sketches of Eastern life earned the book's success on their own.
britannica-1911-ward-william-george:
William George Ward, who lived from 1812 to 1882, was an English Catholic thinker. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica uses his life to show an age of faith in flux. He had a rare gift, near a passion, for pure mathematics. For most other fields he felt open scorn.

Ward won posts at Oxford while sending in blank exam papers. The Tractarian movement drew him by its war on half measures. Hearing Newman preach made him a follower at one stroke. Yet he came at the cause by logic, not by history. He took church orders, then edited the party paper British Critic. His fierce attacks on the English Church shocked even his own side. His tale shows zeal outrunning tact.
britannica-1911-washington-george:
George Washington, who lived from 1732 to 1799, was the first president of the United States. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his family roots. He was born at Bridges Creek in Virginia in February 1732. Study had linked his kin to an English house at Sulgrave.

Two brothers of that house reached Virginia in 1658. Land on the Potomac passed down to the president father. Of the boy early life little is truly known, the entry says. Tales of a hatchet and a cherry tree are called false coinage. A popular life writer made those tales up after his death. Schooling was thin and flawed, save in mathematics. He taught himself much of that field by his own work.
britannica-1911-wedge:
Wedge names a piece of wood or metal, broad and thick at one end and narrowing to a thin edge at the other. This 1911 Britannica entry treats both the tool and the word. A wedge is used to split wood and rock, to hold two pressing surfaces apart, and in general to press hard within a tight space. Though at times counted among the simple mechanical powers, it is really, the entry says, an application of the inclined plane.

The word itself is old English, with kin in Dutch, Danish, and Lithuanian, and no tie to the word weigh. The entry also gives a second sense from weather science. There a wedge is a narrow strip of high pressure caught between two storms. It slides along between a storm that is leaving and one that is coming.
britannica-1911-weybridge:
Weybridge is a town in the Chertsey district of Surrey, England. It lies 19 miles west-south-west of London, on the London and South-Western railway. Its people numbered 5,329 in 1901. The town stands in the flat valley of the river Wey, a mile above the point where the Wey joins the Thames. The river is locked up to Godalming, and cuts help its boats. Weybridge has grown in new times from a village into a town of homes.

The church of St James is new, but it holds many old stones in memory of the dead. One of them is a work by Sir F. Chantrey for the duchess of York, who died in 1820. A column on Weybridge Green also marks her memory. The top of that column once stood at Seven Dials in London.
britannica-1911-wheatstone-s-bridge:
Wheatstones Bridge is a tool for work with electric flow that finds the push back in a wire. Six links join four points in a lozenge shape. When no flow shows in one cross link, a plain rule links the four arms. That rule lets a user solve for one arm from the rest.

The entry is clear that the plan was not first made by Wheatstone. It came from Christie in eighteen thirty-three, though Wheatstone used it in his own work. A plate shows the cell, the gauge, and the four arms. The text then proves the rule with the laws of flow.
britannica-1911-whetstone-george:
George Whetstone, an English stage writer and author, gets a full life in the 1911 Britannica. Born near fifteen forty four, he was the third son of a rich house near Stamford. He spent a small share of wealth fast and lost a court fight for more. In fifteen seventy two he joined an English force in the Low Countries. There he met the poets Gascoigne and Churchyard.

His first book of tales in prose and verse came out in fifteen seventy six. A two part play on Promos and Cassandra came next, drawn from Italian tales. That tale in prose form may have fed the plot of Measure for Measure. Later works span tales, tracts on rule, and tales of war, with a last book in fifteen eighty seven.
britannica-1911-whitefield-george:
George Whitefield, an English religious leader who lived from 1714 to 1770, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born on December 16, 1714, at the Bell Inn in Gloucester. His father kept the inn. At school he gained skill in speech and a love of plays.

Whitefield entered Pembroke College, Oxford, in 1733 and joined the Methodist circle there. Ill health sent him home, but a bishop made him a deacon in 1736. His preaching tours drew huge crowds at once. In 1737 he sailed for Georgia as a missionary. Back in England, shut out of pulpits, he began to preach in the open air.
britannica-1911-william-of-orange:
William of Orange is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a prince known as the Silent, born in Nassau in fifteen thirty three. A will made him heir to rich lands and a princely title as a boy. His kin on one side had served the great emperor with trust.
