The entry tells how the emperor took the boy to be raised at court in Brussels. There he was schooled in the old faith, though his house held the new. High gifts won him the trust and love of that emperor in youth. A rich match to an heiress was set for him at age seventeen. His stand for Dutch freedom fills the main tale that follows.
britannica-1911-winter-john-strange:
John Strange Winter was the pen name of Henrietta Eliza Vaughan Stannard, an English novelist born in 1856. The 1911 Britannica article says she was born on the thirteenth of January 1856. Her father was rector of Saint Margaret's at York. She began young to write tales for the magazines. Her tales were tender in tone and dealt chiefly with army life. Two of them, Bootles' Baby and Houp-la, came out in The Graphic in 1885. They made her name.

Winter then wrote some sixty more books, light and gay in cast. The best of them deal with camp life, like the first pair. She was a tireless writer on themes that touch on women. In 1892 she was the first head of the Writers' Club. From 1901 to 1903 she led the Society of Women Journalists. In 1884 she wed Arthur Stannard, a civil engineer.
britannica-1911-wither-george:
George Wither is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, where he appears as an English poet and writer of satire. Wither was born at Bentworth, near Alton, on the eleventh of June 1588. He died in 1667. The hosted text reaches his article after the tail ends of a few entries that come before it in the volume.

The account follows his schooling and his slow start in life. He spent two years at Magdalen College, Oxford, after entering at the age of fifteen. His neighbours urged his father to put him to a trade instead. He later studied at an Inn of Chancery and gained a place at court. The text notes his elegy of 1612 on the death of Prince Henry.
britannica-1911-zahringen-village: Zahringen is a village in Germany, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the grand duchy of Baden, under the west slope of the Black Forest. The village lies two miles from Freiburg, on the rail line from Heidelberg to Basel. About twelve hundred people lived there in 1900. Above the village, on a spur fifteen hundred feet above the sea, lie the ruins of Zahringen castle. That castle was once the stronghold of the ducal line that bore the same name.
by-conduct-and-courage:
G. A. Henty wrote a sea tale for boys, in a text dated 1902. Its hero starts as an orphan, by the first chapter's name. The king's service takes him next. Sea fight, a step up in rank, and a pirate hold mark the early turns.

A tight escape and a lone command raise the stakes. A grand haul crowns that run of heads in the copy held here. The front pages of this copy are filled with a roll of Henty's past tales — Egypt, Carthage, Jerusalem, and Alfred's days among them — each with its price in shillings. That roll sets the frame: true past times, a brave lad at the core, and foes on sea and shore. Conduct and courage, as the title vows, form the twin tests the lad must pass.
by-shore-and-sedge:
Bret Harte gathered three California tales in By Shore and Sedge, pieces from the mining frontier he made famous. An Apostle of the Tules opens on a camp meeting in Tasajara Valley in October 1856, four hundred settlers camped in a dreary marsh for a religious revival. Harte watches preachers, sick families, and scoffing boys with his usual mix of irony and pity.

Sarah Walker and A Ship of '49 complete the volume, the last reaching back to the gold rush year itself. Harte's California is a place of sudden gatherings, rough faith, and stranger kindness. These shorter pieces show his method at its purest: a vivid scene, a twist of character, and sentiment kept on a tight rein.
cambridge:
Gordon Home wrote a picture guide to Cambridge for the Beautiful Britain set. King's College old gateway fronts the book; it now leads to the University Library. King's Chapel shows past it in the plate note. Six short chapters fill a slim book of sixty-four pages.

First thoughts set town and gown side by side. Early Cambridge comes next. Great colleges take the long third part. Small colleges take the fourth. Library, Senate House, Pitt Press, and museums fill the fifth. Town churches close the frame. Plates show St John's library pane, King's choir, and Trinity's great gate. Gate of Honour at Caius and Emmanuel's old court stand in the run. The round Norman Holy Sepulchre church and St John's Bridge of Sighs dress the cover side. Walk pace and gate lore form the stock.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alain-rene-le:
Alain-Rene Le Sage was a writer born at Sarzeau, Morbihan, in 1668, who died at Boulogne-sur-Mer in 1747. Son of a notary who died early, he left the Jesuit college of Vannes penniless, his guardian having squandered his fortune. Marriage came at twenty-six; practised law briefly, then devoted himself to literature.

The Abbe de Lyonne gave him a small pension and encouraged Spanish study. He translated Spanish plays without public favour. His farce Crispin rival de son maitre won marked success in 1707 and stays on the stage. Actors' enmity drove him to the Foire theatre, for which he wrote about a hundred plays. Besides Crispin, Turcaret, Le Diable Boiteux, and Gil Blas deserve special mention. Turcaret ou le Financier, 1709, is a prose comedy about a financier. Gil Blas, despite assertion, is no Spanish plagiarism but an original work counted among France's romance masterpieces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alger-of-lieg:
Alger of Liège, learned French priest born at Liège about 1055, died at Cluny in 1132. He studied at Liège, became Deacon of St. Bartholomew's, and about 1100 Canon of St. Lambert's cathedral, where he stayed twenty years. In 1121 he retired to Cluny's monastery and died there.

His treatise against Berengarius's heresy, De sacramento corporis et sanguinis Domini, won high esteem from Peter of Cluny and Erasmus. His other writings: De misericordia et justitia, a Fathers anthology with brief commentaries, a free-will treatise, and one on the Mass's sacrifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-hallows-c:
All Hallows College prepares priests for the missions in English-speaking countries. In 1840 the young Dublin priest John Hand lived with a Vincentian community, unbound by its rules. He resolved to found a missionary college. The project seemed fanciful for one so young, unknown, and penniless, but Hand trusted Heaven and Irish generosity. He won Gregory XVI's approbation at Rome. With O'Connell's aid he leased a mansion and twenty-six acres north of Dublin, once the Priory of All Hallows' land.

On 1 November 1842, with Archbishop Murray's encouragement, Hand formally opened the college and gave it its present name. For four years he served as president, directing studies, establishing finances, and organizing staff. Then, worn out by labours, above all by collecting funds house to house and parish to parish, he died in the spring of 1846. He left the harvest to others. His ideal was that All Hallows should be apostolic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-ledge:
The altar ledge began as a step raised slightly behind the plain table-shaped altar, holding candlesticks, flowers, reliquaries, and other ornaments. Later the tabernacle joined the altar as a stationary appendage, with further steps at its sides and behind it. These steps are also called degrees or gradini, their fronts sometimes beautifully painted and decorated.

Brunelleschi's Santo Spirito in Florence shows gradini with beautiful miniature groups from the Passion of Christ. The ledge thus marks the altar's growth from bare table to a stepped setting for ornaments and tabernacle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altarage:
Altarage comes from the low Latin altaragium, revenue reserved for the chaplain, or altarist, as against the parish priest's income. The distinction once guarded the chaplain's livelihood apart from the parish priest's own benefice and income. Today it means the fees a priest receives from the laity for functions performed for them, such as marriages, baptisms, funerals, and other rites.

It is also termed honorarium, stipend, stole fee, or altarage itself in modern use. Each name marks the same payment: a free offering for a priest's personal service at life's turning points.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anselm-of-lie:
An eleventh-century Belgian chronicler, Anselm of Liège was born in 1008 and died about 1056. Liège's famous episcopal school educated him, and he became canon and dean of the cathedral, where Bishop Wazo was his friend. His chronicle, the Gesta Episcoporum Tungrensium, Trajectensium, et Leodiensium, ranks among the best of its period for literary merit and historical value.

It carries on Heriger of Lobbes's work, which covered the first twenty-seven bishops, from Saint Maternus to Remaclus. Anselm wrote at the request of his godmother, Countess Ida, Abbess of Saint Cecilia at Cologne, adding the lives of twenty-five more bishops, down to Wazo. Wazo gets a very full and particular account. The latest edition of the Gesta appears in Monumenta Germaniae Historica: Scriptores, VII, 161-234, and also XIV, 107-120, from 1883. Anselm's style is clear, and his zeal for church reform matches his critical intelligence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-josep:
Antoine-Joseph Mege, a Maurist Benedictine born at Clermont in 1625, spent his life in prayer, preaching, and study. He joined the Benedictines at Vendome in 1643, taught theology at Saint-Denis, and served as prior at Rethel. Late in life he withdrew to Saint-Germain-des-Pres near Paris, dividing his days between prayer and books.

His chief work commented on the Rule of Saint Benedict, attacking the strict reading of Abbot Rance of La Trappe. Maurist superiors banned the commentary in 1689 at the urging of Bossuet. He also translated Saint Ambrose on virginity and wrote a work on Christian morals, leaving a small but sharp body of monastic writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-berlage:
Anton Berlage, a German dogmatic theologian born at Munster in 1805, taught at his native city's academy until his death in 1881. Early teachers drew him toward risky speculation, but study at Tubingen under Drey, Hirscher, and Mohler turned him to a historical method. Ordained in 1832 without seminary training, he lectured first on apologetics and morals, then on dogma alone.

His seven-volume Catholic Dogmatics, published between 1839 and 1864, gathered his teaching in clear and elegant form. Pupils praised his concise and direct lectures, and his spirit shaped the whole faculty at Munster. The entry presents a teacher whose steady orthodoxy steadied German theology in a restless age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-col:
The Apostolic College means the Twelve Apostles as a body commissioned by Christ to spread the reign of God over the whole world. They are founders, foundation, and supports of the visible church on earth, and the name apostle marks their commission. An apostle is a missionary sent by proper authority to carry the gospel to new lands, a meaning fixed by the sending of the Twelve. To call them a college implies they worked together under one head for one purpose.

Referring readers to the article on Apostles for scriptural treatment, this entry deals with dogmatic aspects, the doctrines behind accredited envoys and teachers. Christ, it argues, founded a teaching, governing, and serving apostolate whose charter lies in the gospel commissions. The piece suits readers who want the theology behind the Twelve, not just their names and stories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-banns-of-marr:
Banns of marriage are the church's public announcement of the names of people planning to marry. The word comes from Latin bannum and Old English bannan, to summon. Their object is to uncover any impediment to the marriage and to tell all interested parties of its near celebration. From Christian society's start, marriage counted as a public religious act under church control.

Notice to the bishop dates to the second century, and later the parish priest took up the duty with reputable parishioners' help. Publishing names in church seems to have begun in France near the end of the twelfth century. It was already Gallican custom in 1215, when Innocent III mentioned it to Beauvais's bishop. That same year the Fourth Lateran Council made banns a general law of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-age:
Canonical age is the year fixed by church law at which a person becomes able to take on duties. He may enjoy privileges, enter states of life, hold office, or receive sacraments. Each such act needs growth of mind and body fitted to free acceptance, with knowledge of its duties. The Church sets the age at which one is generally thought qualified. Less growth suffices for baptism than for marriage or priesthood, and higher offices demand more.

Jurists split life into seven ages. They are infancy to seven, childhood to fourteen, puberty to twenty-five, and majority to forty. Manhood runs to fifty or sixty, old age to seventy, and decrepitude to a hundred or death, each year complete. Old discipline varied by time and place. Gratian set seven for tonsure and the first minor orders, twelve for acolyte, twenty for subdeaconship, and thirty for deaconship, later 25.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carthage:
Carthage was a Phoenician colony that long rivaled Rome for mastery of the civilized world before a Roman army destroyed it in 146 B.C. Julius Caesar refounded it in 44 B.C. as a Roman colony, and it became capital of Africa Nova, a province that grew rich and flourishing. African Christianity opens in 180 with martyrs at Scillium and Madaura, and within twenty years a thriving church stood at Carthage.

Tertullian, born at Carthage about 160, defended the faith in his Apology of about 197, claiming Christians had filled every corner of African life. Cyprian, elected bishop in 249, stands with Tertullian as the great figure of the early church there. Later sections trace the primacy of Carthage, its councils, and its bishops. Leo XIII restored the archdiocese in 1884 under Cardinal Lavigerie, who revived Christian life on the ancient site.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-dufre:
Charles Dufresne du Cange was a historian and philologist born at Amiens in 1610 and dead at Paris in 1688. His father, a magistrate, had him taught by the Jesuits at Amiens. He studied law at Orléans and joined the Bar before the Parlement of Paris in 1631. The law did not satisfy him, so he returned to Amiens, married in 1638, and in 1645 bought his father-in-law's post as Treasurer of France.

Neither office nor a family of ten children kept him from scholarship. Conversant with many languages, he was consulted from all sides and gathered much through correspondence. His energy went largely to the history of France and of Constantinople. Two great works grew from that preparation, above all his glossary of medieval and late Latin writers, published at Paris in three folio volumes in 1678.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-b:
An entry on Christopher Bainbridge, Archbishop of York and cardinal, born near Appleby about 1464. He entered Queen's College, Oxford, became its provost before 1495 and a doctor of laws, and later gave generously to the college. He held many benefices, including the London treasurership and the Mastership of the Rolls. Henry the Seventh named him Bishop of Durham in 1507, and the pope moved him to York in 1508.

Sent by Henry the Eighth as ambassador to Rome in 1509, Bainbridge was made cardinal by Julius the Second in March 1511 for winning Henry to the pope against France. He led a papal expedition that besieged Ferrara with success, and he sought the title Most Christian King for Henry after Louis of France forfeited it. In July 1514 his steward, the priest Rinaldo de Modena, poisoned him in revenge for a blow, and Bainbridge was buried in the English Hospice at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cities-of-ref:
The cities of refuge were towns where Jewish law gave asylum to anyone who had killed another without intent, sheltering him from the avenger of blood. Under blood-revenge, a victim's kinsman held it a duty to kill the slayer, intentional or not. The six biblical cities were Cedes in Galilee, Sichem in Mount Ephraim, and Hebron in the south, west of Jordan, with Bosor, Ramoth in Galaad, and Gaulon in Basan to the east.

Three western cities seem to have come first, probably under Josias, with the eastern three added when Jews spread wider after the Exile. Protection was conditional: the fugitive had to prove his deed unpremeditated, then stay within the city's bounds, unable to return home or buy off the avenger. An intentional killer found no refuge even at God's altar, and might be dragged from it to death, as Joab was.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-marriag:
In municipal law marriage is not a contract in the strict sense but a civil status. It unites one man and one woman legally for life, with rights and duties assigned by the law of matrimony. It is presumed to serve the State's highest interest, so the law encourages it, holds it permanent, and dissolves it only by death or, where statutes allow, by divorce. Consent of the parties is essential to a valid marriage.

In England solemnisation before a clergyman was required until 1836, except for Quakers and Jews, when civil and dissenter marriages were legalised. Common-law ages of consent were fourteen for males and twelve for females, and the act of 1753 voided underage marriages lacking parental consent. The article surveys formalities, annulment for deception or duress, and foreign rules, from Scotland's irregular marriages by mere consent to Germany's higher ages and Quebec's parental consent under twenty-one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-college:
Robert Schwickerath's wide survey starts from the word college itself, from the Latin collegium. At first it meant a community, a corporation, or a body of colleagues in a common pursuit. Rome knew guilds of artisans as collegia, plus groups joined for worship or mutual aid. Official bodies bore the name too, such as the College of Pontiffs. The sense survives in modern bodies like the College of Physicians and the College of Surgeons.

From the fourteenth century the word often meant a community of secular clergy living on a foundation for religious service. Schwickerath treats England, where the collegiate system still marks Oxford and Cambridge, and notes Winchester College, founded in 1379 as the first college outside a university. He follows the humanist influence, the colleges of Paris, and the American college, long the main home of liberal education and now in a state of transition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concubinage:
H. A. Gaynor's entry defines concubinage today as a more or less permanent state of a man and woman living in illicit intercourse. Strictly it covers unions where neither party is bound by vow, marriage, Holy Orders, or kinship. Dwelling together does not matter. Repetition or continuance of illicit relations between the same persons forms the essence. The term, however, has not always meant the same thing.

In the Old Testament a legitimate spouse of lower rank, or a bondwoman, might be called concubine without denying her marriage. The label marked her lesser share in rank, property, and household rule. Roman law and early church records used a like sense: a quasi-wife, recognized by law under set terms. Toledo's council of 400 legislated for laymen on the matter. With Rome's fall and Roman law's decline, lawful concubinage faded, and the word took its modern illicit sense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-o:
This reference entry covers two councils held at Orange in southern France, the first in 441 and the second in 529, and explains why the second matters far beyond its region. It sets each meeting in its place, names its president and bishops, and lists the subjects its canons addressed.

The first council, under Hilary of Arles, issued thirty canons on the sacraments, sanctuary, relations among bishops, catechumens, and the marriage of clergy. Far more important was the second council, presided over by Caesarius of Arles, the first in Gaul to issue a decision on a matter of faith. Its rulings on grace and free will shaped Western teaching for centuries, and the entry points readers to the acts and modern studies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deluge:
A long scriptural entry treats the Deluge, the catastrophe fully described in Genesis chapters 6 to 9 and recalled across Scripture from Wisdom to Second Peter. It considers the biblical account, its historicity, the Flood's universality, and collateral questions in turn. Genesis tells how God, seeing human wickedness, spared Noah's family, commanded an ark, and sent forty days' rain, with waters prevailing 150 days.

Critics read the account as a mosaic of two flood stories, Yahwistic and Priestly, differing in authorship and detail. Historicity weighs four theories, from mere fancy to borrowing, against flood legends worldwide. Universality asks whether the Flood covered the whole earth or destroyed all men over part of it. Time, place, and natural causes follow, with dates from rival texts and Babylonian parallels in the Tigris-Euphrates valley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demiurge:
A philosophy entry defines the demiurge, literally a public worker, a word first used for any craftsman serving the public. Soon other words took the common artisan, while demiurge was reserved for the Great Artificer, the Architect of the universe. At first writers added of the world to distinguish him, but gradually demiurge alone meant the Maker of heaven and earth, as in Plato's Timaeus.

Strictly the word never meant one producing from nothing, for which Greeks used ktistes, but only a maker who shapes and models given matter. Heathen philosophy always presupposes matter, and its world-maker need not be the supreme God. In Gnosticism the Demiurge became a central figure. He stands apart from the Supreme God, and often hostile to him, as the flawed maker of the material world. Other writings, by contrast, identify him with the Highest God himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
An ecclesiastical judge is a churchman holding church jurisdiction, whether in the broad sense or the strict. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that the official body set by lawful authority to administer justice is called a court, tribunal, or audience. Every court holds at least two sworn officers, the judge who decides and the clerk who keeps the record of proceedings and judgment.

As a rule, however, a church court forms a collegiate tribunal, whose members either join the president in deciding as judges or advise him as councillors and assessors. The entry cites Hergenrother-Hollweck, Laurentius, and Sagmuller on the shape of church courts. It gives students of canon law the personnel of justice in short compass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-james-c:
Henry James Coleridge, a writer and preacher born in Devonshire in 1822, was grandson of the poet's brother, son of a King's Bench judge. After Eton and a career at Trinity and Oriel, Oxford, he took Anglican orders in 1848 and joined the Tractarian ranks and helped start The Guardian as the High Church organ. Shaken by Newman's secession, the Gorham judgment, and the condemnations of Pusey and Ward, he was received into the Catholic Church in 1852 after a retreat at Clapham.

Ordained in 1856, Coleridge entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1857 and in 1865 became the Jesuit editor of The Month, adding The Messenger in 1877. He projected the Quarterly Series and wrote The Public Life of Our Lord, lives of Francis Xavier and Teresa, and the gospel harmony Vita Vitae Nostrae. Failing health forced his resignation from The Month in 1881, and after a seizure in 1890 he finished his work at Roehampton before dying in 1893.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-ma:
This article treats marriage chiefly as a lasting condition, with its moral and social aspects, rather than as a mere ceremony. Marriage is usually defined as the legitimate union of husband and wife. Legitimate means sanctioned by natural, evangelical, or civil law, and husband and wife implies mutual rights, life in common, and an enduring bond. Those last marks set marriage apart from concubinage and fornication.

The definition is broad enough to cover polygamous and polyandrous unions allowed by civil law. The theory of primitive promiscuity, debated by writers from 1860 to 1890, finds little support in historical times. The entry then weighs deviations from marriage. It argues that Christianity gave the world its highest ideal of unadulterated monogamy, with equality between the two parties, an influence spreading far beyond Christian lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-lamy-b: Jérôme Lamy Besange, born at Linz in 1726 and dead in 1781, taught Scripture at Salzburg for twenty-four years. His published works are an Introduction to the Old Testament in two volumes, an Introduction to the Four Gospels, an Introduction to the Acts of the Apostles. There is also a commentary on the Passion called Fasciculus Myrrhae, and a rendering of the seven penitential psalms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-lafarge:
John LaFarge was an American painter, decorator, and writer who revolutionized stained glass. Born in New York in 1835 to a French naval officer father, he studied at Mount St. Mary's and Fordham, meant to study law, but after Paris study with Couture turned to art. His early Newport landscapes already showed originality in color values and the influence of Japanese art, which he pioneered studying.

Experimenting with color, he rivaled medieval windows. He added new resources by inventing opalescent glass and methods of superimposing and welding it, seen in the Battle Window at Harvard and the Peacock Window at Worcester. His mural work began at Trinity Church, Boston, in 1873, and in his seventy-first year he painted lunettes on the history of religion for the St. Paul capitol. His books on painting, Japan, and the masters matched a wide-ranging mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kimberley-in-:
Kimberley in Orange is a South African vicariate, a missionary district, that grew out of the Eastern District and then the Vicariate of Natal. It became separate in 1886, covering Basutoland, Griqualand-West, Bechuanaland, and the Orange River Colony, though Basutoland split off as its own prefecture on 8 May 1894.

Before diamonds, the white settlers were almost all Boers and Catholics were few. Diamonds found about 1867 drew crowds to Kimberley from 1870, most of them Irish and English. Early priests worked in thin soil. Father Hoendervangers followed troops as a military chaplain in 1854 and built a Bloemfontein church. His successor Father Bompart served a flock of eight or ten poor Catholics, often near starvation, among neighbours hostile to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-knowledge:
Knowledge is treated here as a basic fact of awareness that cannot be strictly defined, only clarified. The article opens from everyday speech: knowing a man, knowing a fact, knowing a lesson, and knowing a science each mean something different.

Those uses fall into two kinds: sense knowledge of particular things, and understanding of general laws. Many tongues mark the split with two verbs, like Greek gnonai and eidenai or German kennen and wissen. Knowledge always joins a knowing subject to a known object, whether event, theorem, mind, or God. Three parts follow: the essentials of knowledge, its kinds, and the problem of knowledge itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liberatus-of-:
Liberatus of Carthage, a sixth-century archdeacon, wrote a history of Nestorian and Monophysite troubles. In 535 he travelled to Rome as legate of an African synod of 217 bishops, to consult Pope Agapetus I. Like most Africans he opposed Justinian's 544 edict against the Three Chapters, and African bishops often used him as ambassador in its disputes.

 He meant to show how misjudged was the Three Chapters' condemnation by the emperor. The work, A Short Account of the Nestorians and Eutychians, runs from Nestorius's ordination in 428 to Constantinople II in 553. Since he names Theodosius of Alexandria as still alive, it was written before 567, while he also records Pope Vigilius's death in June 555. His sources are Cassiodorus, synod acts, and contemporary letters. Despite his controversial purpose and anger at Monophysites and backers of the condemnation, his history is well and fairly written, an important document for the two heresies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liege:
Liege, canonical name Leodiensis, is now the capital of its Belgian province of the same name. The diocese's first capital was Tongres, northeast of Liege. Its land first belonged to Trier, then Cologne, but Tongres gained autonomy after the fourth century's first half. Its bounds, those of the Civitas Tungrorum, were unchanged until 1559. Thus Tongres stretched from Chimay to Stavelot, Aachen, Gladbach, and Venlo, taking in Latin and Germanic peoples.

 St. Servais, installed in 344 or 345, was the first bishop, present at Rimini's council in 359-360. The Franks' conversion began under Falco and went on under Domitian, Monulphus, and Gondulphus. St. Amandus (647-650) and St. Remaculus (650-660) quit the chair in discouragement and built monasteries. St. Lambert (669-705) finished the pagans' conversion and was probably murdered about 705 for defending church property. His successor St. Hubert built a basilica to house his relics, which became the city's nucleus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liguge:
Liguge is a Benedictine Abbey in Poitiers diocese, founded about 360 by St. Martin of Tours. When St. Martin became Bishop of Tours and set up Marmoutiers nearby, Liguge's fame declined. Among his successors were St. Savin, who became a hermit, and Abbot Ursinus, in whose reign Defensor compiled the Scintillarum Liber.

Saracen invasion, Aquitaine wars, and Norman invasion nearly wrecked the monastery, which by the eleventh century had fallen to a dependent priory of Maillezais, finally a benefice in commendam. The commendatory prior Geoffrey d'Estissac, friend of Rabelais, built the existing church. In 1607 Liguge passed to the Jesuit college of Poitiers. At the Revolution the buildings and lands were sold. In 1852 Bishop Pie set up a colony of monks at Liguge. When, in 1880, the monks were driven out under the Ferry laws, many retired under Dom Bourigaud to Silos in Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-henri-d:
Louis Henri de Lestrange, in religion Dom Augustine, was a Trappist abbot and founder, born in Ardeche in 1754 and dead at Lyons in 1827. Fourteenth child of a court officer, he was ordained in 1778 and made vicar-general of Vienne, with a bishopric in view.

Fleeing that prospect, he entered La Trappe in 1780. When revolution suppressed the orders in 1790, he led twenty-four monks to Val-Sainte in Switzerland, then planted houses in Spain, Piedmont, Belgium, and England. Driven out again in 1798, he scattered his monks to Poland and Podolia, regained Val-Sainte in 1802, sent a colony to America, and founded Cervara in Genoa in 1804.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manuterge:
Manuterge was the towel a priest used in liturgical service. Two kinds existed. One served the sacristy, for washing hands before Mass, before Communion outside Mass, and before baptism. It might also dry hands after customary washings after Mass. No rules fixed its material or form, and it often hung over a roller with ends sewn into a loop.

Hand washing before Mass reaches back to early Christian days and appears in ninth- and tenth-century sacramentaries. The second manuterge served at Mass itself, drying hands at the Lavabo after the Offertory, as the priest recited the Lavabo psalm, and for a bishop before the Offertory and after Communion. Kept on the credence table with finger bowl and cruets, it was usually small, about eighteen by fourteen inches, washing only thumb and two fingertips. Lace or embroidery trimmed its ends, and fifth-century ordination statutes already named it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maynooth-coll:
Maynooth College, the National College of Saint Patrick at Maynooth in County Kildare, twelve miles from Dublin, was founded in 1795. Ireland then still had its own Parliament, and though Catholics could not sit in it, the spirit of toleration from America and France seeped into its debates. During their brief parliamentary liberty from 1782 to 1801, Irish Protestants backed national brotherhood and produced Edmund Burke and Henry Grattan, to whom the college's founding is chiefly ascribed.

Other forces helped. The United Irishmen preached universal toleration. London wished to shield young Irish priests from revolutionary contagion on the Continent. Soldiers were also needed in wartime from a class that supplied Ireland's best recruits. In 1794 Dr. Troy memorialized the viceroy, and the college opened the next year. The entry follows its early years as a home-grown seminary built by a rare alliance of Protestant goodwill and government interest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mixed-marriag:
Mixed marriage, in Latin matrimonia mixta, technically means a marriage between a Catholic and a non-Catholic baptized in some Christian sect. The term is also often used for unions between Catholics and infidels. The Church has resisted such unions from its earliest days, because Christ lifted wedlock to sacramental dignity.

A Catholic wedding a non-Catholic was rightly judged to cheapen wedlock's holy nature, since it joined in sacred things with one outside the fold. St. Paul insists strongly on Christian marriage's unity of faith. The article sets out the canonical discipline. Such marriages need dispensation, the Catholic party must promise to keep the faith and raise the children Catholic, and the non-Catholic party must be informed of these promises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-and-can:
Marriage, in this entry's moral and canonical treatment, is the union by which a man and a woman form one principle of generation. They do so through mutual consent, sharing life, raising children and supporting each other in lasting affection. It is a contract by nature above human law, instituted by God and subject to divine law. No human power can rescind it.

Its primary end is the begetting and raising of children of God. Mutual society and help and a lawful remedy for concupiscence are secondary ends. Marriage is monogamous and indissoluble, dissolved only by death once consummated. The entry then works through impediments, consent and form. It sets out how the Church judges validity and what follows when a union fails.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-st-mary:
Mount Saint Mary's College, the second oldest Catholic collegiate institution in the United States, stands near Emmitsburg, Maryland. It lies in the Archdiocese of Baltimore, on high ground at the foot of the Blue Ridge. The site is prized for beauty, health and room for exercise. Its theological seminary has run alongside the college since its foundation.

Directed by an association of secular clergy with lay professors, it is governed by a board chaired ex officio by Baltimore's archbishop. It counted sixteen professors with 298 college students and 54 seminarians in 1909-10. Founded in 1808 when the Sulpicians moved their preparatory seminary from Pigeon Hill, it began with eight students under its first president, John Dubois. It grew through four departments teaching arts, commerce and modern languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystical-marr:
In Old and New Testament, God's love for man and his dealings with his chosen people are often pictured as bridegroom and bride. Christian virginity, too, has been seen from the earliest centuries as a soul's special offering to its spouse, Christ. That sense seems to lie behind talk of the mystical nuptials of Saint Agnes and Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

Later the phrase mystical marriage took two senses, one wide and one restricted. In the wide sense, found in many saints' lives, Christ appears in vision, calls a soul his bride, gives the customary ring, and the Virgin, saints and angels attend a ceremony. The rite symbolises a purely spiritual grace: a sudden growth of charity and familiarity with God, and his special care thereafter. The restricted sense marks a rarer, higher union.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-old-hall-st-e:
Old Hall, or Saint Edmund's College, near Ware in Hertfordshire, carried Douai's work for southern England after the Revolution. Founded on 16 November 1793, Saint Edmund's feast, it began when Bishop Douglass gathered four Douai students at a house already holding a Catholic school from 1749.

A legacy of ten thousand pounds left by John Sone let Douglass build a college blessed in 1799, with chapel and refectory added in 1805. Seminary of the London district until 1850, it then passed to Westminster and Southwark, flourishing under Thomas Griffiths from 1818. Thomas Griffiths, president from 1818 to 1834, later became vicar apostolic of London.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orders-of-st-:
Orders of Saint George share only their patron, the soldier martyr of Lydda, and otherwise stand as independent bodies across countries and centuries. Byzantine art showed George as a horseman in full arms, and crusading knights, recognizing their own gear, adopted him as patron of knighthood.

From that popularity sprang secular and religious associations alike. England's Garter, still seated at Saint George's chapel, Windsor, joins the 1818 order of Saint Michael and Saint George for foreign service, with Bavarian, Russian, and other orders catalogued. Saint George, a martyr of Diocletian’s persecution in the fourth century, is the patron in question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oscott-st-mar:
Oscott, or Saint Mary's College, began in 1793 when English Catholic nobility and gentry formed a committee to school their sons and train clergy on English soil. Buildings meant for the bishop's house at Oscott, a hamlet four miles north of Birmingham, were handed to the plan. John Bew became president in February 1794, the first three boys arrived in May, and the college opened formally in November.

Early years were gloomy until Bishop Milner took the college with its debts in 1808 and revived it. Under Henry Weedall, president from 1824 to 1840, numbers outgrew the old buildings. A stately new Gothic college rose near Sutton Coldfield, and Bishop Wiseman succeeded Weedall in 1840. The entry follows presidents, buildings, and the college's growth into a leading English Catholic seminary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patron-and-pa:
Patronage, or ius patronatus, is a set bundle of rights and duties falling to a definite person, the patron, chiefly over assigning and running a benefice. It comes not from hierarchical rank but from the Church's lawful grant in gratitude to a benefactor. Since patronal rights touch the spiritual order, decretals call patronage a right annexed to spiritual things. It falls under church law and courts, though property questions draw civil law and courts deep into the matter.

Eastern founders could nominate a temporal administrator and suggest a cleric to the bishop. In the West, Orange in 441 gave a bishop building in another diocese the right of presentation, and Toledo in 655 gave each lay church-builder the same, without ownership. Among Germanic peoples, temple and church rights of builders and lords grew into the full medieval patronage system, whose kinds, transfer, and loss later pages sort in detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perge:
Perge was a chief city of Pamphylia, set between two rivers about sixty stadia from the sea. Its ruins still show a theatre, a wrestling ground, a temple of Artemis outside the walls, and two churches. Paul and Barnabas passed through on their first missionary journey, probably without preaching, and it was there that John Mark left them for Jerusalem. On the return from Pisidia, Paul preached at Perge.

As a church centre the city lasted long. Greek lists call it metropolis of Pamphylia Secunda into the thirteenth century. Le Quien counts eleven of its bishops, from Epidaurus at Ancyra in 312 through figures at Nicaea, Ephesus, Chalcedon, and Constantinople. Among them were a condemned Monothelite, Apergius, and an Iconoclast, Sisinnius Pastillas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-privilege:
Privilege, from Latin privilegium, like a private law, is a lasting grant made by a lawgiver outside the common law. It is given by special favour and gives the favoured an edge over the unfavoured. Since the favour lasts, it differs from a permission or a single dispensation.

It is granted by a superior with authority over the law, so it bears a weight near a law's, and others must respect its use. A privilege departs from the common law, whether it merely adds to it or cuts against it. Privileges take many kinds. Some are built into the law, clausa in corpore juris, such as clerics' privileges, while others come by special rescript. Some are added to the law, praeter jus, touching what the law leaves alone. Others stand against the law, contra jus, forming an exception that lets one do or skip what the law forbids or commands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-putative-marr:
Putative, from the Latin putativus, means supposed, reputed or commonly believed. This short encyclopedia entry applies the word to marriage in canon law. A putative marriage is an alliance commonly reputed valid, and sincerely believed by at least one party to be valid in the Church's eyes, because it was entered in good faith. In reality it is null and void, since a diriment impediment, a bar that annuls marriage, stands in its way.

The Church still treats such a marriage as standing in her external forum, her public legal order, until its invalidity is proved. Children born of it keep the rights of legitimacy. Gasparri's work on marriage and Rosset's treatise supply the entry's authorities. Readers of canon law find here a brief, exact note on how good faith softens the harsh edge of an invalid union.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ritual-of-mar:
The ritual of marriage in the Rituale Romanum of today is remarkably simple. It consists of a declaration of consent by both parties, ratified by the priest with the words Ego conjungo vos in matrimonium. Next comes a blessing of the ring. The bridegroom receives it back from the priest and places it on the ring finger of the bride's left hand. A final benedictory prayer completes the ceremony.

The rite should be followed by the Nuptial Mass. It has a blessing after the Pater Noster and a shorter blessing before the benediction. At that Mass the couple are advised to receive communion. A special rubric from the Council of Trent orders that laudable local customs beyond this form should be kept. The contracting parties themselves are the ministers of the sacrament. Its words must be spoken in the vernacular.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabbatine-pri:
The Sabbatine Privilege takes its name from the apocryphal Bull Sacratissimo uti culmine of John XXII, dated 3 March 1322. In it, the pope tells how the Mother of God appeared to him, praising the Carmelite Order. The Virgin asked John, as Christ's representative, to ratify indulgences already granted in heaven. These were a plenary indulgence for order members and a partial indulgence for confraternity members. She herself would descend on the Saturday after their death and free those in purgatory, conducting them to heaven.

Our first information of this Bull comes from the Carmelite Balduinus Leersius, who died in 1483. Its authenticity was keenly contested in the seventeenth century but vigorously defended by Carmelites. Chief opponents were Joannes Launoy and the Bollandist Daniel Papebroch. Today scholars universally regard it as inauthentic, even the Carmelite Zimmerman's Monumenta joining in rejection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacrament-of-:
For Catholics it is certain that Christian marriage between baptized persons counts as a true sacrament under the New Law, strictly understood. Trent defines in canon one of session twenty-four that matrimony is truly one of the Seven Sacraments, instituted by Christ and conferring grace. Anyone denying this is anathema. The occasion was the Reformers' denial of marriage's sacramental character.

Calvin, in his Institutes, allowed matrimony was instituted by God but asked what sober man could call it a sacrament. Agriculture, architecture, and shoemaking are also God's ordinances but not sacraments. Luther called marriage an external worldly thing like clothes and food, subject to worldly authority. Trent's fathers evidently had Luther's passage in mind. But Trent was not first. Florence's Decree for the Armenians had already called matrimony the seventh sacrament, a figure of Christ and the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacrilege:
Sacrilege generally means violating or mistreating a sacred object. Loosely, any offence against religion counts as sacrilege. Theologians agree that only what has been dedicated to God's worship by a public rite counts as sacred. Public authority must intervene; private initiative does not suffice. Giving a thing sacred character is a juridical act of the Church.

Three kinds are enumerated: personal, local, and real. St Thomas teaches that a different holiness attaches to persons, places, and things. Suarez accepts the division as agreeing with the canons. Personal sacrilege means dealing so irreverently with a sacred person that honour due is breached. It is committed chiefly in three ways. Laying violent hands on a cleric, violating ecclesiastical immunity, and sins against chastity by the consecrated are its chief forms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-eugeniu:
Eugenius was unanimously elected Bishop of Carthage in 480 and died 13 July 505. The election was deferred by Arian opposition. The bishop's wise government, charity, austerity, and courage under persecution won even Arians' admiration. In defence of the Word's Divinity he was imitated by his flock. Many were exiled with him after he admitted Vandals against royal edict.

Both sides claimed the name Catholic. The conference ended when the chief Arian bishop withdrew, pleading he could not speak Latin. Enraged, Huneric exiled bishops to Corsica and African deserts. Among the latter was Eugenius, who dwelt in Tripoli's desert. Setting out, he wrote a consolation letter to Carthage's faithful. Gunthamund allowed Eugenius to return. After eight years' peace Thrasamund exiled Eugenius to Vienne. There Eugenius built a monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-selge:
Selge, a titular see in Pamphylia Prima suffragan to Side, stood in a fertile plain on the south slope of the Taurus mountains. It boasted a founding by the seer Calchas, but it was probably a Spartan colony in truth. Hard to reach, it still grew into the most populous and powerful city of Pisidia. Its army of 2,000 soldiers stayed in constant strife with neighboring cities.

Selge sought Alexander's friendship as he passed through Pisidia. In 208 BC it was besieged by Achaeus and forced to pay a heavy war tax. Its coins show it flourishing under Trajan. By the fifth century it was only a small city, yet still able to beat off a Gothic attack. Four bishops are named, and ruins of temples, an aqueduct, a stadium, and a theatre remain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ou:
Jean Eudes founded the Institute of Our Lady of Charity at Caen, Normandy, in 1641, under the title of Our Lady of Refuge. Out of compassion for women abandoned to a life of sin, Eudes first gathered penitents under good and zealous women. A house opened at Rennes, and the institute spread until seven communities stood in France when the Revolution broke out.

The Order of the Good Shepherd sprang from this parent institute. The sisters do not limit their work to reclaiming the fallen; they also receive girls in danger of being lost or brought up immorally, forming a class of preservation. Government reformatories attach to some monasteries. Each house keeps its own novitiate and independence, while the mother-house remains at Caen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-for-p:
Founded on 8 March 1698 by four laymen and the clergyman Thomas Bray, the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge is the greatest society within the Church of England. Bray, the Bishop of London's commissary in Maryland, drove the plan to consult together to promote Christian knowledge. Backed by bishops including Gilbert Burnet of Salisbury, the society first aimed at educating poor children, founding six London schools within two years and nearly 2,000 charity schools by 1741.

Later the society turned to training teachers, maintaining Saint Katharine's College, Tottenham, and supporting diocesan training colleges. Its schools work passed to a new National Society and, after 1870, to the State. As the Church of England's great publishing house it printed cheap books, tracts, and pictures, circulating over 11 million publications besides Bibles, prayer books, and tracts in 1905. It also ran evening schools, prison instruction, hospital visits, medical missions, emigrant aid, and a training college for lay workers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-carthage:
St. Carthage — Mochuda is another form of his name — was born about 555 to a good family in what is now County Kerry, Ireland. This entry follows a youth who herded swine near Castlemaine, then became a monk in a neighbouring monastery under St. Carthage the Elder, later receiving priest's orders. In 580 he resolved on a hermit's life, building a cell at Kiltallagh, where pilgrims soon flocked to his fame.

After a few years, two neighbouring bishops, jealous of him, forced him to quit his hermitage, and he went on a visit to Bangor, where he spent a year. On St. Comgall's advice he went back to Kerry, founding churches at Kilcarragh and Kilfeighney. He then visited Waterford, Clonfert-molua, and Lynally, whence, on St. Colman Elo's recommendation, he settled at Rahan near Tullamore. There he founded his monastery of Rahan about 590.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cyprian-of:
St. Cyprian of Carthage, Thaschus Caecilius Cyprianus, was bishop and martyr. This entry follows a man whose birth date and early life are unknown. By his conversion to Christianity he had, perhaps, passed middle life. A famous orator and pleader, he had considerable wealth and undoubtedly held a great position in Africa's metropolis.

His deacon, St. Pontius, whose life of the saint survives, tells us his manner was dignified without severity, cheerful without effusiveness. His writings show his gift of eloquence. He was no thinker, philosopher, or theologian, but a man of the world through and through, an administrator of vast energies and forcible, striking character. Caecilianus, an aged priest he seems to have lived with, brought about his conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-elphege:
Elphege, martyred archbishop of Canterbury, died at his captors' hands because no ransom would be paid for him. Born in 954, he left his widowed mother and inheritance for Deerhurst monastery, lived as an anchorite at Bath, became its abbot, then bishop of Winchester in 984. In 1006 he became archbishop and travelled to Rome for the pallium. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his murder at Greenwich to 19 April 1012.

Danes sacked Canterbury in September 1011 and carried him prisoner. Drunk and enraged at the refused ransom, they pelted him with ox bones and stones until one Thurm finished him with an axe. Canute later moved his body to Canterbury, where his principal feast falls on 19 April. Earlier, Elphege had confirmed Olaf of Norway at Andover in 994.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-george:
George, martyr and patron of England, is among the most famous saints about whom the least can be safely said. Delehaye's careful investigation sums the firm record in one line: he suffered at or near Lydda, Diospolis, in Palestine, probably before Constantine. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 insists his historical existence is not in doubt, despite absence from Syrian and primitive Hieronymian martyrologies.

The earliest known narrative, surviving partly in a fifth-century palimpsest, is full of incredible marvels: three deaths by chopping, burial, and fire, each undone by God's power. Gelasius's decree of 495 already counted his Acts apocryphal, revering his name while leaving his deeds to God alone. Nor was he the martyr who tore down Diocletian's edict, nor Gibbon's Arian bishop in disguise. The entry leaves a name, a shrine, and a legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-tweng:
John Twenge, prior of Bridlington, is the last English saint canonized, a canon regular famed for miracles. Born near Bridlington in 1319 to the Yorkshire Twenge family, which later gave two priest-martyrs and helped found York's Bar Convent Institute, he studied at Oxford, then entered Bridlington Priory. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Bridlington to 1379.

Charged successively with community offices, he was finally, despite reluctance, elected prior, holding office until death. Even in life he enjoyed a reputation for holiness and miraculous power. Once he changed water into wine. Once five Hartlepool seamen, fearing shipwreck, called on God in his servant John's name, and the prior himself appeared in canonical habit, bringing them safely to shore. After death, miracles by his intercession spread rapidly, and Archbishop Neville ordered evidence gathered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-juliana-of:
Juliana of Liège, nun of Mont-Cornillon, spent her energies winning the feast of Corpus Christi for the Church. Born at Retinnes near Liège in 1193, she lost her parents at five and entered Mont-Cornillon convent. She progressed rapidly, reading Augustine and Bernard with pleasure, and loved Mary, the Passion, and above all the Blessed Sacrament. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Fosses to 5 April 1258.

She took the veil in 1206 and served the sick in the hospital there. Early she bent every energy to introducing Corpus Christi's feast. Chosen superioress unanimously in 1230, she soon faced heavy trials. The convent's general superior Roger had bought his post by intrigue and bribery in 1233. A vicious, scandalous man, he hated her virtue and reproaches, and stirred the populace against her. She fled to Eve of Liège's cell, then to a canon's house, and was vindicated in time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stonyhurst-co:
Stonyhurst College in Lancashire descends from a school founded at St Omer in 1592. It served English boys barred from Catholic schooling at home. This entry follows the college through exile after exile, driven from St Omer in 1762, sheltered at Bruges, then dispersed when the Jesuits were suppressed in 1773.

Staff and pupils regrouped at Liège, then settled at Stonyhurst Hall in 1794. The curriculum first followed Jesuit classical ideals, then opened to modern languages, science, and public exams. Observatory, library, masters, alumni, and the school magazine all appear here. Together they picture a school whose roots run back more than three hundred years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-scots-col:
Scotland's college at Rome, gift of Clement VIII, is traced here from bull to buildings. The foundation bull of 5 December 1600 granted all privileges already enjoyed by Greek, German, and English colleges. Endowments followed, including an abbey's revenue in the Neapolitan kingdom and a monthly pension from the Dataria. The old Scotch Hospice's revenues joined later.

First students arrived in 1602 and lodged two years in the Via Tritone before moving in 1604 to Via Quattro Fontane, near the Quirinal Palace. Modest first buildings gave way, about half a century before 1913, to Poletti's handsome and commodious college, admired for graceful architecture. Rectors, students, and Scottish mission links complete the story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trinity-colle:
A college for Catholic women in Washington, D.C., chartered in 1897 with power to confer degrees. It grew from the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur's wish for a select day-school at Brookland. At the Catholic University's suggestion it became a college matching the women's colleges already founded in the United States.

Cardinal Gibbons, the university's chancellor, warmly backed the plan, and Sister Julia, provincial superior, secured thirty-three acres between Michigan and Lincoln Avenues. The corner-stone was laid on 8 December 1899, and South Hall was dedicated in November 1900. The finished building holds residence halls for two hundred students and a library of 12,000 volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Cambridge's origins lie in obscurity, and no certain date can be fixed for the foundation of the great seat of learning now known as the university. In Elizabeth's day wild legends circulated, with Oxford claiming Greek professors who came with Brutus of Troy. Cambridge traced itself to Cantaber, a Spanish prince said to have reached Britain in the year of the world 3588. The chronicler Peter de Blois, assigning learned monks to Cambridge in 1110, is no more trustworthy.

The entry sifts these fables and follows the real growth of schools, colleges, and faculties from the twelfth century onward. It covers the coming of the religious orders, the founding of colleges, the struggles with town and crown, and the later reforms that shaped the modern university. Readers get both a debunking of antiquarian myth and a solid outline of Cambridge's rise.

St Francis Xavier's at Antigonish, Nova Scotia, was founded in 1885 as St Francis Xavier's College by Bishop MacKinnon of Arichat, now the Diocese of Antigonish. A legislative act of 1866 had empowered it to confer degrees, and a statute of 1882 granted full university powers. The new charter of 1909 gave it all the powers any university could reasonably ask of the state. That included the right to confer every usual degree and to hold property of any value.

The supreme governing body is a board of twelve governors, with the Bishop of Antigonish as chairman by office. In 1912 the college counted twenty-five professors, lecturers, and tutors, and in 1911 and 1912 it counted 356 students, mostly from the Maritime Provinces. The entry sketches a young Catholic college serving Scottish and Acadian communities on Canada's Atlantic edge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ushaw-college:
Ushaw College, or the College of St Cuthbert, is a combined college and seminary for the six dioceses once comprised in England's old Northern Vicariate. Its government rests in a united board of those dioceses' bishops, with a president, a vice-president, and about thirty professors. Students average over 300, split into three courses: a preparatory course of about eighty boys, a humanity course of about 130, and a philosophical and theological course of about 100.

Its history begins with the suppression of the English college at Douai, which for 200 years had embodied the Catholic faith for England, one of the French Revolution's many far-reaching results. English Catholics urgently needed a home successor to continue Douai's work. The entry follows the college's founding at Ushaw, its buildings, and its staff, giving the story of a seminary born from exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-validation-of:
Validation of marriage repairs a union that is null, and this entry sets out the canon law of the cure. When nullity comes only from defective consent in one or both parties, a simple renewal of consent suffices. When some church impediment makes the marriage invalid, it may be healed by simple dispensation or by sanatio in radice, healing at the root.

In the first method, once a dispensation from the impediment is granted, a fresh consent of both parties validates the marriage. If the impediment touched only one party and the other knew nothing of it, both probably must still renew consent. True renewal requires the parties to know of the nullity, unless sanatio in radice is used. The entry works through the cases with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-ann:
Anne de Xainctonge was the Dijon-born foundress of the Sisters of St Ursula of the Blessed Virgin. Born in 1567 to a councillor of the Dijon parliament, she watched the Jesuit college from her family's house and conceived a new idea: religious women who were not cloistered. Running public schools where girls would be educated, not sold an education.

Against the prejudices of her time and her parents' opposition, and guided by Jesuit directors, she opened her first convent at Dôle in Franche-Comté on 16 June 1606, with two companions. The company took Our Lady as general and St Ursula as lieutenant, with the Rule of St Ignatius as its pattern. For fifteen years she founded new houses across eastern France and Switzerland. Her beatification cause was later wrecked when wars and the Revolution destroyed its documents, then re-established.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-ant:
Anthony Page was an English martyr executed at York in April 1593. Born at Harrow-on-the-Hill in 1571, of gentle birth, he entered Christ Church, Oxford, in 1581, then the English College at Reims in 1584. He was ordained deacon at Laon in 1590 and priest at Reims in 1591.

His contemporary Anthony Champney described him as wonderfully meek, modest, and pure, of more than common learning and piety, endearing himself to all by candour of mind and sweetness of behaviour. Condemned for being a priest under the statute of 27 Elizabeth, he was hanged, disembowelled, and quartered. The entry gives his death date uncertainly, as 20 or 30 April 1593.
childe-harold-s-pilgrimage:
Lord Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage is a long poem in four cantos, addressed first to Ianthe. A dedication in verse praises the young girl's guileless heart before Harold appears. The pilgrim himself is a satiated young lord who leaves England to wander. Spain and Portugal, fresh from Peninsular war, fill the first canto.

Greece under Turkish rule fills the second, with lament for her fallen glory. The third canto crosses Waterloo's field to Switzerland, Byron's own exile written into Harold's. The fourth wanders Italy: Venice, Florence, and Rome in decay. Byron published the cantos over six years and woke famous after the first. Harold's gloom became the Byronic hero, copied across Europe. The poem mixes travel description, history, and confession in Spenserian stanzas of sustained splendour, and it made modern tourism melancholy.
cicero-de-natura-deorum-yonge:
Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods, written in 45 BC, stages a debate on religion among Rome's educated elite. C. D. Yonge's translation, from the Harper edition of 1877, is the text here. Cicero sets the scene at a friend's villa and mostly listens.

An Epicurean speaker argues the gods exist but care nothing for human affairs. A Stoic answers that divine reason runs the world and watches over it. An Academic skeptic then takes both cases apart, finding each one wanting. The dialogue is the fullest surviving survey of ancient thought on the gods, and its balance made it a school text for centuries.
cicero-philippics-yonge:
Cicero's Philippics are fourteen speeches against Mark Antony, delivered in 44 and 43 BC after the murder of Julius Caesar. C. D. Yonge's English translation is the text here, drawn from the fourth volume of his Orations. Cicero named them after Demosthenes' speeches against Philip of Macedon.

An old man with no army, Cicero used speech alone to brand Antony a public enemy and rally the Senate against him. The gamble worked for a season, then failed: the triumvirs proscribed him, and Antony had him killed in December 43 BC. The speeches are his last stand for the republic. They cost him his life and fixed his fame.
cicero-tusculan-disputations-yonge:
Cicero wrote the Tusculan Disputations in 45 BC at his villa in Tusculum, in the last stretch of his career. C. D. Yonge's English translation is the text here. The work holds five days of talk with friends on how to face life's hardest blows.

Each day takes one fear: death, pain, grief, the passions of the soul, and the question whether virtue alone makes a happy life. Cicero argues death is no evil, pain can be borne, and grief yields to reason. His answers lean Stoic, though he keeps his Academic freedom to doubt. The talks became a handbook of calm for later ages.
courage:
The rectorial address given at St Andrews University on May 3, 1922, by J. M. Barrie bears the single word Courage as its title. Hodder and Stoughton printed it at Toronto in the same year. Barrie speaks to the red-gowned students as one who came from their own ground.

He says the folk he has cared for most were simple, not great. He wishes he could hand the students a staff for the hard march of life ahead. Talk of the Chancellor, the Principal, and late work in lamplit rooms fills the witty middle. The speech mixes jest with grave counsel, and it asks the young to face fear with a brave and honest heart.
critical-miscellanies-vol-3-of-3-essay-4:
John Morley's essay on the life of George Eliot fills this file, the fourth essay of his Critical Miscellanies, volume three. Macmillan issued the volume at London and New York in 1904. The contents list shows the essay runs from page 93 to page 131.

Morley opens with Eliot's own plea against raking a dead writer's desk for print. He weighs Mr Myers's essay and a letter to Mr Harrison. Her love of Hebrew study, her vast reading, and Romola all come in for remark. The years of her work, 1856 to 1876, frame the survey. He calls her a teacher by art, not by doctrine, and one who disliked vehemence. The piece is biography judged by a critic.
diary-of-a-pilgrimage:
Jerome K Jerome's Diary of a Pilgrimage, first published in April 1891 and reprinted steadily for decades, sends Jerome and his friend B to Germany for the Oberammergau Passion Play. The title page lists him as author of Three Men in a Boat, and the comedy runs on the same rails: packing, trains, and German hotels. A friend's patent tea-basket, complete from caddy to methylated spirit stove, opens the preparations.

At Oberammergau the jokes quieten before the play's sincerity, and Jerome writes about it with unexpected respect. Along the way he complains of phrasebooks full of raspberries, figs, and medlars no traveler ever wants. The diary mixes farce and genuine feeling in the proportion that made Jerome beloved.
doe-osti-17038191-efficient-training-alg:
Brian Bartoldson of Lawrence Livermore sums up project 24-ERD-010 in September 2026, on training large scientific AI models with less computing. Training and running such models eats time and power, a core concern for the Energy Department. His team cut waste in data, model parts, and raw computation.

One method halved the computing time to train a math reasoning model, with almost no accuracy loss, against a leading approach. Another beat standard chatbot training quality in one fifth of the training steps, and that method now ships in widely used open source AI software. Other gains sped text generation up to seven fold and hardened image text models against manipulated pictures.
doe-osti-17134352-energy-101-storage:
Tony Jimenez of the National Laboratory of the Rockies gave an Energy 101 talk on storage to the Islesboro Energy Committee in Maine on 18 June 2026. The slide deck is a plain language primer for a community audience. A note on the slides says generative AI aided research on lithium ion battery recycling, with all citations checked by the author.

Four parts structure the talk: a storage technology overview, battery technology, markets and value streams, and storage sizing. Technologies range from flywheels to electrochemical batteries. Key measures include energy density, power density, round trip efficiency, and self discharge. Sizing is explained with a fuel tank comparison: a 1 megawatt, 2 megawatt hour battery can give full power for two hours, or half power for four.
doe-osti-17152721-dynamic-optical-pressu:
Rohan Jillapalli, Tetiana Bowley, and Steve Gilbertson of Los Alamos present a slide deck, dated 24 September 2026, on a dynamic optical pressure gauge for shock experiments. Shock studies on inert materials need pressure readings, not just velocity. The standard manganin gauge reads pressure through resistance change, and it has limits the team wants to beat.

The proposed design adapts the ruby fluorescence pressure gauge, well known in static high pressure work, to fast dynamic events. Slides lay out the motivation, the optical concept, and planned background experiments. A diagram of a typical shot setup places velocity probes, fiber gauges, and the detonator around the charge, with pressures near 10 gigapascals marked. Next steps test whether fluorescence can track pressure during the shot itself.
doe-osti-2574385-polar-bear-innovative-c:
Final technical report DE-FE0032290, from the Energy and Environmental Research Center at the University of North Dakota, covers August 2023 to July 2025. Authors Darren D. Schmidt, Alyssa C. Regorrah, Youcef Khetib, and Bradley G. Stevens report on Polar Bear, a patented system for capturing vapors from oil storage tanks. Thousands of small wells vent such vapors because standard recovery units cost too much at their scale.

Tanks breathe as levels and temperatures change, so the vapor carries unwanted oxygen. The design splits the stream: oxygen-rich gas becomes on-site fuel, while the liquids-rich part is recovered with oxygen kept low. Prototype tests matched the process models well, lifting the technology from readiness level 5 to 6. Trials with nitrogen and liquefied petroleum gas mixtures tracked the gas balance. The team expects under 2,000 parts per million of oxygen to remain in the recovered liquid portion in field use.
doe-osti-2583550-quantifying-time-to-cha:
July 2025 study by Ed Watt, Mohammad Bani Shamseh, and Pranav Gadamsetty of NREL, prepared for the Department of Energy, times the dead air before an EV charge actually starts. Plugging in begins a negotiation: cable check, signal level attenuation, authentication, payment, parameter discovery, and pre-charge phases pass before electrons flow. Drivers experience the sum as 'time to charge,' and it varies wildly.

The team measured each phase's duration across test data from multiple sources and communication protocols. Some phases dominate the wait. Cable check and pre-charge get phase-by-phase diagrams, and session setup and power delivery times are charted across the fleet of tests. Recommendations target the longest phases, where standards or implementation changes would cut the most seconds. As charging networks compete on experience, the handshake before the charge is becoming part of the product.
doe-osti-2587508-theoretical-and-methodo:
Teresa Portone and Rebekah White wrote this report, SAND2025-10780, printed in September 2025 at Sandia National Laboratories. It examines the theory and practice of hierarchical Bayesian inference. The goal is to capture model-form uncertainty: the error that comes from the model itself being wrong, not just from noisy data. Such methods stack layers of probability distributions, with hyperparameters governing the spread of the discrepancy terms.

The authors work through where the machinery strains. One thread asks when data can actually inform a scale parameter that sets the size of model error. Their numerical exploration suggests it may take near-degenerate cases for the data to speak. Two demonstration problems carry the argument: a spatially varying linear model, and subsurface contaminant transport. Calibration plots compare the method's predictive quantiles against held-out data. The report is aimed at analysts who build uncertainty estimates for high-stakes simulations.
doe-osti-2587776-monitoring-l2-milestone:
Kathleen Shoga, Matthew LeGendre, and Ned Bass wrote this milestone summary, LLNL-TR-2010795, in September 2025. All three work at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. It closes Advanced Simulation and Computing milestone 9234, Converged HPC Center-Wide Data Analytics, completed on August 31, 2025. The milestone's promise was one shared data store for monitoring Livermore Computing, the laboratory's supercomputing center.

In the past, the center's data lived in separate silos. One held benchmark scores, one held facilities data, and one held metrics reported by applications. The new store brings them together. Staff can now match changes across the center and see how they affect use and reliability. Most data moves through Kafka into Elastic databases. Logstash feeds both Elastic and Splunk. Splunk stays in use by a few groups for functions the new tools do not yet match. The stated goal is to move away from it.
doe-osti-2589365-electron-ion-collider-e:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-228940-2025-TECH gives the early design of an injection beamline for the future Electron-Ion Collider. Lead author H. Oh and a large team describe the line that will carry hadrons from the existing AGS complex into the new Hadron Storage Ring. The added section is called the Y-Line Extension.

The design covers repeating cells, matching sections at both ends, and beam shape values at the injection point. Magnet settings, element positions, and first instrument placements are tabulated. Many bending elements are refurbished combined-function magnets from an older arc, which bend the beam and focus it at once. Names used for elements are early labels, not final site names. Builders and reviewers can check the layout against collider requirements from this record.
doe-osti-2998067-nine-canyon-long-durati:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory feasibility study, by Mukesh Gautam, Di Wu, Swasti Saxena, and co-authors, dated August 2025, weighs long-duration energy storage at the Nine Canyon site near Kennewick, Washington. Energy Northwest, a joint agency of 29 public utilities serving over 1.5 million customers, wants a storage system of 50 to 200 megawatts that can discharge for at least 10 hours.

The site offers a strong natural asset: hilly ground rising more than 1,000 feet across a 5,120-acre lease, of which only about 75 acres are built on. A substation and transmission corridor already serve the existing wind project there. Gravity-based storage from partner ARES North America, which lifts and lowers heavy masses on the slope, fits that terrain. The study tests whether the hill, the grid links, and the duty cycle add up to a buildable project.
doe-osti-2999120-keeping-lammps-cutting-:
Anders Johansson of Sandia National Laboratories reports on keeping a famous simulation code current, in SAND2025-12694R, printed September 2025. LAMMPS is a molecular dynamics program, now about 30 years old, that follows atoms as they move and interact. Materials researchers worldwide build on it. The project set out to fit LAMMPS to the newest machine learning methods and the newest computer hardware.

Plans for a unified active learning system gave way to sharper chances. On hardware, the team linked LAMMPS to a specialist code for the Cerebras wafer-scale AI chip, which had hosted record-breaking atom simulations. On software, they prepared the ground for PyTorch ahead-of-time compilation of modern neural network force models. In extreme cases that route ran nearly 20 times faster. A benchmark study across all current exascale supercomputers rounds out the report, which aims to keep LAMMPS a first-choice tool.
doe-osti-3001535-passband-signal-detecti:
Gavin Parpart, Peter Martin, Stephen Jones and PNNL colleagues move radio signal detection onto hardware in a September 2025 report. Crowded spectrum is a headache for military and civilian users: someone must notice which signals are present. Deep learning classifies radio emissions well, but the models usually live on servers. At the edge, on a software defined radio in the field, size, weight and power budgets bite hard.

The design adapts an object detection approach, in the YOLO family, to spectrogram like views of passband signals. It runs on a deep learning processing unit inside a field programmable gate array system on chip. Chapters cover preprocessing, the backbone network and detection heads, and scoring with receiver operating curves. Raw IQ samples feed the pipeline from radio front ends. The goal is a detector that rides with the sensor, flagging signals in real time instead of shipping data home.
doe-osti-3020488-resilience-through-data:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Nawaf Nazir and Veronica Adetola, dated November 2025, applies formal methods, meaning mathematical proof techniques, to the controllers that run industrial equipment. Programmable logic controllers are exposed to attack: an intruder can poison the data arriving over the network, or compromise the controller while it runs. Either path can make machinery behave badly while looking normal.

The proposed defense builds control logic from temporal logic rules that state what must always, or never, happen. Software tools translate those rules into a model checker, NuSMV, where the desired behaviors are proven against the system definition. Verified designs are then translated back into deployable controller code, with automatically generated runtime monitors watching for intrusions. The report walks through the threat model and each stage of the pipeline.
doe-osti-3020806-history-of-the-chemical:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-26/6, Volume 2, draws lessons from the Chemical Stockpile Emergency Preparedness Program, which for decades prepared communities around United States chemical weapons storage sites for a possible accident. With the stockpile destroyed, this 2026 final volume preserves what the program learned. Volume 2, by Ken Lerner and co-authors, focuses on practice rather than chronology.

A central lesson concerns planning zones. Because preparedness resources were finite, the program concentrated them where a hazard to the public was reasonably possible: an immediate response zone and a protective action zone around each site. The zones decided where sirens and tone-alert radios were installed, which households received information mailings, and which schools got protective ventilation. The volume explains how such choices were made and defended, as guidance for future emergency programs facing the same trade-offs.
doe-osti-3021634-vitrification-of-inorga:
Vitreous State Laboratory final report VSL-18R4380-1, by Keith S. Matlack, Wing K. Kot, and Ian L. Pegg of The Catholic University of America, studies how to vitrify spent inorganic ion exchange media. Published in June 2018 and released under HFO-73192, the work serves Hanford tank waste treatment. Ion exchange materials such as chabazite pull radioactive cesium from tank waste, but then the loaded media itself becomes waste that needs a permanent form.

The team blended AY-102 tank waste simulant with chabazite and glass-forming additives, and computed melter feeds that would produce 100 kilograms of target glass at 15 weight percent total solids. Composition tables give the analyzed glass chemistry, including zirconia near 17.4 percent. The results show the spent media can be folded into the glass waste stream rather than handled as a separate disposal problem.
doe-osti-3021949-history-of-the-chemical:
